Sports.title: Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsed
Sports.content:
Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped.

In a letter to the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, the influential European Football Clubs (EFC) group warned that its cooperation with future tournaments would hinge on Infantino backing down. It said the threat would hold unless a joint venture between EFC and Fifa – a framework for which has already been agreed – is completed before television rights can be sold for the 2028 Women’s Club World Cup.

The letter, dated 31 July and signed by the EFC chief executive, Charlie Marshall, said Infantino’s actions could constitute a “substantial breach” of the bodies’ existing memorandum of understanding (MoU) and suggested this could be grounds for its termination. It floated the idea that EFC and its clubs may push back against the international match calendar and its player release rules, which are crucial to ensuring national team tournaments can function. Infantino shelved the privately backed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE) in the early hours of 1 August after widespread condemnation.

Fundamental to EFC’s complaints was the impression FFE would bring all broadcasting, commercial and sponsorship rights under its own umbrella. The letter asked Fifa to confirm this and said it would take decisive action if these elements were not included in the long-proposed joint venture, whose creation is enshrined in the MoU and intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions. It witheringly wrote that the tie-in had, “unlike the FFE proposal, made no meaningful progress over the past year”. EFC already has a similar joint venture with Uefa, named UC3, which was launched in 2025.

A potentially incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”

In theory the threat still holds although Fifa, in a response to EFC’s letter since Infantino climbed down, is understood to have promised a swift meeting to keep the joint venture on track. EFC’s position followed concerns raised by a vast number of clubs around Europe, who were angered by the lack of consultation around the design of FFE. One major European club expressed concerns in its own letter saying it would support EFC in any “firmer collective action” if necessary and called for “more rigorous and transparent governance processes”.

Any European withdrawal from Club World Cups would in practice mean those tournaments could not run. EFC and Fifa operated last year’s Club World Cup, the first to take place with 32 teams, using a short-term prototype for any future joint venture. No hosts have yet been announced for the new-look Women’s Club World Cup or the next edition of the men’s tournament in 2029.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea won the Club World Cup in July 2025 by beating Paris Saint-Germain in the final. Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty Images

EFC’s letter also raised the continuing delay, first reported in February, in distributing £185m of solidarity money to clubs that did not participate in the Club World Cup. Transparency over the event’s financial performance was also requested.

“We ask that you urgently share the final surplus revenue generated by the 2025 Fifa WC, together with a full profit and loss statement, so that all revenues, expenses and costs can be properly assessed in line with our partnership in this competition,” it said. “The absence of information on this matter, as with the lack of a solution on CWC solidarity for over a year, is also of serious concern and disappointment to EFC and our member clubs.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is understood there is increasing optimism that this issue is on the verge of resolution, although a notional average £50,000 windfall for every global top-flight club, if the pot was divided equally, pales in comparison with the £84m reward long since banked by last year’s winners, Chelsea.

Referring to clubs releasing players for international duty, EFC continued: “Our memorandum of understanding, set to expire on 30 December 2030, includes EFC’s and its member clubs’ acceptance of the international match calendar and the release rules. Both are directly relevant for Fifa’s non-European member associations and to any value FFE may have.” It said Fifa’s apparent commercial vision for FFE constituted a “serious breach of trust” and warned the MoU could be jeopardised.

The letter demonstrates the extraordinary level of leverage EFC, which is chaired by the Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, can claim over Fifa and its increasing influence on football’s future. The organisation, set up in 2008 as a lobby group for clubs around the continent, now has well over 800 members although only a minority hold full voting rights. Some stakeholders elsewhere in football’s ecosystem have expressed fears about the level of power it has assumed. A separate representative body, the Union of European Clubs, was created in 2023 to represent smaller sides but is not recognised by Uefa.

One potential consequence of EFC’s discussions with Fifa could, in the medium term, be its expansion into a group representing clubs around the world. More immediately, last month’s letter demanded that Fifa deliver on a previous promise to fully integrate Al-Khelaifi into the Fifa council, which is purportedly its main decision-making body.

Sports.title: Liverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos
Sports.content:
Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.

Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.

Elaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo, and Bryan Baum, co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will also join the Liverpool board. Bezos is considered a passive investor and will not have a seat on the board.

Despite the involvement of Bezos, the third richest man in the world with $272bn (£201bn), Eduardo Saverin, worth an estimated $33bn and the Mittal family, worth around $17bn, FSG will remain in operational control of Liverpool as well as majority owners. 1892 Holdings’ investment remains subject to regulatory approval, which could take up to 90 days, and will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. There is also no change to the leadership or day-to-day running of Liverpool.

FSG insist the deal is not part of an exit strategy from a club they acquired in 2010 for £300m after the near-ruinous ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett. The transaction does not compel FSG to sell more of the club to 1892 at a future date, or include obligations for 1892 to increase their stake, but it does give Bhatia’s consortium options to purchase more of Liverpool should the majority owners eventually decide to sell.

It is the makeup of Bhatia’s consortium, rather than any financial need, that FSG claim attracted them to the British-Indian businessman’s proposal. The FSG leadership team of principal owner John W Henry, chair Tom Werner and president Mike Gordon have spent almost a year getting to know Bhatia and believe the deal will create further opportunities for Liverpool in global business, technology and investment, including in the important markets of India and Asia.

View image in fullscreen The sale will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Gordon, who has resumed a more hands-on role at Liverpool following the departure of Michael Edwards as chief executive of football at FSG, said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.

“As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.”

With Premier League and Uefa financial regulations linking a club’s spending to turnover, the new investment will not have an immediate benefit for head coach Andoni Iraola and his Liverpool team. However, the commercial opportunities presented by the involvement of Bezos, Bhatia and Saverin will enable the Anfield club to grow their annual revenue significantly. Liverpool’s annual revenue increased to a record £703m in the year ending May 2025.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Speaking on behalf of 1892 Holdings, Bhatia said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.

“To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come.”

Bhatia was involved in QPR for almost 19 years and took on numerous roles, from chair of the club to chair of the club’s community trust, until transferring his shareholding in July. He is likely to have a more visible presence at Anfield than fellow members of his consortium or FSG.

Sports.title: Raúl Jiménez’s injury-time penalty salvages point for Wolves against Blackburn
Sports.content:
Raúl Jiménez marked his return to Wolves with the stoppage-time equaliser that saved them from an embarrassing start to their return to the Championship. The Mexico striker, who scored against England during the World Cup, came off the bench to convert a penalty given for handball by Ryan Alebiosu that would have had VAR questioning whether the defender was in the area when Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross struck his arm.

One minor consolation from Wolves’ relegation is that the video assistant referee is no longer their problem. Jiménez, who had bought scarves for all supporters in the South Bank in gratitude for their welcome home, tucked away his first goal in this second spell for the club he graced during their recent heyday before leaving for Fulham.

“He’s an important striker,” César Peixoto, Wolves’ new head coach said. “He lives for scoring and making goals. Raúl is a key player for us. He helped the team inside and outside the pitch but we have to go slowly with him because he is 35 years old and comes back from the World Cup. We want him to stay good and scoring for us is good for him and for the team.”

Goals from Sean McLoughlin and Andri Gudjohnsen allowed Blackburn to provide Wolves with a reality check after Marshall Munetsi had scored early. Confidence is a fragile commodity and, after their decision to replace Rob Edwards with a manager with no experience of English football, the Wolves board know that their supporters’ patience is thin. Leading Gil Vicente to sixth place in the Portuguese first division does not make Peixoto a guaranteed winner.

Conceding the equaliser, through Jiménez’s first goal for Wolves in 1,311 days, denied unfancied Blackburn a deserved victory after Wolves lost their shape. Tony Mowbray, their head coach, felt the penalty decision was harsh. “I’ve just been shown an angle by my analyst where he [Alebiosu] is outside the box; another angle I’m told shows he’s just inside the box. I just felt like more and more decisions were starting to sway their way,” the former West Brom manager said. “It’s harsh to take because I don’t think they deserved that second goal.”

Molineux was awash with fading golden sunlight and rising optimism at kick-off. A summer that started with such a surprising managerial departure was promising to end with renewed faith in the team’s direction of travel, until Peixoto’s admired high press came unstuck as his team started to “play with their hearts more than their heads”.

View image in fullscreen Marshall Munetsi (right) celebrates scoring Woves’ first goal with Fer López. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

The Blackburn defence had split generously to allow Munetsi a clean run through on to Fer López’s sumptuous pass. The left-footed finish from the Zimbabwean, himself coming back to Molineux after a loan at Paris FC, strengthened the feelgood factor.

Peixoto’s tactics do currently lead to gaps on transition. Blackburn, who have not done so much in the transfer market to suggest they should aim higher than last season’s 20th place, got behind Wolves on several occasions. It was no great surprise when, from Ryoya Morishita’s superb right-wing cross, McLoughlin headed beyond Dan Bentley to equalise.

Some of Wolves’ best business this summer has been bringing players back to Molineux. While Jiménez started the night on the bench, after a late start to pre-season following his impressive World Cup for Mexico, López was the classiest player on view. Back from a loan at Celta Vigo, he has been invited to make the No 10 position his own, and the Spaniard nearly regained Wolves the lead only to curl his shot wide.

View image in fullscreen Blackburn’s Andri Gudjohnsen gives his side a 2-1 lead early in the second half. Photograph: Simon Davies/ProSports/Shutterstock

Blackburn continued to benefit from Wolves’ soft centre however. Oladapo Afolayan’s shot needed tipping over by Bentley before the right winger again got space down Wolves’ left – where David Møller Wolfe, in for the injured Hugo Bueno, showed he is still not match fit after his World Cup endeavours with Norway – to cross for Gudjohnsen to turn in Rovers’ second goal. “The team lost some organisation and played with their heart rather than their head and brains,” Peixoto said. “It’s a lesson for us in the future, we need to stay with mental stability for the 90 minutes.”

By the hour mark, the South Bank were swirling their Jiménez scarves above their heads and chanting “Si Señor” in honour of the veteran striker who was such an esteemed figure at Molineux for five of the club’s best years in modern times. Before his horrific head injury, he was the pivotal attacking player as Nuno Espírito Santo’s team reached the later stages of the FA Cup and Europa League. The scene was set for the Mexican. Could he deliver? Si, señor.

Sports.title: ‘Not going to be an issue’: Mikel Arteta relaxed about Arsenal contract situation
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has said he is relaxed about his Arsenal contract expiring at the end of the new season and believes his side will need to be better than last year to defend their title successfully.

The Premier League champions will face Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City in the Community Shield in Cardiff on Sunday and are heavy favourites to win back-to-back league titles for the first time since the 1930s. The departure of Pep Guardiola from their traditional rivals City means Arteta is now the Premier League’s longest-serving manager, with the Spaniard having joined in December 2019.

He signed a three-year contract extension in September 2024 after Arsenal finished as runners-up to City and had been expected to agree a new deal over the summer that would make him one of the highest-paid managers in the world. Arteta acknowledged on Friday that his priorities have been elsewhere this summer as he attempts to strengthen his squad before the new season but reassured supporters that he is fully committed to the club.

“They don’t have to worry about any of that, because I want to be here. I am extremely happy. I feel very grateful to work with the people that I work with and when we have the possibility, we will resolve that. And that’s it,” he said.

Asked if he expects talks over a new contract to continue after the transfer window, Arteta added: “There is always another priority, I think. And that’s the way we have been treating it, I think because everybody feels comfortable that the time on the contract is not going to be an issue. I think because my will, certainly, is to be here and I am very happy here. My feeling from the club is the same one. That is why everyone is doing things in a really organic way.”

Arsenal have opened negotiations with Bayer Leverkusen over a move for Jarell Quansah as they seek cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber, while they are still in the market for another attacker if they can offload Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus. After missing out on Vinícius Júnior when the Brazil forward opted to sign a new deal with Real Madrid, Arteta defended Arsenal’s strategy this summer and is hoping that they can still add to their squad.

“I am really happy with the squad, the players that I have and I am really happy with the ambition of the club. There is zero question about that. We have shown that in the manner we have tried to act,” he said.

“But I think we need to do it our own way. We have super strengths and we have other areas we need to be very conscious [of] because we don’t have the elements or the structure that other clubs have. We need to do it our way. We are always on it that way and we will do what we believe is the right thing to do. To have the best possibility to compete in every competition that’s for sure.”

Arteta added: “We’re going to prepare to elevate our level, expecting that the rest will do the same. That’s traditionally what happened in the league in the last few years, and that’s the way we have planned the season, and the way we want to evolve the team.”

Sports.title: Chelsea expect Enzo Fernández to stay after Manchester City opt not to meet deadline
Sports.content:
Manchester City did not make a £120m bid for Enzo Fernández before Chelsea’s 5pm deadline on Friday but Enzo Maresca still expects a busy end to the transfer window, as the club seek incomings and outgoings. Chelsea, meanwhile, now expect the Argentina midfielder to stay at Stamford Bridge.

Maresca takes charge of City for the first time in a major match on Sunday against Arsenal in Cardiff in the Community Shield but is a long way from finalising the squad he will have for the season. Fernández, who played under Maresca at Chelsea, remains a target for City, who could still test the water despite missing the deadline.

“For sure there are things we need to do, how many I don’t know, can be one, can be two, depends also if players want to leave, so we can see,” Maresca said on Friday, having suggested City would not agree to Chelsea’s demands. “It’s 48 hours for the final, my first final in this club, I would like to win my first trophy, so my focus isn’t on players that can leave or players that can arrive, my focus is on the game.”

City have rejected two bids from Barcelona for Rodri but anticipate a third, and are expected to sell Tijjani Reijnders in the coming days. They are also in the market for reinforcements as they aim to challenge on four fronts. City are close to signing the 18-year-old Morocco international Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille but are willing to bring in others.

Rodri, who has a year remaining on his contract, returned to the club on Friday after his holiday which followed a triumphant World Cup, but Maresca would not be drawn on the midfielder’s immediate future with a third Barcelona offer expected.

“The transfer window is open, we can buy players, we can sell players, anything can happen. I just saw Rodri now in the building, I gave him a big hug, he looks good, so we’ll see what happens.”

Reijnders is set to join the Saudi Pro League side Al-Qadsiah after the two clubs agreed a £51m fee for the Dutchman, who moved to City last summer from Milan but wants more regular playing time.

“They all work every day, they all do sessions every day and at the end of the week they all want to play a game,” Maresca said. “When they don’t play they struggle to understand or they struggle to see the reason why, and I can understand that after one season some of them would like to play a little bit more. It’s a normal situation.”

James Trafford has already been sold to Leeds, while Omar Marmoush, Rico Lewis and Savinho are others who spent much of Pep Guardiola’s final season on the periphery and could be sold.

Sports.title: Arsenal open talks with Bayer Leverkusen over deal for Jarell Quansah
Sports.content:
Arsenal have opened talks with Bayer Leverkusen over a move for Jarell Quansah as they intensify efforts to bring in cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber.

The England defender, who left Liverpool last summer for an initial £30m and was part of Thomas Tuchel’s World Cup squad, has been identified as an ideal replacement for the France and Netherlands defenders, who will miss the start of the new season due to injury. While Quansah’s preferred position is in central defence, he was also deployed at right-back by Tuchel at the World Cup and was sent off in the last-16 victory over Mexico.

It is understood that Leverkusen are reluctant to sell the Warrington-born 23-year-old, who signed a five-year deal when he left Anfield last July, and would want at least €50m (£43m). Arsenal – who saw a bid of £30m for Aston Villa’s Ezri Konsa rejected earlier in the window – are not thought to want to pay that much but now could test the German club’s resolve by submitting a similar offer. Liverpool had a €70m buyback option on Quansah but that has now expired.

Arsenal are still believed to be interested in Konsa, who also filled in at right-back for England during the World Cup but is better known as a central defender. Villa value the 28-year-old at £60m.

Mikel Arteta said this week that Saliba’s back injury would take “some time to heal” and he was unsure about when he would be available again. Arsenal also have concerns over Timber, who pulled out of the Netherlands squad on the eve of the World Cup after failing to recover from a persistent groin injury that forced him to miss most of the run‑in last season.

“Jurriën is progressing really well,” Arteta said after Arsenal’s friendly defeat by Borussia ­Dortmund last Sunday. “He’s on the pitch, he’s doing quite a lot right now, but it’s still weeks away. I cannot tell you how much.”

Arsenal would still like to sign a new attacker before the end of the window and could allow Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus to depart in order to free up more funds. ­Galatasaray have offered £38m for Martinelli, although the Brazil ­forward has turned down a move to Turkey. Napoli have shown an ­interest in Jesus.

Ethan Nwaneri could also be sold, with Milan, Fulham, RB Leipzig and Borussia Dortmund among those who have been linked with the 19-year-old.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The future of Myles Lewis-Skelly is unclear after he was offered to Chelsea and Manchester United this week. Arteta refused to address the rumours after he scored in the friendly against Como – managed by Cesc Fábregas – on Wednesday.

“I’m not going to talk about speculation,” he said. “If there is speculation about our players, it’s a good sign. That means our players attract attention and are doing a good job.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Rangers and the paradox of a painful exit that boosts their trophy chances
Sports.content:
AND NOW FOR SOME PERSPECTIVE

All new managers want to hit the ground running. But landing with a dull thud has never been a barrier to future glory, certainly not at Ibrox. Take Graeme Souness, whose start as Rangers’ player-manager put the ‘pish’ in ‘inauspicious’. On his league debut, away to Hibs, he was sent off in the first half after a revenge attack on the wrong mullet. Rangers lost 2-1 and were beaten in the third game as well. Graeme out! Rangers won the League Cup and finished the season as champions for the first time in nine years.

Dick Advocaat had a similarly awkward start in 1998. In his first game, played at Tranmere’s Prenton Park, Rangers went 3-0 down to Shelbourne in the first leg of their Big Vase tie. They went through comfortably in the end but lost the first league game a few days later. Dic- Advocaat out! Rangers had to settle for a domestic treble that season. Different times, when toys were played with for more than a few seconds before being launched from the pram with maximum force, followed a few seconds later by a handful of freshly sourced excreta. In 2026, alas, hot air and horse pucky are an acceptable substitute for reasonable discourse. And so, after failing to win any of his first four games as Rangers manager, Derek McInnes is “out of his depth” and a “dead man walking”.

Que Sera, Sera? Eff that! Turns out the future is ours to see after four games, two of them in a competition Rangers had no chance of winning anyway. Football Daily hasn’t a clue if McInnes is up to the Brobdingnagian challenge of managing Rangers, one that most tea-timely newsletters don’t really understand. But we do know that a culture of self-fulfilling poppycock, where ostentatious negativity is football’s version of the fatberg and many people would rather be right than happy, is a stain on our daily bread.

That said, what a roflcopter of a start! Given the events of last season, it was never going to be an equanimity-cultivating experience for a new Rangers manager to see Russell Martin’s start and lower it. Rangers have one point from two league games and are out of Bigger Vase after the most costly 1-1 draw against Polish opposition on British soil since Brian Clough called somebody a clown. Paradoxically, the aggregate defeat to Jagiellonia Bialystok – and subsequent drop into Tin Pot – has increased Rangers’ chances of winning a trophy under McInnes. Time will tell whether those chances have increased from 0.0000001% to 0.0000002%, from 9% to 9.4% or from some other figure to some other figure. Right now, the supercomputers know, and the bairns in the prams certainly don’t.

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 10: Fulham
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 15th (NB: this is not necessarily John Brewin’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 11th

Prospects

Marco Silva cutting the cord after five years by the river came as little surprise. If his time at Craven Cottage was successful in re-establishing Fulham as a Premier League club, he rarely concealed his ambitions to manage in European competition. He was frequently explicit in his disappointment that the club’s ownership did not meet him halfway by funding a stronger squad. Silva’s powers of rebadging and replenishing talent will be missed now that he has decamped to Benfica. Under him, Fulham played entertaining football, a collection of ugly ducklings showing their renewed worth for a club that, despite falling short of European qualification, looked upwards rather than downwards at the relegation battle. They were often a pleasure to watch, and ornery opposition for all-comers.

Álvaro Arbeloa is a very different type of appointment, with far less experience than his predecessor in frontline coaching terms, even if he arrives with Real Madrid on his CV. His arrival, though, has opened up a working relationship with the Spanish aristos, Gonzalo García and César Palacios arriving to work with a coach who helped them through the ranks in Madrid. By little coincidence, all three share the same agency as their representatives. There have been links with Endrick and Thiago Pitarch, two further young Real jewels, leading to a sense of Fulham becoming some form of Madrileño nursery, a Santiago Bernabéu on Thames. Should that play out, it would represent another sea change.

Silva preferred to work with hard-bitten pros. A couple of his leading men, Raúl Jiménez and Harry Wilson, have departed. The latter played the best football of his career last season but, like his manager, got a better offer elsewhere, from Leeds. Fulham’s latest approach is to source young players and polish them up. Can they have the same successes as mid-tier peers such as Brentford, Brighton and Bournemouth, where the approach is far more data-driven? Will supporters be looking upwards rather than downwards? A previously enigmatic club just got more enigmatic.

Off-field picture

In May, the club were runners-up at the football business awards, for stadium experience, as the Riverside Stand’s opulent hospitality completed its first full season in service. Fulham need the Riverside to deliver as a revenue stream, as financial results for the 2024-25 season showed a pre-tax loss for the year at £44.5m, and that was lowered by the sale of João Palhinha in July 2024. There has been no such windfall since. The Khan family ownership continues to back the club, its overall investment estimated at about £900m, with staff costs at 117% of turnover. Therein lies the reasoning behind Silva not receiving the backing he desired.

Owner-fan relationship

The most expensive season ticket at Craven Cottage comes in at £3,084 for access to the Riverside’s facilities, the highest in the Premier League. Shahid Khan and his son Tony, the vice-chair and director of football operations, are unpopular among committed supporters for price rises and pandering to tourism. Khan’s boat Kismet was named superyacht of the year in 2025, its main salon inspired by the Palace of Versailles, and can be chartered for more than $3m per week. Though the balance sheets confirm Khan’s outlay in funding a continued Premier League status, fans would prefer he recognised not everyone lives the high life.

The manager

Where Silva had an unremarkable playing career, Arbeloa featured among the elite, a World Cup and Champions League winner. He also had the ear of Florentino Pérez, the perennial Real Madrid president asking him to replace Xabi Alonso mid-season in the 2025-26 campaign. That did not pan out and he took his first job away from Madrid, where he was a well-regarded youth coach, in south-west London. Khan Sr’s comment that Arbeloa “believes in giving young players a chance” is pertinent for Fulham’s change in direction. Crucially, as befitting traditions at Craven Cottage, the new man from Salamanca believes in open, attacking football, offering some continuity from Silva’s reign.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Gonzalo García surges forward during Fulham’s Costa del Sol Trophy match against Málaga. Photograph: Joaquin Corchero/AFP7/Shutterstock

Gonzalo García’s reputation was made by his performances at last summer’s Club World Cup, where he won the tournament’s Golden Boot. Comparisons were made to Raúl, a considerable accolade at the Bernabéu. Goals followed in the Champions League against Juventus and Borussia Dortmund but García eventually lost out to the star system of Vinícius Júnior and Kylian Mbappé. His reputation in Spain is as a hard worker off the ball, necessary for a Premier League player. Last season, Rodrigo Muniz’s injuries meant the old soldier Jiménez shouldered the burden at centre-forward. García is younger and fresher but the hype surrounding his arrival gives him much to live up to.

Stat attack

Fulham had the oldest side in the Premier League last season, which may help explain why they had arguably the least intense press. Marco Silva’s side recorded the fewest high turnovers, which occur when a team recovers the ball to start a new open-play possession sequence in the final 40 metres of the pitch. Real Madrid are hardly known for being a high-pressing side but they comfortably outperformed Fulham on this metric. It will be fascinating to see how Arbeloa approaches this.

Set for a breakthrough

Jonah Kusi-Asare’s arrival last summer from Bayern Munich is further mining of a super-club’s youth department. Bayern inserted a buy-back clause for a player they picked up from AIK. The Sweden Under-21s player has been compared to Alexander Isak, and made seven substitute appearances last season – without scoring – before an initial loan became a permanent move. At 6ft 5in he offers a different profile of striker to García. Hayden Mullins, the former under-21 coach now Newport manager, saw the best of Kusi-Asare last season, the 18-year-old scoring five goals in six matches.

World Cup impact

García made his debut for Spain in a pre-World Cup friendly against Iraq but failed to make the eventual champions’ tournament squad. Antonee Robinson had a fine tournament for the USA until the co-hosts perished in the last 16 at the hands of a Belgium team featuring Timothy Castagne. Luc de Fougerolles, yet to play a Premier League game for Fulham, showed off teenage defensive talents in Canada’s run to the knockouts. To complete a successful quintet – saving the best till last? – Sander Berge had a fine tournament as Norway also reached the quarter-finals.

Sports.title: Former Arsenal star Francis Coquelin suffers 'suspected broken eye socket' as veteran is rushed to hospital after brutal clash of heads in Ligue 2 fixture
Sports.content:
Former Arsenal midfielder Francis Coquelin was taken to hospital after a frightening clash of heads in a league match in France.

Coquelin, now 35, had been making just his second appearance for Ligue 2 side Laval on Friday night.

The midfielder went down in the early stages of the match after clashing heads with Wilitty Younoussa, who was making his debut for Nantes.

Medical staff were called onto the pitch to attend to the players, with Coquelin and Younoussa both ultimately forced to leave the pitch on stretchers.

Reports in France stated that Coquelin was conscious as he was taken to hospital but has undergone a scan amid concerns he had suffered a broken eye socket.

'After his heavy collision with Younoussa, Coquelin was taken to the hospital but conscious,' French journalist Raphael Faurie-Pacaud wrote.

Francis Coquelin was stretchered off after a clash of head in a Ligue 2 match in France

Coquelin, seen playing for Arsenal in 2016, suffered a suspected broken eye socket

'Suspicion of an orbital floor fracture for the player who was making his first appearance with the Tango at Le Basser.

'He could be sidelined from the field for several months.'

Laval head coach David Vignes confirmed post-match he believes the injury was 'pretty serious' and would rule Coquelin out for the foreseeable future.

Coquelin had rejoined Laval in the summer, with the midfielder having started his career at the club.

The 35-year-old had been part of the youth set-up at Laval, before being signed to Arsenal's academy.

Coquelin went on to play 160 times for Arsenal and won the FA Cup twice, while he also had loan spells at Lorient, Freiburg and Charlton.

He spent three years at Valencia after leaving Arsenal, before a four-year spell at Villarreal, where he was part of their Europa League winning team in 2020-21.

Coquelin spent the last two seasons at Nantes and was facing his former side on Friday for the first time when his injury occurred.

Laval ultimately earned a 2-1 victory in the Ligue 2 match following a stoppage time winner.

Sports.title: Golden girl Keely Hodgkinson has to settle for silver as British star loses her 800m European Championship crown with second-place finish - with Olympic champion jokingly removing her medal in disappointed post-race interview
Sports.content:
Audrey Werro is fast becoming an unsolvable riddle for the leading lady of British sport. For the second time in 10 weeks, this Swiss phenomenon left Keely Hodgkinson staring at her heels in a race that lived up to its billing as the best of the European Championships.

To the most talented Audrey since Hepburn went the 800m gold medal. To Hodgkinson, there was presumably no silver lining to be found in finishing a close second on home soil.

If there is to be any consolation, it is that Werro, aged 22, clocked a championship record of 1:54.81 on a chilly, breezy evening in Birmingham to beat her. But warmer thoughts will be harder to find for Hodgkinson.

Instead, the Olympic champion must process the dawning of a serious rivalry and one that is not currently swinging in her favour. This one was settled by the margin of 0.2sec.

In the long run, Hodgkinson might view such moments as the competitive nectar needed for the breaching of new frontiers, of course, but the sting in the present will be real. Not many athletes have the finishing speed to match Hodgkinson, but in their past two races Werro has kicked away from her with the force of a donkey.

The decisive move here came after 500 metres, when Werro put the hammer down.

Hodgkinson, who had been near enough level at the bell after a 56sec opening lap, went with her, and they both separated from Femke Broeders-Bol in third, but the Brit had no answer. She never got her nose in front, and those moments of futility can leave lasting doubts in an athlete.

The 24-year-old, who was chasing a third straight European title, was evidently in little mood to indulge the celebrations of on-track interviewer Iwan Thomas. He assumed she would be thrilled with silver, but Hodgkinson responded: ‘I think I would be happier with a gold.’

Kely Hodgkinson was forced to settle for second in the women's 800m final on Friday

Hodgkinson jokingly took off her silver medal at the European Championships in Birmingham

She later added: ‘I think with that level of competition, any medal is a really good achievement and another one to add to my collection so I can never be disappointed with that. But I'm defending champion so I wanted to do that.

‘I knew it was going to come down to the wire but I really thought I was going to win today. But it wasn't meant to be. I didn't do anything wrong, it was just one of those things.

‘Congrats to Audrey. I am sure we will have more battles.’

That much seems certain. And for two women striving to break the oldest world record in track athletics, that will be a good thing.

But Werro has the edge. Having been beaten twice by Hodgkinson during the indoor portion of the season, she gained spectacular revenge in Stockholm in June when the Brit set a personal best of 1:54.33. Not only was that a win against a full-form Hodgkinson, Werro’s time of 1:53.98 was the third quickest in history. A month later, Werro ran quicker again with a 1:53.80 – if anyone is to better the dubious mark of 1:53.28 set by the Czech Jarmila Kratochvilova in the Eighties, Werro might have the edge.

To think, Werro was only cleared to race in this final on appeal after being tripped in her semi-final. It was a marginal call but also the correct one, so there should be no controversy around what it led to.

For Hodgkinson, the bigger picture will make for strange viewing. After the injury troubles of 2025, her times in 2026 have moved sharply on an upward trajectory, including the indoor world record in February, so she rightly resents any suggestion of ‘failure’ at losing a race or two. She was borderline tetchy in using that label prior to these Championships.

But in athletics, the clock is a secondary adversary to the field and Werro’s emergence is a huge fly in the ointment. For the rest of us watching, we can presumably take great pleasure in where it leads, because athletics needs rivalries. In these two gifted runners, it has one that has the potential to go on for years.

Sports.title: Manor Solomon opens up on his friendship with West Ham favourite Yossi Benayoun, not realising the rivalry with Tottenham and Championship ambitions after move
Sports.content:
Manor Solomon scrolls through the thousands of pictures on his phone before finding the one he’s after. Even amid the endless stream of snaps and selfies from over the years, he knows exactly where it is. He presses his finger to the screen and up it pops.

Two old images, one stitched above the other, taken 11 years apart, showing the same two men. At the bottom, a six-year-old Solomon stands in front of Israel icon and former West Ham favourite Yossi Benayoun.

‘I was in a football camp during the summer and he came to visit us as a surprise,’ says Solomon, sat around a wooden table in the sunshine at West Ham’s Rush Green training ground. ‘I had a picture with him. My father just got him outside of the room asking for a photo with me.’

Above it, the two of them once again, wearing the same colours of their country, this time as team-mates after 17-year-old Solomon was called up to the Israel national team.

‘We trained together. We shared the dressing room together. It was really amazing to share the dressing room with him. He’s really a hero. He's the hero of Israeli football. Him and Eyal Berkovic. They are the best footballers we've ever had in Israeli football.

‘He was my idol. First of all, he's Israeli. He made it to England. He played in the Premier League. He played for Liverpool, Arsenal, Chelsea, West Ham, the biggest clubs in England.

Manor Solomon has signed for West Ham from Tottenham this summer

‘Back then I was really little and I was looking up to him. If he made his dream come true, coming from Dimona, a small city in Israel, playing in the Premier League for the biggest clubs, maybe one day I can be the same.

‘I really love this game. He was a winger, a number 10, similar to me. Different, but similar. I always looked up to him and said: if Yossi did it, maybe in the future I will be able to get closer to him. I never thought I would get because he was for me the best one.’

Benayoun had two spells with the Hammers, helping the club to the FA Cup final in 2006, before returning on loan from Chelsea in 2012.

They are friends now. Solomon phoned him up when he knew he was leaving Tottenham and interest in him from West Ham and others started to surface.

‘I had a few options,’ he says. ‘I asked him what he thought was the best option because I want to hear his opinion. Obviously, he’s played for West Ham. And he told me that he sees me in English football. For him, I'm really suitable and I really fit English football. And West Ham can be a really, really good place for me.’

Solomon’s arrival means he’s the first player to make the switch from Spurs to West Ham since Callum Davenport in 2007. When Mohammed Kudus made the move the other way last summer, he was the first to do so since Scott Parker in 2011.

The 27-year-old, though, revealed he was not aware of the rivalry between the two. ‘I didn’t know it,’ he laughs. ‘So, let’s say I came from Manchester United it would be different?’

Oh yes.

‘Coming from Spurs… because they hate each other?’

Oh yes.

‘Okay. Yeah, I didn’t know. I know everyone in London hates each other, especially the big clubs. Tottenham, Arsenal, Chelsea, West Ham. They all hate each other but I didn’t know how big this is.’

Oh yes. So, any message to the West Ham fans so they take it easy on you?

‘It doesn't matter where I came from. It doesn't matter. I think if I came from Spurs, I came from Liverpool, I came from Fiorentina, for me it doesn't matter. I'll just try to give my best regardless of where I came from.’

Solomon says he was unaware of the rivalry between Spurs and West Ham

There is another rivalry he’s aware of, though.

‘I've heard about the rivalry between West Ham and Millwall,’ says Solomon. ‘I heard it's really big. I think it's one game before the national team break. So, there's plenty of games until this one. I think a friend of mine told me about the rivalry because I didn't know it before. And then also here at the club everyone told me it's a big rivalry. Of course, West Ham is the big club between the two. But Millwall fans I know are really harsh and tough. So for sure against West Ham it will be even bigger.’

Solomon’s time at Spurs was blighted by injury, but he does know what it takes to help fire a club to promotion. He was on loan at Leeds when they won the Championship in 2024-25, scoring the stoppage-time winner at Plymouth that secured the title.

‘There is a big difference between the Championship and the Premier League,’ he adds. ‘West Ham is a big club that can be back in the Premier League and then remain there for a really long time.

‘Everyone knows that West Ham belongs in the top half of the Premier League. Three years ago they won a European title. I'm sure if the club goes in the right direction, this club will fight again for Europe in the Premier League.’

Sports.title: Supercomputer backs Arsenal to retain Premier League title, predicts how Liverpool, Chelsea and Man City will get on under new bosses - and names the surprise team in Europe who might get relegated
Sports.content:
Supercomputer backs Arsenal to retain Premier League title, predicts how Liverpool, Chelsea and Man City will get on under new bosses - and names the surprise team in Europe who might get relegated

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The opening day of the Premier League season is fast approaching, with a supercomputer backing Arsenal to defend their title in the 2026-27 campaign.

Mikel Arteta's side ended a 22-year wait to be crowned champions last term, with the Gunners holding off Man City after finishing as runners-up in three successive seasons.

Arteta will look to become just the fourth manager in Premier League history to retain the title, following Sir Alex Ferguson, Jose Mourinho and Pep Guardiola.

According to Opta's supercomputer, which has conducted 10,000 data-led simulations of the campaign, Arsenal are the overwhelming favourites having been given a 38 per cent chance of lifting the trophy again in May.

By contrast, Liverpool were given a 28.5 per cent chance of retaining the title last year under Arne Slot, with the Reds ultimately finishing down in fifth.

A concern for Arsenal, however, has been highlighted over the back injury sustained by William Saliba with Arsenal's win percentage dropping from 68.7 to 47.6 per cent in the Premier League when the Frenchman is unavailable.

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta will look to be just the fourth boss to lead his side to back-to-back Premier League titles

Manchester City are seen as the second most likely team to be crowned champions

Man City are viewed as Arsenal's most likely challengers again, despite the departure of their legendary manager Pep Guardiola.

Enzo Maresca's side have been given a 20.5 per cent chance of glory following a summer of change, with Elliot Anderson the headline addition at £116m, although Rodri could follow Bernardo Silva in leaving the club.

PREMIER LEAGUE TITLE PROJECTION Arsenal – 38% Man City – 20.5% Liverpool – 9.2% Man United – 6.2% Aston Villa – 4.8% Chelsea – 4.1% Tottenham – 2.9% Source: Opta

Liverpool are third most likely champions at 9.2 per cent, despite new boss Andoni Iraola admitting in pre-season that his side 'cannot sustain the level we want' at this time.

The Reds are followed by rivals Manchester United, with Michael Carrick given a 6.2 per cent chance of winning the league.

Despite Aston Villa selling Morgan Rogers for a British transfer record £117million to Chelsea and the departure of Youri Tielemans to Man United, Unai Emery's side are fifth favourites at 4.8 per cent.

They are narrowly ahead of Chelsea under new boss Xabi Alonso at 4.1 per cent, with the Blues having a clear fixture schedule after missing out on Europe last season.

It is a similar situation at Tottenham, who are seen as having a 2.9 per cent chance of claiming the title under Roberto De Zerbi.

Tottenham have been among the biggest spenders in the transfer market this summer, with Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes among marquee signings at £100m and £85m respectively.

The spend comes with Spurs having recorded back-to-back 17th placed finishes in the top flight, with the Premier League status only confirmed on the final day of last season.

Hull City earned promotion to the top flight via the playoffs, but are seen as favourites to go down

Fulham are viewed as potential surprise strugglers under their new boss Alvaro Arbeloa

At the other end of the table, the three newly promoted sides have unsurprisingly been viewed as the most likely to go straight back down to the Championship.

Hull City, who came up from the play-offs, are deemed the most at risk of relegation at 38.7 per cent.

Ipswich and Coventry follow on 31.2 and 27.9 per cent, respectively.

The three clubs can take heart from Sunderland, who were viewed as the side most likely to finish bottom last season only for the Black Cats to qualify for Europe after a memorable campaign.

PREMIER LEAGUE RELEGATION RISK Hull City – 38.7% Ipswich Town – 31.2% Coventry City – 27.9% Sunderland – 25.9% Fulham – 23.4% Leeds United – 22.5% Crystal Palace – 20% Source: Opta

Sunderland's participation in the Europa League and their limited transfer activity this summer could have an impact on their prospects this campaign.

Opta's supercomputer has the Black Cats as fourth most likely club to be relegated at 25.9 per cent,

It follows Sunderland's underlying numbers last season, where they had the third lowest open-play expected goals, as well as facing the third-most shots and the fourth-most shots on target in the top flight.

Fulham are the next club at risk at 23.4 per cent, following a summer which has seen Marco Silva leave and be replaced by Alvaro Arbeloa.

Leeds United and Crystal Palace follow at 22.5 and 20 per cent, respectively.

Nottingham Forest and Brentford are next at 18.1 and 16.3, followed by Everton and Bournemouth on 13.6 and 13.1.

Sports.title: Katarina Johnson-Thompson's heptathlon hopes get off to worst possible start as a DRONE crashes into the track before hurdles event - with British star, 33, underwhelming after first day
Sports.content:
Katarina Johnson-Thompson's heptathlon hopes get off to worst possible start as a DRONE crashes into the track before hurdles event - with British star, 33, underwhelming after first day

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

A drone crash was the least of Katarina Johnson-Thompson’s concerns as she made an underwhelming start to her challenge for a European Championship medal in Birmingham.

After three disciplines, the 33-year-old was placed 15th and offering little indication she has fully recovered race sharpness from the calf niggle that ruled her out of the Commonwealth Games.

Serving as a portent of the hiccups that lay ahead, Johnson-Thompson’s first event, the 100m hurdles, was delayed during surreal scenes when a drone fly-by went hilariously wrong. In attempting to pass underneath the barriers, the driver lost his bearings and crashed into one of the hurdles.

When the gun finally set the field loose, Johnson-Thompson clocked 14sec – her worst time in 14 years of competing in major championships. From there, she regained some ground by clearing 1.83m in the high jump, allowing the two-time world gold medallist to climb to 10th, before tumbling four spots with a disappointing 12.79m in the shot put – 165cm short of her best.

Poland’s Adrianna Sulek-Schubert leads from Ireland’s Kate O’Connor.

Meanwhile, World Athletics president Lord Sebastian Coe has played down rumours that low crowds in Birmingham could harm London’s bid to host the 2029 World Championships.

"Maybe we need a stretcher? Medics?" 🚨



This scenic drone shot was going so well... 💥🤕 pic.twitter.com/UJEIm32LhJ — BBC Sport (@BBCSport) August 14, 2026

Katarina Johnson-Thompson's heptathlon hopes got off to a strange start when her 100m hurdles race was delayed by a camera drone crash

The Alexander Stadium, with a capacity of 23,000, was almost half-empty during some sessions earlier in the week, which has sparked awkward questions at a time when UK Athletics is bidding against Rome, Nairobi and Munich for the bigger event in three years.

Asked if pictures of empty seats in Birmingham might influence panel members looking at London’s presentation, Lord Coe said: ‘Look, it’s horses for courses. We had London (Olympics) in 2012, London (world championships) in 2017, London will point to having sold out Diamond League five months before the event took place. So I think it was a challenge. It’s always a challenge starting a championship on a Monday morning.’

Sports.title: How 'Gladiator' Amy Hunt became Britain's newest sprint superstar - as self-styled 'track goddess' eyes fantastic four golds in Birmingham and nipping at the heels of the international elite
Sports.content:
The fingers told the story of Amy Hunt’s incomplete mission in Birmingham on Thursday evening. First, she showed two for the gold medals she has collected so far in her domination of European sprinting and then she held up four to signify a job half done.

Even in this city of bovine obsessions, there presumably isn’t a bull stubborn enough to wager against that target being met over the weekend.

On Saturday, she will team up with Dina Asher-Smith in the 4x100m, for which the British quartet are favourites, and they will go again in the mixed relay on Sunday. Given the male talent pool includes Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu, respectively the European gold and silver medallists, Hunt’s chances of delivering on her astonishing projections are more than strong.

By now, folk are aware enough of her remarkable talents, both for the winning of races over short distances and her willingness to accompany the golds with spoken nuggets. In an era when too many of her contemporaries hide their personalities behind thick shields, Hunt, 24, is the open book athletics needed; a Cambridge graduate who isn’t afraid to share idiosyncratic declarations of self-confidence and one who, repeatedly, has backed up big talk with big performances.

By Thursday night, with the 200m title added to the 100m gold won on Monday, she was channelling Russell Crowe’s Gladiator on the track with the cry: ‘Are you not entertained?’ It was later followed by a charming explanation to reporters that her father is so obsessed by the film that his parting words to his daughter, prior to each race, include another Maximus classic: ‘Strength and honour.’

Added to the 200m world silver medal Hunt in Tokyo last year, the honours are adding up. So too is the strength of conviction that Olympic prizes and Asher-Smith’s British sprint records could soon be under threat by the next British speedster off the rank.

Newly crowned double European sprint champion Amy Hunt is the open book that athletics needs

On Saturday, she will team up with Dina Asher-Smith in the 4x100m

Hunt signalled she is halfway to her target of four gold medals after adding 200m glory to her 100m triumph

It is an enticing thought, especially as we approach the halfway point of the LA Olympic cycle. But there are a couple of caveats at play – by timings, the best of Asher-Smith, 30, remains some way ahead of what we have seen so far from Hunt, and more pertinent, the places on an Olympic podium are further clear again.

Some context here: Hunt’s best at the 100m is 10.97sec, which was delivered in Stockholm earlier this year, and at the longer distance she clocked 22.08sec in Tokyo last year. Fast as the sporting world likes to move on, let’s not forget Asher-Smith went 0.15sec faster in winning the 100m world silver in 2019 and was 0.2sec quicker while winning 200m gold at the same championships.

Asher-Smith, a world-class athlete at her best and, more importantly, an expert at managing the rounds at a championship, is no soft target. In other words, Hunt will need to maintain this steep trajectory to even get close to breaking her national records.

The other conversation involves catching the world’s elite and perspective is needed – in 2026, when we have seen the best of Hunt in the 100m, she only ties 25th in the global list, more than 0.3sec off the top, and her standard for the 200m places her 10th, more than half a second off Julien Alfred.

The purpose of mentioning these deficits is not to dilute any hype, but an accurate scaling of where she stands when non-European bibs are in the race might be necessary. In doing so, it should also be recognised, with some excitement, that Hunt is not close to being the finished article. That is a good thing.

Adam Gemili, her former training partner and an excellent analyst of the biomechanics in sprinting, told the Daily Telegraph that he can foresee Hunt reaching the 21.6s in the 200m, her stronger discipline.

The long stride of a 5ft 11ins runner has a certain ring of Usain Bolt about it; the trade off is slower starts in the 100m, but there are those around UK Athletics who believe she can the top-end speeds of the best women in the world. On the latter, it was demonstrated in how she ran down the field in the shorter distance on Monday and again when she passed Asher-Smith on the straight on Thursday.

Hunt's best times are still slower than Dina Asher-Smith at her peak and improvement will be needed to catch the world's best

It is exciting that Hunt is not the finished article with Adam Gemili forecasting she can go 21.6s in the 200m

Those strengths offer fascinating possibilities, as does her comfort in the unique challenge of a championship, where the pressure is greatest and fatigue accumulates between rounds. As Hunt previously demonstrated by describing herself as an 'academic badass and track goddess', some athletes are more born to the spotlight than others. Lord Sebastian Coe, president of World Athletics, has been among the luminaries at the European Championships to identify that ease with her circumstances as a decisive trait.

Doubtless it will be tested in more extreme circumstances at the world championships next year, by which point more time will have been afforded to understanding Hunt’s peculiar issue with low blood pressure. She revealed it in the wake of winning the 200m, with the consequence that felt close to fainting during a race in London earlier this year. Less than ideal.

But Hunt has overcome all manner of problems to get this far. It should not be forgotten that after breaking the under-18 world record for the 200m, she spent years tormented by injuries. A ruptured quadricep while at university left her in such a state that she needed help from her mother to get out of the shower.

These days, she might require assistance carrying the medals and little else.

Sports.title: Revealed: Cristiano Ronaldo signed prenup agreement with new wife Georgina Rodriguez, as marriage certificate and full details of their wedding at £30m mansion emerge
Sports.content:
Revealed: Cristiano Ronaldo signed prenup agreement with new wife Georgina Rodriguez, as marriage certificate and full details of their wedding at £30m mansion emerge

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez got married at their new £30million mansion near Lisbon in front of just four witnesses and their children, it emerged today.

Cristiano's doting mum Dolores Aveiro and his three siblings Hugo, Elma and Katia, were not present at the intimate civil ceremony, which took place at 1.30pm on Tuesday.

Georgina's sister Ivana, Cristiano's long-time friend Miguel Paixao and a Spanish couple named as Jose Rodriguez Sangil and his wife Monica Goncalez Martinez were the only witnesses.

Registrar Maria Manuel Ferreira de Campos Folhadela de Oliveira travelled from the northern Portuguese city of Porto to Cascais to officiate the ceremony.

And the star couple, who married exactly one year to the day after they announced their engagement on social media, have decided to keep their prenuptial assets separate despite tying the knot after a decade-long romance.

Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodriguez married with four witnesses in Cascais, Lisbon

The marriage certificate for Ronaldo and Georgina's wedding has now emerged

The couple posted photos of them wearing their wedding rings after the small ceremony

They signed a prenup agreement to define their property regime on August 10, a day before the ceremony, at a public notary's office in Lisbon.

Cristiano Ronaldo's representatives confirmed earlier this week the footballer and his long-time partner married on August 11 in an 'intimate' ceremony in Cascais after the couple posted photos of them wearing their wedding rings on social media.

It followed speculation which turned out to be false that they were due to marry at Funchal Cathedral in Cristiano's native island of Madeira on Saturday.

No details had emerged about where in Cascais they had wed or who exactly was at the ceremony apart from their children.

Overnight respected Portuguese newspaper Jornal de Noticias published a copy of the marriage certificate showing it took place at Cristiano's massive mansion in the upmarket residential area of Quinta da Marina.

And it also evidenced the fact so few people were invited there appeared to be no place for Cristiano's mum, who gave the union her blessing shortly afterwards by posting a heart emoticon on her son's Instagram in response to his wedding announcement, or the rest of his family apart from his children.

Jose Rodriguez Sangil was described as a Spanish jeweller by Portuguese press.

The marriage document listed Cristiano's full name and age of 41 as well as his birthplace and the names of his parents, including his late father Jose Dinis.

Cristiano's massive built-from-scratch mansion in Quinta da Marina was the venue

The home boats an impressive infinity pool, underground car park and a private cinema room

Ronaldo wore his wedding ring on his finger as he returned to training in Saudi Arabia

The same details were listed for 32-year-old Georgina, born in the Argentinian capital Buenos Aires, and referenced by her full name of Georgina Luisa Rodriguez Hernandez. They will both keep their pre-marriage names.

The marriage certificate was recorded as number 1,493 of this year but appears to have been listed at Porto's Registry Office instead of Cascais which is the municipality where the wedding took place.

Cristiano and Georgina are now back in Saudi Arabia where the Portuguese international plays his club football for Al Nassr ahead of the start of the new season tomorrow.

Sports.title: Paul Scholes names £60m Arsenal star they should 'get rid of' instead of Myles Lewis-Skelly amid Man United and Chelsea links
Sports.content:
Paul Scholes names £60m Arsenal star they should 'get rid of' instead of Myles Lewis-Skelly amid Man United and Chelsea links

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Man United legend Paul Scholes believes Arsenal would be making a mistake if they sold Myles Lewis-Skelly this summer - and highlighted another player the Gunners should move on instead.

Lewis-Skelly, 19, enjoyed a breakout campaign in 2024-25, and while he struggled for gametime last time out, he played an important role in the end-of-season run-in.

However, with the £75million addition of Bruno Guimaraes adding to the likes of Martin Zubimendi, Martin Odegaard, Declan Rice, Mikel Merino and Eberechi Eze as options in central midfield, it has raised uncertainty over the 19-year-old's future.

Reports then broke earlier this week suggesting Arsenal had offered Lewis-Skelly to both Chelsea and Man United.

And, speaking on The Overlap Fan Debate, brought to you by Sky Bet, Scholes felt that if Arsenal sanctioned his departure it would be a big mistake.

‘I prefer Myles Lewis-Skelly in centre midfield to Zubimendi,’ Scholes said.

Paul Scholes believes Arsenal would be making a mistake if they sold Myles Lewis-Skelly

Lewis-Skelly has been linked with a move to both Chelsea and Manchester United this summer

‘I think Zubimendi struggled last year. If there’s one player you are going to get rid of, it would be him [Martin Zubimendi].'

Scholes also pointed to a wider issue if Arsenal were to sell their academy graduate, who can play at left-back and in central midfield.

He added: 'It reminds me a little bit of when Danny Welbeck left Manchester United. I hated it, didn’t like it.

'Now, Danny was a little bit older than Myles Lewis-Skelly, but when you’re losing your own players, it’s disappointing.'

Jamie Carragher agreed with Scholes' thoughts and admitted he was left shocked by the reports.

He said 'Do you think it’s from his side or the club’s side? That’s the thing that was a little bit strange about it. It felt almost like Arsenal offered Manchester United Myles Lewis-Skelly.

'It wasn’t Myles Lewis-Skelly saying I want to leave or his people putting something out. That’s where the shock came from.

'I still can’t believe it. Obviously, last season wasn’t great for him for the whole season, but when a young player has already put in performances like I’ve seen him put in at the Bernabeu...

'He was running the game at the Bernabeu from left-back and then his performance in the Champions League final in central midfield against Paris Saint-Germain.'

Scholes felt Arsenal should move on Martin Zubimendi instead of the young Englishman

Carragher continued: 'You can’t play at that level unless you’re pretty special at that age. All young players have ups and downs. Last season he didn’t play as much as he probably would have liked.

'But, as you just said, his ceiling is so high for the performances he’s already put in as a kid. I couldn’t believe that Arsenal would even think about letting him go.'

When pressed on Lewis-Skelly's future earlier this week, Gunners boss Mikel Arteta refused to give anything away.

'I’m not going to talk about any speculation,' he said. ‘If there is a speculation about our players, that’s a good sign. That means that we attract attention and they’re doing a good job.’

Sports.title: Keely Hodgkinson misses out European Championships gold medal in thrilling 800m final
Sports.content:
Keely Hodgkinson misses out European Championships gold medal in thrilling 800m final

The women's 800m was one of the most anticipated events of the European Athletics Championships, as it promised a thrilling three-battle between Keely Hodgkinson, Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol

View 2 Images Keely Hodgkinson went into the final as a two-time defending champion (Image: Julian Finney/Getty Images)

Great Britain's Keely Hodgkinson narrowly missed out a home gold medal in the women's 800m final at the European Athletics Championships. Hodgkinson, 24, came second behind the supreme Audrey Werro in her bid a three-time European champion at Alexander Stadium in Birmingham.

‌



Swiss sensation Werro recovered from a dramatic fall during her semi-final on Thursday afternoon to clinch the gold medal with a rapid time of 1:54.81. Hodgkinson made the fastest start under the Friday-night lights but had the 22-year-old on her shoulder.

‌



On the final lap, Werro made her move and gained the lead. Hodgkinson pushed to make it a dramatic finish but couldn't pip her rival to the finish line and had to settle for silver.

‌



Meanwhile, Femke Broeders-Bol set a new national record for the Netherlands as she earned bronze. Hodgkinson was all smiles after the final, although she jokingly took her silver medal off during an interview.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



"It was a great race, I love a good challenge and that's what it was," the Atherton-born star reflected. "I have mixed emotions. With that level of competition, any medal is a good achievement. Another one to add to my collection and I can never be disappointed with that.

"I knew it was going to come down to the wire and I really wanted to win. I guess it just wasn't meant to be. There were so many ways it could have played out. Audrey wanted to take it on, with that wind I was happy to let her. We are all great athletes and I look forward to the next match-up.

"I've said all year it's really motivating to be in such a competitive event. I love it, it's such a competitive event. I had a pretty good day, it just didn't quite go the way I wanted it to."

‌



View 2 Images Audrey Werro pipped Keely Hodgkinson to claim gold in Birmingham (Image: Julian Finney/Getty Images)

As for Werro, who ran the fastest time for 43 years earlier this season, she picked up her first senior international gold medal. But the rising star's chances of even racing were plunged into doubt following her aforementioned fall.

Werro was holding the inside line in a crowded field before disaster struck, as she went down due to an 'unintentional touch' involving Werro and France's Anais Bourgoin. Following a review, Werro and Lithuania's Gabija Galvydyte were reinstated to the final.

Article continues below

The organisers explained: "The incident resulted in the fall of two athletes, Werro and Galvydyte. Having reviewed the circumstances, the referee decided to qualify both athletes in accordance with the applicable rules."

Reflecting on Werro's final performance, Paula Radcliffe told BBC One: "Audrey Werro is young still and that was a huge amount of pressure even without the fall, without the bruising and then to pull it together to take the race by the scruff of the neck, which I think Keely did intend for her to do but she thought she could come back at her. But Werro had another gear."

Sports.title: British cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies following tragic accident in Portugal
Sports.content:
British cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies following tragic accident in Portugal

Finlay Tarling, the 19-year-old younger brother of Ineos Grenadiers rider Josh, was competing for the NSN Development Team at the Volta a Portugal when the incident occurred

View 2 Images Finlay Tarling has sadly died (Image: Huw Fairclough/Getty Images)

British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died aged 19 following a tragic accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal. Tarling, the younger brother of Ineos Grenadiers rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on both the road and track.

‌



The Welsh teenager was competing for the NSN Development Team on Friday and the incident occurred on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe. No details regarding the nature of the incident have been released.

‌



NSN announced his death in a statement which read: "We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

‌



Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend. Rest in peace, Fin."

View 2 Images Finlay Tarling pictured with his parents in 2025 (Image: Huw Fairclough/Getty Images)

‌



The Portuguese Cycling Federation also issued a statement which confirmed the race had been neutralised and that the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of 'respect and mourning'.

It said: "The organisation of the 87th Volta a Portugal em Bicicleta Jogos Santa Casa deeply regrets to announce the passing of British cyclist Finlay Tarling, from the NSN Development Team, following a serious accident that occurred during the 8th stage of the race.

"At this moment of profound dismay, the organization of the Volta a Portugal and the Portuguese Cycling Federation express their most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his teammates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones.

‌



"In light of this tragic event, the race will be neutralised until reaching Fafe and, as a sign of respect and mourning, the podium ceremony scheduled for today will not take place. The organisation will provide all additional information as soon as conditions allow it to do so."

Stephen Park CBE, Performance Director for the Great Britain Cycling Team, paid tribute by saying: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

‌



"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man. Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh at this tragic time."

In the comments of NSN's Facebook post, fans from around the world offered their condolences to Tarling's family, loved ones and his team. "This is terrible, shocking news," one wrote. "My deepest condolences to Fin's family, the team, and the whole cycling family."

"Such sad news," another added. "Deepest condolences to Finlay's family and the wider cycling community."

Article continues below

"Deepest condolences to the family, friends and teammates as this is heartbreaking," a third posted. "May you rest in peace."

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta gives injury update on five Arsenal stars ahead of Community Shield
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta gives injury update on five Arsenal stars ahead of Community Shield

Mikel Arteta was without five key players during pre-season but will able to welcome back three of them for Arsenal's clash with Manchester City in the Community Shield on Sunday

View 2 Images Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka have returned to Arsenal training (Image: Manuel Velasquez - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

Mikel Arteta has confirmed that Declan Rice, Martin Zubimendi and Bukayo Saka will all be available to face Manchester City in the Community Shield. The Arsenal boss also provided updates on William Saliba and Jurrien Timber, who are both recovering from long-term injuries which they suffered during the World Cup.

‌



All five players didn't feature in any of the Gunners' pre-season friendlies. Rice, Zubimendi and Saka each made it to the final weekend of the tournament with England and Spain respectively, so they were afforded additional time off in order prepare for what's set to be another gruelling campaign at club level.

‌



Saliba, however, went down with a back problem in the opening stages of France's semi-final defeat to Spain. Meanwhile, Timber picked up a serious groin injury just days before the Netherlands kicked off their campaign.

‌



Arteta was asked to provide an update on the quintet during Friday's pre-match conference and had mixed news. "They [Rice, Zubimendi and Saka] will be available. They trained with us today, they will train tomorrow and if they are in the condition that we expect them to be, they will be involved."

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



The Arsenal manager added: "Jurrien is progressing really well, he is on the pitch, we are ramping up now with certain actions and especially the volume and the load. I think he is on a good trajectory, but there is still a few weeks to go. Wilo, as we all know, it's more a long-term injury."

Asked whether Timber could return before the next international break which starts in September and runs into October, Arteta replied: "We have to wait and see. He needs to start to train with the group in the next week or so hopefully, and then see how he progresses from there.

"It's been a long-term issue, and we want to make sure that every step that we take is the right one, he feels right to do that, because he's such an important player for us."

‌



How should Arsenal line up against Manchester City? Let us know your XI in the comments section.

View 2 Images William Saliba's back injury could rule him out for months (Image: Zhizhao Wu/Getty Images)

Both Rice and Saka had fitness issues during the World Cup and had to be managed by England's medical staff. But Arteta hasn't seen anything from the duo that's worried him.

‌



"We haven't noticed anything; they had individual plans through the time that they had with the national team," he explained. "They've been trying to evolve those issues and they have improved.

"In the rest period that they had, they both had specific programmes for themselves. They've been doing those and so far, what I saw the last two or three days, it was really good."

Sports.title: Value Scope: Each way horseracing tips from Steve Jones for Saturday on ITV
Sports.content:
Value Scope: Each way horseracing tips from Steve Jones for Saturday on ITV

Ripon provides the main handicaps this weekend and our tipping ace has recommendations in both the Great St Wilfrid and its consolation race, the Silver Cup

View 2 Images Steve Jones with his picks for Saturday

Go for Glory in the William Hill Supporting MND Silver Cup. Course form is often crucial on Ripon’s undulating sprint track and GLORY HYDE (2.55) has shown a distinct liking for Yorkshire’s garden racecourse.

‌



She landed back-to-back victories over today’s course and distance in June and she did well to overcome traffic problems on the latter occasion. Her two subsequent runs have not been as good but there have been valid excuses for the below-par performances.

‌



She didn’t have the best of draws for either start – both at York – and that course doesn’t really play to her strengths. Her stands’ side stall for today’s race should be much more of a help and she has a decent amount of gears.

‌

The likely strong pace will suit her perfectly and she looks overpriced returned to her favourite venue. Have 1pt each-way at 14-1. Sky Bet is paying out on six places.

Ripon’s big race is the William Hill/MND Association Great St Wilfrid Handicap where KODIAC THRILLER (3.25) has strong claims.

He has been rejuvenated by a visor in his last couple of starts. His fourth over 5f at Ripon was a good effort as he stumbled coming out of the stalls and then ran into trouble when attempting to get back into the race.
