World.title: NOHIL, partners tackle foot deformities, train specialists in Lagos
World.content:
…400 patients get free medical care

By Chioma Obinna

The National Orthopaedic Hospital, Igbobi, NOHIL, Lagos, in collaboration with Steps2Walk and the Global Health Charity and Training Foundation, GHCTF, has commenced a specialised foot and ankle surgical training and free medical outreach aimed at expanding access to quality orthopaedic care and reducing the burden of untreated foot deformities in Nigeria.



The five-day programme, which began Monday, August 10, combines specialist surgical training, knowledge transfer and community healthcare services, with more than 400 people already benefiting from free screening, consultations and medications.



The initiative also attracted an international faculty of orthopaedic specialists from the United States, United Kingdom, Türkiye and Pakistan, who are training Nigerian healthcare professionals on contemporary approaches to managing foot and ankle conditions.



Speaking at the commencement of the programme, Medical Director of NOHIL, Dr. Wakeel Lawal, described the collaboration as a major opportunity to strengthen specialist capacity and improve access to advanced foot and ankle care in Nigeria.



Lawal said exposure to contemporary global practices would enable participating specialists to transfer the knowledge gained to their various hospitals, thereby expanding access to specialised services and reducing the number of Nigerians who travel abroad for treatment.



He said: “This programme is important because it is not just about treating patients. It is also about transferring skills and knowledge to our specialists so that they can replicate what they have learnt in their various hospitals.



“This will ultimately improve access to specialised foot and ankle services across the country and reduce the need for Nigerians to seek treatment abroad.”



The Foot and Ankle Surgical Course, held at the Pavilion Hall, featured lectures, clinical case presentations and interactive sessions ahead of about 30 live surgical procedures scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday.



Representing Steps2Walk, Dr. John Lewis Ugbo said the organisation remained committed to improving the management of orthopaedic deformities among children and adults in developing countries.



He disclosed that Steps2Walk had provided medical supplies and equipment to support the programme while facilitating knowledge transfer between international specialists and Nigerian practitioners.



Ugbo drew attention to the burden of congenital clubfoot, noting that about three out of every 1,000 births are affected, while warning that delayed or inappropriate treatment could result in lifelong disability and other complications.



He said the programme was designed not merely to perform surgeries but to change the way orthopaedic deformities are identified and managed through early intervention, specialist training and sustainable capacity building.



“It is not just about coming here to do surgeries. It is about changing the approach to the management of orthopaedic deformities through early identification, appropriate treatment and training,” he said.



Ugbo also expressed Steps2Walk’s commitment to establishing a long-term partnership with NOHIL, including continued specialist training, provision of medical supplies and participation of international experts in future programmes.



Meanwhile, more than 400 residents benefited from the medical outreach held at NOHIL, with about 150 health volunteers supporting the exercise.



Beneficiaries received free screening for hypertension, diabetes, prostate health, high cholesterol, malaria and hepatitis B, as well as eye examinations.



Free medications were also provided, while beneficiaries requiring continued care were linked to the Lagos State Health Insurance Scheme.



Speaking during the programme, Permanent Secretary, Lagos State Ministry of Health, Dr. Dayo Lajide, commended Steps2Walk and GHCTF for supporting specialised orthopaedic care in the state.



Lajide described the collaboration with NOHIL as significant, stressing the importance of partnerships in expanding access to quality healthcare.



Also speaking, Dr. Adebayo Akintobi, representing GHCTF, commended the NOHIL leadership and volunteers for their commitment to the outreach.



Akintobi praised the volunteers for their compassion and dedication to the beneficiaries, saying the exercise demonstrated the capacity of NOHIL and its partners to deliver comprehensive healthcare services to a large number of people.



The medical outreach continues today, Tuesday, at the General Hospital, Somolu, where members of the public are expected to benefit from free health screening and other medical services.



The initiative is expected to culminate in the live surgical sessions later in the week, further strengthening local expertise in the management of complex foot and ankle conditions.

World.title: Nestlé backs 50 Zaria women as rural retail initiative hits five-year milestone
World.content:
By Chioma Obinna

Five years after launching its Empowering Rural Women Initiative, Nestlé Nigeria is expanding its support for women-led businesses, with 50 retailers in Zaria, Kaduna State, receiving business training and product grants to strengthen their enterprises.



The latest beneficiaries were equipped with practical skills in bookkeeping, stock management, merchandising, financial management and customer service, alongside Nestlé products valued at three times the value of their existing stock.



The Zaria intervention, which marks the 10th edition of the initiative, also begins a three-month mentorship programme aimed at helping the women apply their new skills, manage the additional inventory and build more sustainable businesses.



Launched in 2021, the initiative targets women retailers with the drive to grow their businesses but limited access to training, mentorship and growth capital.



With the addition of the Zaria beneficiaries, the programme has now reached 482 women across communities in Nigeria, up from 432 before the latest intervention.



Nestlé said monitoring of previous beneficiaries shows that more than 80 per cent have sustained or grown their businesses beyond the initial support. Many have reportedly increased their inventories and turnover, attracted more customers and strengthened their financial and business management practices.



The programme comes against the backdrop of the critical role women play in Nigeria’s retail economy, particularly in rural and underserved communities where small retailers provide a vital link between consumers and larger markets.



Speaking at the Zaria event, Boladale Odunlami, Commercial Manager, Nestlé Nigeria, said women are central to the company’s retail network and deserve opportunities to grow alongside the business.



“Women account for approximately 60% of the retailers in Nestlé Nigeria’s retail network. Every day, they help us reach consumers, build trust within communities and keep our business moving,” Odunlami said.

He added that the initiative was designed to turn women retailers into stronger entrepreneurs while reinforcing the company’s distribution network.



“The Empowering Rural Women Initiative reflects our belief that the women who contribute to our growth should have the opportunity to grow with us. By investing in their skills and strengthening their businesses, we are helping them increase their earning potential while building a stronger, more capable and more resilient retail network,” he said.



Beyond the immediate stock support, the mentorship phase is expected to be critical to the programme’s long-term impact. Mentors will guide participants as they manage their expanded inventory, apply lessons from the training and reinvest profits into their businesses.



Participants will also be encouraged to share experiences and build networks that can continue beyond the formal three-month mentorship period.



Reflecting on the initiative’s five-year journey, Victoria Uwadoka, Corporate Communications, Public Affairs and Sustainability Lead, Nestlé Nigeria, said its success should be measured by what beneficiaries achieve after receiving support.



“The true measure of this initiative is not the support we provide on the day, but what the women go on to build with it,” Uwadoka said.



“Five years on, we are seeing women sustain their growth, expand their businesses and create greater economic security for themselves and their families.”



According to her, the initiative demonstrates Nestlé’s Creating Shared Value approach, where investment in communities also strengthens the company’s business ecosystem.



“As these women build stronger businesses and better livelihoods, they also strengthen the retail network that connects Nestlé to communities across Nigeria. It is a model in which progress for the women and progress for our business reinforce each other,” she said.



The Zaria edition was implemented with the support of Nestlé Nigeria’s partners and local distributors, who will remain engaged with the beneficiaries during the mentorship period.

World.title: Lagos water concession, prepaid meters’ll deepen hardship — CAPPA
World.content:
File image.

… Demands publication of CHEC-Naston MoU, suspension of prepaid metering

By Chioma Obinna

Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa, CAPPA, has warned the Lagos State Government against moves to concession parts of the state’s public water infrastructure, saying the policy could deepen hardship for residents and undermine access to affordable and reliable water.



CAPPA’s warning followed the state government’s signing of a one-year Memorandum of Understanding, MoU, with China Harbour Engineering Company, CHEC, and Naston Engineering Nigeria Limited to scope and define components of a water infrastructure programme within the Lekki Concession Area.



Under the arrangement, the first phase will involve the installation of a transmission pipeline beneath the Lagos Lagoon into the Lekki Concession Area, while the second phase will cover downstream distribution, metering and last-mile connections.



The engagement is expected to produce a technical report and implementation framework for a possible concession agreement between the Lagos State Government and the consortium.



But CAPPA said the development raises serious concerns about the future of public water supply in the state, particularly the possibility of private control over distribution, tariffs, metering and household access.



“There is no publicly accessible record showing the project’s full scope, how the consortium was selected, what obligations the companies have assumed, or how residents have participated in its development.

“The government is already discussing tariffs and a concession while the public remains shut out,” the organisation said.



The group also faulted the lack of publicly accessible copies of the MoU, terms of reference and records of consultations with affected communities.



CAPPA maintained that beyond the transparency concerns, concessioning water infrastructure could undermine the principle of universal access by placing commercial profitability above the needs of residents, particularly low-income households.



The organisation argued that Lagos, with its substantial revenue base, has the capacity and responsibility to mobilise public resources, maintain existing infrastructure, expand water production and guarantee access to safe and affordable water.



“The problem is that successive administrations have failed to fund, maintain, and expand the system at the scale Lagos requires.



“Allowing a public institution to deteriorate and then presenting private control as its rescue is dishonest. It is an abdication of responsibility,” CAPPA’s Water Programme Officer, Holiness Segun-Olufemi, said.



CAPPA also kicked against the planned expansion of prepaid water meters, warning that the system could make access to water dependent on a household’s ability to pay upfront.



Unlike conventional postpaid metering, prepaid systems automatically cut off supply when purchased credit is exhausted.



“For a resource essential to human life, sanitation, and public health, automated disconnections are fundamentally exclusionary and set to worsen the lives of vulnerable groups and low-income earners,” Segun-Olufemi said.



CAPPA drew parallels between the proposed water concession and Nigeria’s experience with electricity privatisation, arguing that consumers have continued to face rising tariffs, metering challenges, estimated billing and unreliable supply despite the transfer of major parts of the electricity sector to private operators.



It warned that Lagos could reproduce similar problems in the water sector, with public funds financing infrastructure while private operators control billing and revenue and households bear rising costs without guaranteed supply.



The organisation said the consequences could be more severe in the water sector because, unlike electricity, water is indispensable to human survival, sanitation and public health.



CAPPA cited experiences in Akilo and Baruwa areas of Lagos where prepaid water meters have reportedly been introduced.



According to the group, residents complained of intermittent supply, delays in activating purchased units, low pressure, restricted supply periods and discrepancies between payments and volumes of water received.



In Baruwa, CAPPA said some households reported spending as much as N60,000 monthly on water, while also alleging sudden disappearance of purchased units, prolonged outages, dirty water when supply resumed and inadequate complaint mechanisms.



CAPPA therefore called on the Lagos State Government to halt further steps towards concessioning the water system and suspend expansion of prepaid metering.



It demanded the immediate publication of the CHEC-Naston MoU and urged the government to develop and publicly disclose a fully funded plan for rehabilitating treatment plants, pipelines, reservoirs and distribution networks.



The organisation also called for a system that guarantees every household access to a basic quantity of water.



It urged communities, labour unions, students, journalists, civil society organisations and residents to demand accountability from the government on the provision of basic amenities.



CAPPA warned that any concession agreement could bind Lagos for decades, potentially outlasting the administrations that negotiated it.



While acknowledging the urgent need for massive investment in the state’s water infrastructure, the organisation said such investment should strengthen the Lagos Water Corporation and expand public capacity rather than create another avenue for private profit from an essential service.

World.title: JKing returns with 6 new songs
World.content:
By Benjamin Njoku

King Izonebi Alfred fondly called Jking, the indescribably talented Nigerian highlife musician, has shaken the music world with six new songs. The six songs — ‘Biri Bein Ghan’, ‘Chief Adowei Binaebi’, ‘Chief Boro Opudu’, ‘Hon.Seles Saboh’, ‘Traditional Series (Bini Ebi)’ and ‘Izon Fiye’ — are thematically and instrumentally built to tell great stories as a guide for any society suffocated by moral and cultural deficit.

In the new songs, Izonebi Alfred is philosophically situated by two quotable statements that ‘philanthropy is the prerogative of a good man with a good heart’, and that ‘taking a recourse to stealing is the prepossession of a man with an ungrateful heart’. Behind these two statements, Alfred musically builds an edifice that asserts a clear moral direction for this generation and beyond.

Alfred’s songs always provoke healthy intellectual, cultural and moral discussions among music enthusiasts. His new songs carry this potential in dimensions never known in the history of highlife music in the Niger Delta. Like waters that brim the riverbank, Alfred’s new songs are loaded and full.

World.title: Nehita Ofure leads emotional stage play ‘Surrounded’ at BFF festival
World.content:
By Benjamin Njoku

Award-winning actress and beauty queen Nehita Ofure Irieme delivered a powerful performance in the stage play ‘Surrounded’, staged at the recently concluded Building Forever Friendships, BFF, Festival 2026 in Lagos.

Her performance was one of the highlights of the festival, with the emotional weight of the story leaving members of the audience in tears.

‘Surrounded’ explores the complexities of friendship, betrayal and emotional healing, presenting a raw and relatable account of what happens when trust is broken and the difficult journey of learning to trust again.

Nehita shared the stage with star actress Ariyike Dimples, who played Elizabeth; Abbeytee, who portrayed Shadow; and Bankole Bayo, who played Chris. Together, the cast brought to life a deeply emotional story about friendship, heartbreak, vulnerability and the importance of human connection.

For the actress and filmmaker, the role offered another opportunity to explore the depth and versatility of her craft, building on her experience as a performer across different creative platforms. She described the experience as both challenging and rewarding, noting that theatre demanded a different level of vulnerability and connection from an actor.

“Playing Ayanfe in ‘Surrounded’ was such a beautiful and challenging experience. Theatre is very different because there is nowhere to hide. You are right there with the audience, and every emotion has to be honest and immediate. The role allowed me to explore pain, betrayal and vulnerability in a very intimate way, and I am grateful for the opportunity.”

She added that the message of the play resonated deeply with her because friendship is an important part of human relationships and emotional wellbeing.

“What I love about ‘Surrounded’ is that it reminds us that friendship can be beautiful, but it can also hurt deeply when trust is broken. We all experience moments when we feel disappointed, betrayed or alone. But the courage to open your heart again is part of healing. I hope everyone who watched the play left with a renewed appreciation for genuine friendship and meaningful connections.

The BFF Festival, hosted annually in Lagos, Nigeria, by Bola Adetoun Jegede, is described as the world’s biggest friendship festival. The gathering celebrates community, emotional healing and meaningful human connections through conversations, games, networking activities and prizes.

World.title: DELTA ROAD LANDING: Private jet crew overwrote black box – NSIB
World.content:
By Dickson Omobola

Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau, NSIB, has disclosed that the flight crew of the private jet that landed on a road in the Ogwashi-Uku area of Delta State overwrote the aircraft’s black boxes.



In aviation, the black boxes, comprising the Cockpit Voice Recorder, CVR, and Flight Data Recorder, FDR, capture cockpit audio, aircraft systems and flight performance data to help investigators determine the causes of incidents or accidents and improve aviation safety.



Addressing newsmen virtually, Friday, Director-General of the NSIB, Capt Alex Badeh Jr, said between the time the incident occurred and when the aircraft departed for Lagos, the crew overwrote the recorded data, making the investigation more challenging.



He, however, said investigators relied on other available evidence to reconstruct the sequence of events and determine what happened.



His words: “I don’t think airlines are doing anything (to hamper investigation into accidents or incidents) deliberately, at least not to my knowledge. But one thing is: the FDR and CVR being overwritten a lot of time. That is an issue that we face. I think that is something we faced with the last one in Asaba.



“They took off and flew back to Lagos and overwrote everything that happened when they landed in Asaba. That aeroplane, being a November registered and operating on a parts 91 certificate, which is a not for profit, just for private operation, not for charter hire, they weren’t subject to the rule that requires them to have the 26 hours cockpit voice recorder…

“Between when the incident happened and when they took off and went back to Lagos, they overwrote everything that happened. That made things a little difficult, but we still worked with other things to figure out what happened. We are still working with other parts to get the data for that. The FDR of that aeroplane did not work as well. I am not sure what happened.”

On June 10, a private aircraft, which had four crew members on board, landed on a road in the Ogwashi-Uku area near Asaba, the Delta State capital.

Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Mr Festus Keyamo, described the incident as a security breach, saying the crew of the private aircraft were in the custody of the Department of State Services, DSS.

World.title: We will not allow Iran march toward a nuclear weapon — Vance
World.content:
US VP Vance

By Vera Anyagafu with agency report

US Vice President, JD Vance has reiterated the US stance against Iran, saying, “We are not going to allow Iran to march toward a nuclear weapon, and we are not going to allow them to threaten our partners with impunity.”



Speaking at a policy event in Washington, Vance said the administration is coordinating diplomatic, economic, and security measures with allies to pressure Iran while keeping the option of further action available, declaring that the US will use all tools at its disposal to confront Tehran.



He also outlined the approach as working with European and Gulf partners on a coordinated response to Iran’s nuclear activities and regional proxies, targeting Iran’s oil exports, drone program, and entities linked to the Revolutionary Guard with sanctions, and maintaining a US military presence in the region to protect shipping lanes and American personnel.



The remarks came amid renewed concerns over Iran’s uranium enrichment and recent attacks on commercial shipping in the Gulf.



US officials have also cited Iranian support for proxy groups in Yemen, Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon as a key driver of instability.



However, Iran’s Foreign Ministry had dismissed Vance’s remarks, calling them, “the same failed policy of pressure and threats.”



Speaking in his capacity as US Senator, Chris Murphy, D-Conn., said Congress must be involved in any escalation and stressed, “We need a strategy that actually reduces risk, not just rhetoric.”



Analysts also stated that the phrase ‘all tools’ is deliberately broad, meant to signal resolve to Tehran while keeping options open for the administration.



Vance said Secretary of State and Defense officials will brief allies in Europe and the Middle East next week, and that the administration is reviewing additional sanctions designations.

World.title: CIPM President calls for people-centred transformation of Nigeria’s public service
World.content:
The President and Chairman of the Governing Council of the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria (CIPM), Mallam Ahmed Ladan Gobir, FCIPM, fnli has called for a fundamental transformation of Nigeria’s public service, anchored on innovation, accountability, participation, inclusion and strategic people management.

The CIPM President made the call while delivering the keynote address at the Ogun State 2026 Public Service Day Celebration Lecture, held at the Cultural Centre, Kuto, Abeokuta, on Thursday, August 13, 2026. The lecture was themed “Transforming the Public Service: Advancing Innovation, Accountability, Participation and Inclusion.”

Speaking to public and civil service leaders, scholars, organised labour, private-sector representatives and other stakeholders, Gobir emphasised that the ultimate purpose of public service is not merely to process paperwork, but to improve citizens’ lives.

He noted that citizens experience government primarily through the quality of public services they receive, stressing that “Government is an idea. Public service is its experience.” He therefore urged public institutions to move beyond measuring activity and processes to measuring the actual value and impact delivered to citizens.

According to him, innovation in the public service must go beyond simply digitising existing processes. He cautioned against “digitising dysfunction”, noting that technology cannot compensate for institutions that have failed to rethink inefficient processes.

He challenged public-sector leaders to ask whether existing procedures still create public value and encouraged institutions to redesign processes around citizens’ needs rather than institutional convenience.

On accountability, the CIPM President described it as “the mathematics of trust,” emphasising that public institutions must earn citizens’ confidence through competence, fairness, transparency, consistency and responsiveness.

He also stressed the importance of meaningful citizen participation, noting that participation should go beyond inviting citizens to events after decisions have already been made. Rather, citizens should have opportunities to influence decisions that affect their lives.

On inclusion, Gobir called for public services to be designed to accommodate citizens across different socioeconomic, geographic, technological and demographic circumstances. He warned that a service cannot be considered truly inclusive if it is technically available but practically inaccessible to significant segments of the population.

The CIPM President further highlighted the critical role of human resource management in public-sector transformation, noting that no institution can transform beyond the capacity of its people.

He called for a strategic approach to talent management, leadership development, performance management and capability building within the public service.

“The greatest infrastructure of a nation is not concrete. It is capability. Only capable people move institutions.”

He urged public-sector organisations to build workplaces where competence, integrity, innovation and excellence are recognised and rewarded, while challenging leaders to develop the right people and capabilities for emerging public-sector needs.

Speaking specifically on Ogun State, Gobir acknowledged the state’s development ambitions and encouraged it to pursue a model of transformation that goes beyond infrastructure and technology to focus on building institutions that are responsive, effective and centred on citizens.

He distilled the lecture’s theme into four key imperatives: innovation must change the method; accountability must change the culture; participation must change the relationship between government and citizens; and inclusion must change the architecture of public service.

He added that leadership remains central to achieving all four imperatives, stressing that institutions do not transform themselves—people transform institutions, and leaders determine whether those people are empowered, constrained, inspired or ignored.

The CIPM President concluded by calling for a public service where innovation becomes an institutional habit, accountability becomes a professional ethic, participation becomes consequential and inclusion becomes a design principle.

He said the ultimate measure of public-sector reform should not be the number of policies or projects launched, but the number of lives improved and the extent to which citizens can access government services without unnecessary friction.

“The ultimate measure of institutional reform will not be the number of policies launched. It will be the number of lives improved,” he said.

The engagement reinforces CIPM’s commitment to advancing professional human resource management and supporting stronger, more capable and people-centred institutions across Nigeria.

World.title: Why Air Peace? The Selective Targeting of Nigeria’s Largest Airline Must Stop
World.content:
Fred Chukwuelobe





Why Air Peace? That is the question Nigerians must ask following the decision by aviation industry unions to picket and disrupt the operations of Nigeria’s largest airline in Lagos and Abuja.

This is not the first time Air Peace has found itself at the receiving end of what appears to be disproportionate industrial action. A few years ago, when the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) was engaged in a dispute with the Imo State Government, Air Peace was also picketed despite having nothing to do with the dispute.

So, what is different this time? And why does Air Peace repeatedly appear to become the target?

The unions have advanced two principal reasons for the latest action: the alleged refusal of Air Peace workers to join the unions and an alleged debt owed the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) by all the airlines in respect of the five per cent Ticket Sales Charge (TSC).

On the alleged debt, the Director-General of the NCAA, Captain Chris Najomo, reportedly said the regulator and all the airlines under the Airlines Operators of Nigeria (AON) had reached an agreement for the settlement of the outstanding owed by all the airlines. If such an agreement exists and the airlines are complying with it, why has the matter suddenly become grounds for industrial action against Air Peace?

Records obtained indicate that the airline has paid billions in Ticket Charges last year and several billions this year and is still paying. It also paid several millions in other charges during the period and so far this year. As the country’s largest airline, Air Peace naturally pays more in statutory charges because of its size and operations.

If the dispute is between a regulator and an airline over payment obligations, when did aviation unions become debt-collection agents for the NCAA?

The situation becomes even more curious when union officials are heard telling Air Peace passengers to “go and buy tickets from other airlines” and “leave Air Peace.”

That is not the language of neutral industrial action. It raises the legitimate question of whether something beyond workers’ rights is driving the campaign.

The second justification – that Air Peace workers must join the unions – is even more troubling. Workers have a constitutional right to freedom of association. Union membership should not be imposed on employees against their will.

Air Peace workers say they have enjoyed cordial relations with management for about 12 years and have regularly received salaries, promotions, healthcare benefits, allowances and other entitlements. They cite, among other benefits, travel privileges for themselves and family members.

One of their leaders, Comrade Aminu Suleiman, put the position bluntly: “We can choose to join or not. It’s not by force.”

Trade unions have historically played an important and legitimate role in protecting workers, negotiating better conditions and defending labour rights. I covered organised labour as a labour correspondent during my years in journalism and witnessed both the positive contributions of unions and instances of abuse and mismanagement of union funds.

But the legitimate role of trade unions does not include forcing satisfied workers into membership simply because their numbers would increase union revenue or influence.

That is where the current dispute becomes troubling, and questions need to be asked about the motives of the unions.

Air Peace is one of the biggest employers in Nigeria’s aviation industry. Bringing its workforce into the fold of organised labour would undoubtedly increase union revenue through compulsory deductions from workers’ salaries. That may be the unions’ objective, but it cannot justify coercion or the targeting of the airline.

And if the real issue is union membership, why only Air Peace? Other airlines also have workers who are not members of these unions. Why were their operations not similarly disrupted?

If the issue is the alleged NCAA debt, why should passengers and workers be punished for a financial matter between a regulator and an airline?

Even more disturbing are allegations that some Air Peace workers were physically assaulted during the picketing. If established, such conduct must be condemned unequivocally.

A picket is not a licence for violence. Industrial action is a legitimate instrument of negotiation and pressure. It does not confer on union members the right to assault workers, intimidate passengers or prevent people from exercising their lawful right to work.

The consequences of the action extend far beyond Air Peace. Passengers were stranded. Flights were disrupted. Airports were thrown into confusion. Businesses suffered losses, while families were left scrambling to reorganise travel plans.

These are not abstract statistics. They are real people bearing the cost of an industrial dispute in which they have no stake. Responsible industrial action should minimise unnecessary hardship to the public while putting pressure on the employer or institution concerned if they have genuine reasons to do so and not this contrived grievance.

I witnessed this during a railway workers’ strike in London last April. The strike affected services, but operations were managed in a way that allowed some services to continue. The objective was to exert pressure without unnecessarily paralysing the entire system. Nigeria must develop the same culture of responsible industrial relations. The ability to cause maximum disruption should not be mistaken for the strength of a union. Air Peace is not above the law. If the airline violates any law or regulation, it should face appropriate sanctions through due process. But regulation must be impartial, and enforcement must not become selective.

No airline should receive preferential treatment. Equally, no airline should be selectively targeted.

That is why the government should investigate the circumstances surrounding the latest industrial action, including the allegations of assault, the basis for targeting Air Peace and whether the unions acted within the law.

Most importantly, the aviation unions owe Nigerians an explanation for targeting only Air Peace.

If Air Peace workers did not invite you, if the NCAA has an agreement with the airlines, and if passengers certainly did not invite you, why did you choose to shut down Air Peace?

Who sent you? That question is not an attack on organised labour. It is a legitimate demand for accountability. Nigeria is already battling serious economic challenges. The country cannot afford industrial disputes conducted in a manner that paralyses air transportation, strands passengers and imposes unnecessary losses on businesses and individuals.

If there are genuine grievances against Air Peace, let them be presented, investigated and resolved through dialogue and due process. If there is a genuine dispute over money owed to the NCAA, let the regulator and the airlines resolve it according to the law and whatever agreement they have reached.

But industrial power must never become a tool for coercion, intimidation, selective targeting or the settlement of unrelated scores.

So, the question remains: Why Air Peace? Until the aviation unions provide a convincing answer, Nigerians are entitled to ask whether this action was truly about protecting workers – or whether there is something else behind the campaign against Nigeria’s largest airline.

Chukwuelobe, fnipr, journalist, public affairs commentator, writes from Lagos

World.title: Galatasaray Issue Fresh Warning to Arsenal over Osimhen
World.content:
Galatasaray President, Dursun Özbek has issued a fresh warning to Arsenal over Super Eagles striker Victor Osimhen, insisting the Turkish champions have no intention of selling the Super Eagles striker.

Osimhen’s name has entered discussions between Galatasaray and Arsenal, with the Premier League champions exploring the possibility of signing the Nigerian forward.

According to The Standard UK, the talks between the two clubs initially centred on Arsenal winger Gabriel Martinelli, with Galatasaray submitting a £38.5 million offer for the Brazil international.

Ethan Nwaneri was also discussed, but according to The Telegraph, Osimhen’s availability was raised during negotiations between the clubs.

It remains unclear whether Arsenal sporting director, Andrea Berta initiated the conversation about Osimhen or whether the Nigerian was offered to the Gunners.

Arsenal have maintained a long-standing interest in the 27-year-old and are still searching for another forward before the transfer window closes. However, Galatasaray’s latest position could make any potential move extremely difficult.

Özbek has made it clear that Galatasaray are not interested in losing their star striker, regardless of the size of the offer. Speaking to 343 Digital, the Galatasaray president delivered a firm message about Osimhen’s future.

“I will not sell Osimhen no matter how much money it is,” the 77-year-old said in quotes revealed by Haber Sariki Mirzi.

The statement comes after Galatasaray rejected a €130 million (£111m) offer from Saudi Pro League club Al Hilal for the Nigerian striker.

The decision underlines just how important Osimhen has become to the Turkish champions following his impressive spell in Istanbul.

The Nigerian joined Galatasaray permanently after his initial loan spell and has continued to establish himself as the club’s most important attacking player.

Arsenal’s interest in Osimhen comes as Mikel Arteta looks to add another attacking option to his squad. The Gunners manager admitted after Arsenal’s final pre-season game against Como that the club remains active in the transfer market, although he warned that finding the right player would not be straightforward.

“I think for the margins to improve, there are very few players in the market that are available to do that and bring that to the club.”

“But again, we are actively looking to improve that and we’re going to try.”

Osimhen would offer Arsenal a different profile in attack, combining explosive pace, physical strength, aerial ability and an aggressive approach to pressing, but with Galatasaray refusing to consider a sale, Arsenal may have to look elsewhere unless the Turkish club’s position changes.

World.title: Herbert Wigwe @ 60: A Legacy of Banking, Service, Nation-building
World.content:
Omolabake Fasogbon





Dr. Herbert Onyewumbu Wigwe, the late banker, entrepreneur and philanthropist, would have turned 60 today, leaving behind a legacy that continues to influence banking, education, healthcare and youth development in Nigeria and beyond.

Wigwe, who rose to become one of Africa’s leading financial executives, was widely known for his role in the transformation and expansion of Access Bank. But beyond banking, he devoted considerable attention and resources to building institutions, supporting young people and creating opportunities for disadvantaged communities.

To his family, friends and associates, he was also a mentor and a firm believer in the ability of people to achieve more when given the right opportunities.

As Co-Founder and Group Chief Executive Officer of Access Bank and later Access Holdings, Wigwe played a major role in the growth of the financial institution from a Nigerian bank into a financial services group with operations across several countries. His ambition was not simply to build a successful Nigerian bank, but to develop an African institution capable of competing with leading financial organisations around the world.

His influence also extended beyond Access Bank. As Chairman of the Bankers’ Committee, Wigwe participated in discussions on major issues affecting Nigeria’s banking industry and economy. He worked with government officials, regulators and other business leaders, believing that the private sector had a responsibility to contribute to national development and help find solutions to the country’s social and economic challenges.

Wigwe’s belief that business success should make a difference in society was reflected in the establishment of The HOW Foundation in 2016.

Through the Foundation, he supported programmes in education, healthcare, mentorship and youth development. Its interventions included educational support for disadvantaged children, programmes in Makoko and for Almajiri children, medical scholarships and specialist oncology training. The Foundation also supported the adoption and rehabilitation of 25 primary healthcare centres in Rivers State.

Perhaps one of Wigwe’s most ambitious projects was Wigwe University, which reflected his strong belief in the power of education to transform Africa. He envisioned a university that would produce confident, entrepreneurial and globally competitive young Africans capable of creating jobs, solving problems and building institutions.

The university received its operating licence in 2023 and, despite Wigwe’s death before it fully opened, went ahead to welcome its first students and continue the vision of its founder.

His commitment to developing a new generation of African leaders also continues through initiatives such as the Fearless Leadership Series and the Wigwe Venture Lab. Wigwe encouraged young Nigerians to think boldly, challenge convention, take responsibility and create solutions. He believed leadership was not simply about occupying an important position, but about making a positive impact on people and society.

Wigwe died in February 2024 while many of his plans were still unfolding, but the institutions he helped to build and the people he supported continue to carry his vision. As family members, friends, colleagues and associates mark what would have been his 60th birthday, his story remains one of ambition, institution-building, philanthropy and service.

His legacy is increasingly being measured not only by what he achieved during his lifetime but also by the institutions he created, the opportunities he provided and the people he inspired.

World.title: Globacom at 23: The Indigenous Imagination That Rewired Nigeria’s Digital Destiny
World.content:
Louis Ibe





There are companies that participate in history, and there are companies that alter its trajectory. At 23, Globacom belongs unmistakably to the latter category. Founded in August 2003 through the vision of Dr Mike Adenuga Jr., Globacom was never merely the entry of another telecommunications operator. It represented something more consequential: the emergence of an indigenous proposition that a Nigerian enterprise could think at global scale, build to international standards, and remain deeply aligned with the aspirations, sensibilities, and realities of its people.

Over time, that proposition has acquired an almost philosophical resonance. Globacom’s journey has been one of enterprise, infrastructure, technology, and cultural imagination. Beneath these visible dimensions lies a more enduring idea: that Nigeria need not remain a passive observer of technological progress. It could be a participant, a builder, and, in certain instances, an architect of the future it seeks to inhabit. In an industry shaped by successive waves of innovation, investment, and competition, Globacom has established a durable institutional presence whose significance extends beyond the mechanics of telecommunications.

Some enterprises are built around market opportunity; others evolve into expressions of deeper conviction. Globacom’s story belongs to the latter tradition. Its defining question has never been merely how to provide connectivity, but what connectivity could enable for Nigeria. That distinction has shaped its technological decisions, consumer philosophy, and its nuanced understanding of the cultural environment in which a telecommunications brand must operate.

That conviction was evident from the outset. Globacom’s introduction of per-second billing reshaped both the economics and psychology of mobile communication in Nigeria, challenging long-standing assumptions about consumer pricing. In a market where the cost of communication had previously constrained access, the innovation made mobile telephony more transparent, accessible, and consumer-centric.

The company subsequently advanced through successive technological generations—from 2.5G at launch to 3G Plus and 4G LTE—reflecting an institutional disposition unwilling to treat technological limitation as destiny. The underlying message was clear: Nigeria need not wait for the future to be imported.

Then came Glo-1. In 2010, Globacom deployed a 9,800-kilometre fibre-optic submarine cable beneath the Atlantic, linking Nigeria and West Africa to Europe. Its significance extended beyond engineering achievement. It was symbolism expressed in fibre and steel—a tangible articulation of a national possibility.

Nigeria would not only consume global digital infrastructure; a Nigerian enterprise could actively participate in building it. Executed without foreign equity or consortium partners, the project remains one of the most compelling demonstrations of indigenous technological ambition in the country’s corporate history. Beneath the ocean, fibre transmitted data; above it, the project transmitted belief in national capability.

Yet Globacom’s indigenous imagination has never been confined to technology alone. From an early stage, it recognised that telecommunications brands do not exist solely in balance sheets, network architecture, or infrastructure assets. They also exist in culture. Musicians, actors, sports figures, and other national icons became more than brand ambassadors; they became channels through which the brand entered the emotional and cultural consciousness of Nigerians. In doing so, Globacom demonstrated a critical understanding of its market: technology is not merely consumed; it is interpreted through culture, memory, aspiration, and identity.

Its engagement with African football, the Super Eagles, the Nigeria Football Federation, domestic leagues, and the Glo Soccer Academy extended this philosophy into sport. Its support for cultural institutions and festivals—including Ojude Oba, Ofala, and Lisabi—further reflected a broader understanding of connectivity. To connect a people is not only to enable communication between devices; it is to connect generations to memory, communities to identity, creativity to opportunity, and tradition to the future.

The widely celebrated $1 million reward to the victorious Super Eagles following their 2013 Africa Cup of Nations triumph belonged to the same continuum. It was corporate patronage, but also an expression of emotional citizenship: an acknowledgment that there are moments when national spirit converges around shared achievement, and that responsible enterprise can participate meaningfully in such moments.

This helps explain why describing Globacom simply as “the Nigerian network” is both accurate and incomplete. It is accurate because the company emerged from an indigenous conception of the telecommunications opportunity and has consistently interpreted the Nigerian market from within.

It is incomplete because its ambition has never been limited to national identity alone. Rather, it has sought to demonstrate that Nigerian origin can coexist with technological sophistication, international scale, continental relevance, and cultural confidence.

Twenty-three years on, that proposition remains instructive. Globacom’s significance cannot be fully captured through subscriber figures, financial performance, infrastructure inventories, or corporate milestones. These are valid indicators of enterprise, but they do not exhaust its historical meaning. Its deeper contribution lies in expanding the psychological boundaries of Nigerian enterprise: challenging the assumption that innovation must arrive with a foreign accent, and demonstrating that indigenous capability can operate within domains once reserved for multinational capital and imported expertise.

The story is also inseparable from the stature of its founder, Dr Mike Adenuga Jr., GCON, whose role in Nigeria’s contemporary economic history has been recognised with distinction. In Nigeria, he holds the Grand Commander of the Order of the Niger (GCON), one of the nation’s highest honours. Internationally, he has been conferred the Commander of the Legion of Honour by France, and the Companion of the Star of Ghana by Ghana. These recognitions stand in contrast to his notably private and understated public persona: while the honours are public, the individual remains reserved, yet the institutional footprint of his enterprise philosophy is widely evident.

Ultimately, Globacom’s most enduring innovation may not be per-second billing, fibre infrastructure, bandwidth capacity, spectrum allocation, or mobile technology itself. It may be the idea embodied in its trajectory: that excellence does not require external validation; that indigenous enterprise need not be constrained by limited ambition; that technological sophistication can coexist with cultural authenticity; and that technology can carry culture as effectively as it carries data.

There is, perhaps, a deeper metaphor at work. The telecommunications network was designed to connect voices, but Globacom’s broader historical significance has been to connect possibility with confidence. It entered a Nigeria still defining the contours of its digital future and helped expand those contours—carefully, deliberately, and irreversibly. Through infrastructure as well as imagination, it demonstrated that the future is not always a distant destination. It can be conceived, engineered, connected, and deliberately brought into being.

Twenty-three years after its inception, Globacom stands as more than a participant in Nigeria’s digital transformation. It is one of the institutions through which that transformation acquired an indigenous vocabulary, a cultural depth, and a renewed sense of self-belief. Its enduring legacy may ultimately be this: the reminder that Nigeria is not merely a consumer of the future. With imagination, discipline, and institutional resolve, it can help build it—and give it a distinctly Nigerian voice.

Ibe is a Reputation Management Strategist and PR Specialist

World.title: Oghenegaren Osievwo-Thompson Blade of Destiny: How 17-Year-Old Prodigy Rewrote Nigeria’s Sporting History
World.content:
On August 9, 2026, 17-year-old Oghenegaren Osievwo-Thompson made history by winning Nigeria’s first-ever gold medal in an international fencing tournament, triumphing in the U-23 men’s epee event at the 2026 Commonwealth Fencing Championships in Lagos. Competing for Nigeria for the first time, the former England fencer finished the tournament completely unbeaten, signaling a promising new era for the sport in the country, writes Kunle Adewale

Oghenegaren Esiovwa-Thompson made history by winning Nigeria’s first-ever international fencing gold medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Fencing Championships. On Sunday, August 9, 2026, the 17-year-old phenomenon dominated the men’s U-23 epee division at Rugby School Nigeria in Atlantic City, Lagos. In his debut tournament after switching athletic allegiance from England, the teenager dismantled the international field to spark nationwide celebration and fundamentally alter the trajectory of Nigerian fencing.

A Historic Homecoming in Lagos

The atmosphere inside the sports hall at Rugby School Nigeria was electric. Standing as Nigeria’s sole representative at the tournament, Esiovwa-Thompson carried the hopes of a nation unfamiliar with fencing podiums. Fencing has long been perceived as an elite, Eurocentric sport, making a Nigerian breakthrough on the Commonwealth stage a distant dream.

By the end of the evening, that perception was shattered. The final scoreline read a staggering 15–5. Esiovwa-Thompson had not just defeated the reigning Asian champion, Lokesh Vemani of India; he had delivered a tactical masterclass.

When the final point landed, the arena erupted into a wall of sound. Amid the roaring fans stood Esiovwa-Thompson’s grandparents, watching their grandson wave the green and white flag.

“I didn’t realise I was the first Nigerian to win gold at the Commonwealth Championships until just before the final,” Esiovwa-Thompson admitted, visibly moved by the gravity of his achievement. “Doing this in front of my grandparents, in front of the fans—it’s overwhelming. Everything is just coming to me now, and I’m proud to represent my country.”

Path of Total Dominance

While the final score suggested an easy victory, Esiovwa-Thompson’s gold medal was forged through a gruelling, flawless campaign. He drew a target on his back early in the tournament during the preliminary pool stages.

Pool Stages and Early Rounds

Placed in Pool 4, the Nigerian teenager refused to drop a single bout. He swept through the group completely unbeaten, earning the top seed and a crucial bye into the knockout rounds.

In the Round of 16, he faced South Africa’s resilient Karabo Mathobela. Showing a mature understanding of distance and timing, Esiovwa-Thompson cruised to a 15–7 victory.

The Indian Gauntlet

What followed was an unprecedented sporting narrative: a lone Nigerian teenager taking on the powerhouse fencing contingent from India.

In the quarterfinal, Esiovwa-Thompson faced India’s Shivaansh Kapoor. In a display of defensive steel and lightning-fast counter-attacks, the Nigerian conceded only two points, winning 15–2.

In the semifinal, the true test came against India’s Ashwini Shaurya. Shaurya pushed the pace, testing the 17-year-old’s composure. Backed by a partisan Lagos crowd, Esiovwa-Thompson adjusted his strategy, finding the target in tight quarters to edge out an intense 15–11 victory.

In the final against top-seeded Lokesh Vemani, Esiovwa-Thompson left no room for doubt. He jumped to an early lead, using his reach and exceptional point control to keep Vemani off-balance, closing out the historic 15–5 win. India’s Godwin Natarajan and Ashwini Shaurya took home the bronze medals.

Anatomy of an Allegiance Switch

Esiovwa-Thompson’s journey to the top of the podium did not begin in Lagos, but rather in the highly competitive British fencing circuits. Before donning the Nigerian green, he was one of England’s brightest prospects.

He tasted international success early, winning the U-13 boys’ epee gold at the prestigious 2022 Wratislavia Challenge. He followed that with a bronze medal in the cadet men’s epee team event in Naples while representing England.

Yet, despite his success within the British system, a deeper calling remained. The decision to switch athletic allegiance from England to Nigeria at such a young age was a calculated risk driven by a singular focus.

“There’s something in me that has always longed to fence for Nigeria,” Esiovwa-Thompson explained. “Even though I grew up in England and won several medals there, I knew representing Nigeria would be the right path to fulfil my Olympic dream.”

Transitioning into a tournament as a country’s sole representative brings immense psychological pressure. However, Esiovwa-Thompson credits his lifelong dedication to the weapon for his unshakable mental focus. “I’ve been fencing longer than I haven’t been fencing,” he remarked. “Because I’ve been fencing all my life, I knew what to do. I knew how to stay calm, stay relaxed, and take every match one at a time.”

Catalyst for Nigerian Fencing

The broader Commonwealth Fencing Championships saw other powerhouses find success. England’s Oliver Strange claimed the tournament’s first gold by defeating India’s Manoj Patil in the men’s U-23 foil final, while India’s Singh Sanasam and England’s Thomas James secured bronze.

Yet, no story captured the imagination of the public like Esiovwa-Thompson’s. Initially flying under the radar, his dominant pool performance quickly made him the star attraction of the tournament. The home crowd responded by turning Rugby School Nigeria into a fortress.

“It was the first time I experienced that kind of support,” the champion recalled. “The cheers from the fans hit me every time I stepped onto the stage. Their support was key to my victory.”

For the Nigerian Fencing Federation, this gold medal is a proof of concept. It demonstrates that with the right talent pipeline, Nigerian athletes can challenge the traditional global hierarchy in combat sports. Esiovwa-Thompson’s triumph provides a blueprint for dual-heritage athletes looking to represent their ancestral home.

Road to Olympic Games

At just 17 years old, Esiovwa-Thompson has achieved something no Nigerian before him has done: winning gold at an international fencing event. But for the teenage prodigy, the Commonwealth crown is simply a stepping stone.

“A lot of training, dedication, sweat, and tears went into this,” he reflected. “I’m just happy I won in front of Nigerians, in front of my family.”

With his technical foundation established in Europe and his heart firmly rooted in Nigeria, Esiovwa-Thompson’s ultimate target remains the Olympic Games. If his dominant performance in Lagos is any indication, the international fencing community has been put on notice. The young epeeist has proven he possesses the composure, pedigree, and passion to carry the Nigerian flag all the way to the world’s biggest sporting stage.

World.title: History Beckons as Cameroon, Malawi Clash
World.content:
Cameroon and Malawi will battle in the final of the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations tomorrow as both teams close in on a first major title.

The 2026 WAFCON is set for a thrilling conclusion as Cameroon and Malawi prepare to face off in the final tomorrow.

With a new champion guaranteed to be crowned, both nations are vying for their first-ever major title. Cameroon secured their place in the decider after a tense penalty shootout victory against hosts Morocco, following a goalless 120 minutes.

Meanwhile, Malawi continued their dream run by defeating Algeria 3-1 to reach their first-ever final. Malawi, making their tournament debut, have been the surprise package of the competition.

They announced their arrival by stunning ten-time champions Nigeria with a 3-2 victory in their opening match, a result that propelled them to the top of their group. In contrast, Cameroon are no strangers to the latter stages of WAFCON.

The Indomitable Lionesses’ journey to the final has been remarkable. They initially failed to qualify for what was a 12-team tournament.

However, the expansion to 16 teams offered them a second chance, which they have seized with both hands to stand on the verge of a historic triumph.

Malawi’s sensational run has been powered by the formidable sibling duo of Tabitha and Temwa Chawinga. Both were instrumental in the semi-final win over Algeria, with Tabitha scoring a brace. Their attacking prowess has made them two of the tournament’s standout performers.

Temwa Chawinga, known for her clinical finishing, currently leads the Golden Boot race with five goals and two assists.

If Malawi are to complete their fairytale and lift the trophy on their debut, the Chawinga sisters will undoubtedly be at the heart of the action.

While Malawi’s attack has grabbed the headlines, Cameroon’s success has been built on a rock-solid defence, marshalled by 22-year-old goalkeeper Michaely Bihina.

The Benfica shot-stopper was heroic in the 1-0 quarter-final victory over Nigeria, making nine crucial saves. She followed that with another clean sheet against Morocco.

Bihina became the star of the semi-final, saving an extra-time penalty before denying three more spot-kicks in the decisive shootout to send her team to the final. Sunday’s showdown will be a classic clash of styles, pitting a potent attack against a resolute defence to determine who will be crowned champions of Africa.Morocco and Algeria will contest the third-place play-off today.

World.title: More than A Charity as Arsenal, Man City Set to Face Off on DStv, GOtv
World.content:
The new football season begins with an early dose of rivalry on Sunday when Arsenal and Manchester City meet in the Community Shield, with both sides eager to begin the campaign with silverware and gain an early psychological advantage.

The game, which kicks off on Sunday at 3 pm, will be available live to DStv Yanga and GOtv Jolli subscribers via SuperSport Premier League (DStv channel 203) and SuperSport Premier League Africa (GOtv channel 65)

The traditional season curtain-raiser carries added intrigue this year, given the fierce battle between the two clubs last season. Arsenal eventually ended a 22-year wait to win the Premier League title, but City ran Mikel Arteta’s side close, remaining in contention deep into the campaign before finishing four points behind the champions.

Recent encounters have also favoured City. Pep Guardiola’s side won the most recent Premier League meeting 2-1 at the Etihad in April and followed that with a 2-0 victory over Arsenal in the Carabao Cup final at Wembley in March. The Community Shield, therefore, gives Arsenal an immediate opportunity to turn the tables, while City will be looking to reinforce their recent dominance in this fixture.

For City, however, this will be a new era. With Guardiola gone, Enzo Maresca takes charge for his first competitive match as manager. Maresca inherits a squad with considerable quality but has also strengthened it in the summer as he begins the task of putting his own stamp on the team. A victory over Arsenal would provide an ideal launchpad for his reign and an early indication that City remain serious contenders on all fronts.

Arsenal will also have a major new addition to showcase, with Brazilian midfielder Bruno Guimaraes arriving from Newcastle United in a £75 million deal.

The highly rated midfielder is expected to bring further quality, energy and steel to Arteta’s midfield, and supporters will be keen to see him make his competitive debut in Arsenal colours.

Beyond the silverware at stake, the Community Shield offers both managers an opportunity to assess their preparations, new signings and tactical adjustments before the Premier League campaign begins in earnest. It is also the first competitive glimpse of players who could play decisive roles in the months ahead.

For Arsenal, the match represents a chance to start their title defence by lifting another trophy and put their recent defeats by City behind them. For Maresca and City, it is an opportunity to begin a new chapter with a statement victory against the champions.

With two of England’s leading clubs facing each other so early in the season, the Community Shield promises considerably more than a ceremonial curtain-raiser. It is a renewal of a rivalry that defined much of last season and an intriguing first indication of how another battle for Premier League supremacy might unfold.

World.title: … S’Eagles Scores Brace, but Gala  Stumble  in Super Lig Opener
World.content:
​Super Eagles striker, Victor Osimhen scored a brace for Galatasaray as they were held to a 2-2 draw by Çorum in their opening match of the Süper Lig season.

​Süper Lig champions, Galatasaray kicked off their 2026/2027 campaign with a fixture against newly promoted Çorum at Rams Park. Going into the match, Cimbom were the overwhelming favorites due to their status as reigning champions and superior squad quality.

​As expected, they dominated the early proceedings, bossing the midfield. Osimhen made his presence felt early on, lurking inside the box and waiting for opportunities to pounce.

​Abdulkerim Bardakcı had the first real opportunity of the game, connecting with a corner kick cross, but he failed to direct his header on target.

​Osimhen earned his first genuine chance in the 15th minute, outjumping his marker to power a header toward goal. However, his effort drifted just a whisker wide.

​The top Nigerian marksman looked sharp all night, constantly calling for the ball. Although he lacked adequate service and had to work hard for scraps, he managed a shot from the edge of the box in the 25th minute, which was comfortably saved by the goalkeeper.

​Ultimately, the first half ended goalless, setting the stage for a dramatic second half.

World.title: The City of Cape Town wants to give you R10 000 to report crime
World.content:
See something, say something. Image: Pexels / Mary Alson

In its crime-fighting efforts, the City of Cape Town (CoCT) distributed notices to residents asking for their help.

The call?

R10 000 for reporting crime that leads to an operational result.



Cape Town Continues its Crime-Fighting Efforts

During an early-morning roadblock on 14 August 2026, the City of Cape Town metro police handed out notices to residents asking for their help.

The notice asks residents to “say something” and “get rewarded.”

In it, the City suggests residents could “earn up to R10 000” if what they report “leads to an arrest, impoundment or confiscation.”



The incidents residents can report include:

Illegal firearms

Dumping and littering

Drug dealing

Stolen property

Metal and cable theft

Vandalism

Gangsterism

To report these crimes, residents can call the city any time, day or night.

They can contact the City on 0800 11 00 77. The line is available 7 days a week, 24 hours a day.



Residents can also use the Citizen Safety App to report crime. The app is available on Android and iOS.

The app is available for what the city describes as “non-life-threatening incidents.”

These include noise complaints, suspicious activity, by-law violations, and illegal dumping.



When filing a report, the app will automatically capture residents’ GPS to hasten response times.

Residents can participate anonymously

According to the notice, you can make a report anonymously, and your identity will be protected.

However, the city highlighted it will only pay a reward when “information leads to an operational result.”



These include arrests, recovering stolen goods, and confiscating contraband or illegal firearms.

Residents also have to be aware that not every tip will net them a big payday even if action is taken.

The notice stresses that it’s possible to “Earn up to R10 000.” However, it doesn’t stipulate the minimum reward a resident could earn from a tip.



Crime in Cape Town

This call to action comes as 21 of the city’s 62 precincts have recorded an increase in crime.

According to data from the South African Police Service (SAPS), the precincts where crime has risen sharply include Makhaza. There’s been an 18.9% increase in crime in the suburb.

Ravensmead follows with a 12.3% increase in crime.



Sea Point on the Atlantic Seaboard and Bishop Lavis on the Cape Flats tie for third place, with crime rising 11.1% in these suburbs year-on-year.

It’s not all bad news. The city’s efforts appear to be making some strides. Fewer crimes were reported in 28 of the 62 precincts.

Top 10 CoCT Suburbs Where Crime Increased

Suburb Increase (%) Makhaza 18.9% Ravensmead 12.3% Sea Point 11.1% Bishop Lavis 11.1% Kensington 10.9% Lwandle 10% Bothasig 9.9% Lingelethu-West 9.7% Atlantis 9.6% Table View 9.2%

During these challenging economic times, this initiative may increase reporting and encourage active citizenship.

World.title: St Stithians teen couple: When does memorial, funeral take place?
World.content:
It’s been over 10 days since the deaths of St Stithians teen couple Cameron Waldeck-Cooks and Ethan Coetzee in an alleged murder-suicide, and South Africans are no closer to knowing the truth about what happened. There has also been no official word on funeral or memorial services that will take place

ST STITHIANS TEEN MURDER-SUICIDE LATEST

This week, Mpumalanga Police spokesperson Colonel Mavela Masondo confirmed that they would not divulge any new information to the public relating to the St Stithians teens’ alleged murder-suicide due to an ongoing investigation.

Cameron Waldeck-Cooks – a Grade 11 learner at the Johannesburg private school – and Ethan Coetzee, a 2025 matriculant, were found dead on the morning on Monday, 3 August at the Waterval self-catering lodge in Mumpalanga.



The bubbly blonde had been invited to participate in a multi-day hike, which she hoped would help her towards her goal of the Gold level of The President’s Award for Youth Empowerment.

According to a statement by Etha’s family, the teen couple appeared happy the night before their death. Their bodies were discovered by Ethan’s father, Graham Coetzee.

Police initially investigated the deaths as an inquest and initially suspected that no foul play was involved.

However, post-mortem findings changed the direction of the investigation regarding to the St Stithians teens.

According to preliminary findings as well as the opinion of an independent forensic pathologist involved, Cameron Waldeck-Cooks died from strangulation/suffocation.

Ethan’s death is believed to be a suicide.



Police have subsequently opened a murder case in connection with Cameron’s death.

No person has been charged with Cameron’s murder, and police have not publicly announced that Ethan was legally determined to be her killer. The investigation continues.

CAMERON WALDECK-COOKS, ETHAN COETZEE: WHEN DOES FUNERAL, MEMORIAL TAKE PLACE?

In a statement to the public, the parents of Cameron Waldeck-Cooks shared that a memorial service would take place during the month of August. A date has yet to be made public.

It’s unclear if she, or Ethan Coetzee, has been laid to rest via a funeral service.

St Stithians, the President’s Award for Youth Empowerment and anti-gender-based violence activists, Women For Change, have paid tribute to Cameron.

A group of cyclists who took part in the Trans Baviaans Race dedicated their mountain biking race to Cameron. The teen’s dad, Derrick Cooks, was moved by the gesture, sharing: “What you and the team did for Cam is incredibly special….knowing you carried her with you means everything. Cam would have absolutely loved this”.

World.title: Eskom announces 13-hour power outage in Gauteng on Sunday
World.content:
Eskom says the interruption forms part of essential maintenance on distribution power lines in the Winterveld area. The power utility explained that the work is necessary to maintain network reliability and prevent future unplanned outages. Eskom apologised in advance for the inconvenience the maintenance would cause to affected customers and thanked residents for their cooperation during the works.

The outage will run from 8:00 to 21:00 on Sunday, 16 August, affecting customers in Blocks CV, EW and N, as well as Central City, Central House, Kwiksave and Shoprite in Block CV. Eskom has urged all affected customers to treat electrical appliances and wiring as live at all times during the interruption, warning that power could be restored without notice before the announced end time. The utility also cautioned that the maintenance schedule could be disrupted by circumstances beyond its control, meaning the outage may not proceed exactly as communicated.

Eskom has encouraged customers to use several official channels to stay informed or report supply-related problems. These include the “MyEskom Customer” self-help app, WhatsApp on 0860037566, and the USSD code *120*37566#. Customers can also access the Alfred chatbot through Eskom’s website or check billing queries online through the Eskom customer portal on weekdays between 8:00 and 16:00. For urgent supply-related enquiries, Eskom’s contact centre remains available 24 hours a day on 08600 37566.



The planned maintenance forms part of Eskom’s broader efforts across the Gauteng cluster to maintain ageing infrastructure and reduce the frequency of unplanned outages, which have repeatedly disrupted households and businesses in the region. While scheduled interruptions cause short-term inconvenience, Eskom maintains that this kind of preventative work is critical to improving long-term supply stability.

Warning for residents

Residents in the affected areas are advised to plan ahead, particularly for activities reliant on electricity, and to keep devices charged ahead of the outage window. Businesses operating in Block CV, including retailers such as Kwiksave and Shoprite, may also need to make contingency arrangements for the duration of the interruption.

Eskom has reiterated that safety remains a top priority during all maintenance work and has asked communities to report any downed lines or electrical hazards immediately through its emergency channels rather than attempting to intervene themselves

World.title: Chiefs 0-2 Sundowns – Ex-Pirates and Amakhosi stars make bold prediction
World.content:
Former Kaizer Chiefs and Orlando Pirates stars Junior Khanye and Benedict “Tso” Vilakazi have predicted Amakhosi to suffer defeat against Mamelodi Sundowns this weekend.

Chiefs host Masandawana at FNB Stadium on Saturday in a highly anticipated Betway Premiership clash.

The Glamour Boys currently sit at the top of the league standings after winning their opening two matches of the season. However, Khanye remains unconvinced by what he has seen from his former club.



Speaking on iDiski TV, the former Chiefs midfielder questioned whether new head coach Fernando Da Cruz is effectively communicating his instructions to the players.

“I don’t think there’s coordination between the players and the coach. He needs an interpreter to translate. There are certain instructions that have to be given immediately,” Khanye said.

“The team is not stable. You see Thabo Moloisane getting benched by Zitha Kwinika. The combination of Kwinika and Miguel Inacio has not been tested. Their midfield is very static, there’s no movement.”

Sundowns tipped to beat Chiefs

Khanye was also critical of Sundowns despite their impressive squad and quality, suggesting that Miguel Cardoso’s tactical experiments have affected their performances.

“Since winning the star, his head has gotten bigger. He can’t be experimenting and making six changes,” he said.

Despite his criticism of both teams, Khanye believes Sundowns have enough quality to overcome Chiefs.



“In terms of quality, Sundowns are ahead. It might be 2-0 or 2-1, but Sundowns will win,” he added.

Vilakazi, meanwhile, believes Chiefs will need to adopt a more defensive approach if they are to stand any chance of taking points from the defending champions.

The former Pirates captain urged Da Cruz to seek advice from former Chiefs coaches who have successfully frustrated Sundowns in previous meetings.

“Fernando Da Cruz needs to call ex-Kaizer Chiefs coaches and ask them about the tactics they used to draw with Sundowns in the last game, in terms of their physicality and low block,” Vilakazi said.

He believes Chiefs must be physical and disciplined on defence, but ultimately backed Sundowns to claim victory.

Vilakazi predicted a 2-0 win for Masandawana.

World.title: Constitutional Court sets aside Shell offshore exploration
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Constitutional Court on Friday ruled in favour of coastal communities and environmental groups, overturning oil and gas exploration rights that were granted to energy giant Shell more than a decade ago.

The landmark ruling ended a years-long battle over Shell's plans to conduct offshore seismic surveys along South Africa's Wild Coast.

The Constitutional Court overturned the Appeals Court ruling that gave the British oil heavyweight another chance to renew its permit.

It agreed with a lower court's 2022 judgement that the exploration authorisation granted by South Africa's government in 2014 was unlawful.

The Apex Court said in a statement that "any other remedy would allow financial investment to outweigh grave Constitutional violations".

It added that such an outcome would signal that "the rights of affected parties are subordinate to commercial interests".

Shell had planned to map more than 6,000 square kilometres off the Indian Ocean coast, which boasts pristine beaches and rich waters hosting exquisite marine life.

The seismic survey is conducted by bouncing sonic waves off the sea floor and using the reflection to build up a 3D image.
