World.title: It is time we look past the binary of ‘good’ and ‘bad’ men
World.content:
During the #MeToo movement in India, around 2018, there were few articles in the press written by Indian men that engaged seriously with what women were saying about sexual violence and with the social conditions that allow it to persist. But instead of a failure of individual men to support women, the gap reflected a difficulty in thinking about gender-based violence as something produced by individual acts as well as by social relationships and assumptions about masculinity.

By and large, men’s responses then, as now, following the Bombay High Court’s commendable decision to reverse Tarun Tejpal’s acquittal, have instinctively been to become defensive or huddle together rather than open up, meet women on their terms, and think through and talk about sexual violence.

What we can say

On August 11, a senior Supreme Court advocate argued in The Tribune that because criminal law can punish only conduct that satisfies the legal requirements of an existing offence, we should suspend judgment on the Tejpal case and wait for the decision of the Supreme Court, where Mr. Tejpal has appealed. A court cannot convict someone for conduct that does not constitute an offence under the law — and due process and the presumption of innocence are legitimate subjects of discussion. However, it does not follow that the only appropriate response outside the courtroom, as the advocate says, is to say “we do not know”. We can still distinguish between what a criminal court is legally entitled to conclude and what the social dimensions of a case allows society to conclude.

In 2022, Andrea Waling, honorary adjunct at the Australian Research Centre in Sex, Health and Society, Melbourne, reported in a paper in the Journal of Men’s Studies “five key framings” in #MeToo coverage based on 163 media reports: “men are victims of masculinity requiring intervention, men are positioned as inherently ‘good’ or ‘bad’, boys and men are lost and need to be found, men are performative in their ‘awakenings’, and men’s take up of protector or allyship roles may in fact be attempts to be false heroes”.

“The findings of this work note several tensions and contradictions that highlight an overall lack of coherency and agreement regarding men’s engagements with, and roles in, the #MeToo movement,” she added.

Misleading distinction

The fact is, men saying “I support women” is not the same as men asking uncomfortable questions about masculinity, desire, entitlement, friendship, professional hierarchies, male conversations, complicity, and the ways ordinary men may participate in cultures that make sexual violence possible without themselves being predators per se. This is also the territory the #MeToo movement opened up in India but which men have seemed the least willing to enter. In an article in The Indian Express in 2018, Rimjhim Jain wrote that men were the “missing piece” of India’s #MeToo movement and that their silence has allowed the problem to continue to be framed as something women themselves have to resolve. That has not changed.

Men have remarkably little practice talking about sexual violence as a male problem. Instead, there is copious male discourse about false accusations, due process, the presumption of innocence, men being afraid to interact with women, and so on. Laws also reflect the society that makes them and criminal cases cannot encompass conduct the law already does not criminalise. However, none of this means other questions are illegitimate, or even less important. In particular, men still need to ask what it is about the specific social organisation of relations between men and women that produces the situations the law eventually confronts.

That in turn requires us to move beyond the misleading distinction between “men like us” and “other men” and to recognise that sexual violence is not the preserve of ‘monsters’. It can also emerge from ordinary assumptions about, say, flirting, persistence, seniority, alcohol, women’s accommodation of male behaviour, and men being disinclined to intervene when another man crosses a line. This is also why a group response by men can become a form of mutual psychological protection: “Let us establish that we are not all monsters,” they seem to say, “before we discuss what the group itself has to examine”.

Sexual violence cannot be understood using abstract political analysis alone. Instead, it demands attention to intimate behaviour. Put another way, it is not enough to identify The System as being patriarchal; at some point you have to ask how you should behave. How the men around you behave. What you have laughed at. What you have ignored. And whom you have believed — or not. A criminal trial has to determine whether particular conduct satisfies a particular legal standard but society can, and should, also ask what kinds of behaviour it ought to have learned to recognise as unacceptable before they reached the threshold of criminal proceedings.

Original insight

Fixating on the intellectual objects on the basis of which the High Court reversed the lower court’s decision in the Tejpal case, such as evidence, testimonies, criminal laws, standards of proof, judicial reasoning, and so on, also allows men a way to avoid confronting the larger question #MeToo posed. That is: what forms of sexual coercion, intimidation, and entitlement exist in the gap between behaviour that is socially acceptable and conduct that a criminal court can recognise and punish? As at the height of the #MeToo years, this question remains relevant, and in India still barely charted.

In fact, that the legal system reached different conclusions at different times validates #MeToo’s original insight, that there is a distinction between what a criminal court can establish in an individual case and what a society needs to learn to identify and change.

Women have exercised much of the intellectual labour of making this subject discussable whereas men have often treated it as something to consume rather than participate in. Today there are also sophisticated feminist analyses of consent, coercion, power, institutional complicity, testimonial injustice, workplace hierarchy, etc. One would like to see a corresponding body of male self-reflection asking what it would mean for men to understand themselves — ourselves — differently.

The author thanks Srividya Tadepalli for her feedback.

mukunth.v@thehindu.co.in

World.title: The day Hyderabad celebrated two Independence Days on August 15, 1947
World.content:
“Sheher khamosh tha. Sab jagah khamoshi thi (the city was silent. There was silence everywhere),” recalls Oudesh Rani Bawa, who remembers being a six-year-old and standing on the street in Gowlipura as residents gathered to hear the day’s developments on the GEC Radio. Hours earlier, in a pre-dawn swoop at 3 a.m. on August 15, 1947, Congress workers Krishnacharya Joshi, Dr G.S. Melkote and Ramananda Tirtha were picked up from Narayanguda and shifted to the Central Jail in Musheerabad.

Also read | Independence Day 2026 updates

Between the silence and the crackdown, the whiff of freedom and Independence was very much in the air on the day India became free, but Hyderabad did not. Hyderabad witnessed two different Independence Days that day. The calm also belied the unfolding reality, as an exodus of Hindus began amid growing fears over the Razakar menace spreading across rural areas.

“The party’s [Communist Party] decision was to hoist the flag wherever there were party people. I raised the flag in Goshapet High School in Dhoolpet, and it was very tense at that time. Women went from place to place shouting slogans about Bharat and throwing flowers as if it was a festival. Young boys also joined, shouting jai, jai…” recounts Brij Rani Gour in her memoir. Gour, the sister-in-law of Oudesh Rani Bawa, was picked along with Yashoda Bai for hoisting the flag at the school.

They were heeding a call by Congress leader Ramananda Tirtha, who had appealed to people to unfurl the flag wherever they could. “Observe Independence Day. We in Hyderabad cannot share the joy with the rest of our fellow countrymen who are our own citizens of Independent Democratic India… we refuse to be slaves,” he had said.

The flag-hoisting programme was part of the ‘Join Indian Union’ campaign launched by the Congress. While the Nizam’s government maintained a firm grip over Hyderabad and sought to enforce its will, the same was not the case in many parts of the dominion. Workers skipped work, schoolchildren stayed home (it was a Friday), and cinema halls remained shut. Trains passing through the Nizam’s dominion were stripped of the Indian Union flags. As the Bombay-Madras Express steamed into the Gulbarga station at 2 p.m. on August 15, 1947, the Nizam’s Police got to work removing all the flags pasted on the train.

The crackdown against the flag and those planning to hoist the tricolour had begun much earlier, when Arya Samaj leaders such as Narendraji, Dattatreya Prasad and Gangaram were arrested and sent to jail on July 30, 1947.

However, on the day, a different kind of freedom was being celebrated elsewhere in the city. At Darussalam, Razakar leader Kasim Rizvi unfurled the yellow Asafia flag, calling it “the emblem of political power of Muslims”. A salvo of 110 guns was fired on the occasion.

A more public celebration unfolded near Abids Shop, where ‘Independent Hyderabad Day’ was marked by decorating shops in the locality and installing a tall new flagpole for the Asafia flag. On the parallel road, however, there was silence, with traffic diverted and buses barred from plying on the route. Silence prevailed again in another part of the city, where the police enforced a curfew in Secunderabad that remained in force until August 20, 1947.

At the Ordnance Depot in Secunderabad, then a British enclave because of the stationing of the Indian Army, the flags of both India and Pakistan were hoisted.

At 3 p.m., a public meeting got underway at the Exhibition Pavilion, organised by Anjuman-e-Majlis-e-Azad. Raja Pratapgirji Bahadur delivered the main address, appealing to all communities living in the State to unite so that everyone could enjoy the fruits of freedom. The meeting also passed a resolution reaffirming the participants’ allegiance to the throne and the Nizam.

But not everything was deadly serious. At the Paramount Cinema in Secunderabad, a new movie was in town — Wasiyat Nama. A newspaper described the reception to the film as one of “unprecedented enthusiasm” for the 3.30 p.m. matinee show on August 15. The movie was a two-year-old adaptation of Bankim Chandra Chatterjee’s Krishnakanter Will.

The Nizam’s government had been preparing for the day, issuing a ruling that said: “In exercise of its power conferred by Rule 58 sub-rule (1) (b) of the Defence of Hyderabad Rules, the President of the Council is pleased to order that no flag of any foreign State shall be ceremoniously flown in any public meeting nor shall any salutation of such flag be made. Contravention of this order shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term that may extend to three years or with fine or both.”

The ruling remained in force for 13 more months, until Hyderabad became part of India in September 1948.

World.title: Evidence demands CBI probe into Coimbatore SC youth murder case
World.content:
Demanding CBI probe into the death of a Scheduled Caste youth Amudhan (19), son of Kennedy and Sumathi of Kallakurichi district, who was brutally murdered by an armed gang of students of a private engineering college in Coimbatore on August 10, Evidence, an NGO in Madurai, has also urged the newly elected Tamil Nadu government to deal with an iron hand in curtailing drugs in the State.

Speaking to media persons on Friday, A Kathir, executive director of Evidence, an NGO, said that the young boy, who was studying third year engineering, was killed in a brutal manner.

“The murderers, who were drugged, had used rods, logs and other weapons. It had happened in a broad daylight close to the college grounds in Coimbatore district....”

He further charged that the police and the college authorities appeared to be keen on ‘hiding’ the real facts and presented a different tale.

He said the cause of death had arisen after Amudhan had disclosed the names of students, who were addicted to drugs to a four-member committee constituted by the college management. Irked over this, the annoyed gang of students had killed Amudhan.

Intervening, the boy’s mother Sumathi said that only after Amudhan disclosed the names of the students, who had access to all kinds of drugs, they had targeted him with deadly weapons. While this was the fact, which had claimed the life of Amudhan, the police and college authorities were giving vague reasons.

She further said, “There was no group among the students and even if there were such claims by the college and the police, my son was not involved in any such groups.”

She pleaded and asserted that the only reason for the death was that he revealed the names to the committee members.

Weeping during the conversation, she said that if the government was really serious to end the drug menace in educational institutions, they should arrest all the 20 suspects, which alone would discourage youth from falling prey to narcotics like ganja and other substances.

Two fact-finding teams from the Evidence, which visited both Kallakurichi district, the native of Amudhan’s family and Coimbatore, where he studied, said that though the Chettipalayam police in Coimbatore district have registered cases under BNS sections 191 (2), 126 (2), 127 (2), 137 (2), 109 (1) and 103 (1) and among others, the investigation appeared to be one-sided so far.

Hence, they had decided to approach the court seeking a direction for CBI investigation and also under the supervision of a High Court judge.

The fact-finding team members said that inquiries by them with some of the students, who had knowledge about the murder incident, said that the police should have registered cases against the college authorities for not taking stringent action against students using narcotics. It was freely available in some of the hostel rooms.

The Tamil Nadu government should immediately release ₹12 lakh as compensation to the family members for the brutal murder as per the law.

Amudhan’s elder brother Charles (21) should be given a government job. The arrested youth should all be booked under the Goondas Act and none of them should be given bail under any circumstances, Mr. Kathir said and appealed to Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay to deal firmly with the ganja menace, especially on higher education campuses, across the State.

World.title: West Asia war LIVE: Iran defiant on strait as Trump tells Americans to accept high gas prices
World.content:
Iran called on the U.S. to accept defeat while President Donald Trump blasted Iran as “evil” and urged Americans ‌to brace for continued high fuel prices. The comments suggested the warring parties remained far apart, with progress toward peace talks and oil tanker traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway both halted.

Also read | What does the U.S.-Iran agreement say? | Explained

“This strait will be opened and ⁠closed only under Iran’s command, and so long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and stop indulging in fantasies, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade,” Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a post on X early Saturday (August 15, 2026), showing little urgency toward restoring prewar trade.

“The Strait of Hormuz ‌cannot be seized by a tweet or an aircraft carrier, by issuing an order or by delivering an election speech,” he said. One out of every five barrels of the world’s oil exports passed through the strait before the U.S. and ‌Israel launched the war on February 28.

Also read | No progress on reviving peace deal with U.S.: Iran

Mr. Trump on Friday (August 14) urged Americans to accept slightly higher gasoline prices while the conflict with ‌Iran ⁠continues. At a political rally in Garden City, New York, Mr. Trump said paying “a tiny little bit more for your ⁠gasoline” is worth the cost of ensuring “a very evil country” could not have a nuclear weapon, one of the president’s stated rationales for the war.

World.title: Trump says will ‘soon’ declare Hormuz Strait U.S. territory
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday (August 14, 2026) said he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz waterway part of U.S. territory after defeating Iran.

Also read | West Asia war updates on August 15, 2026

"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," he said with a chuckle during a political rally at a police academy in New York state.

"It's true," he added.

Mr. Trump, together with Israel, launched a war against Iran on February 28 with the stated aims of ending the country's controversial nuclear program and sparking a popular uprising.

However, Iran struck back by establishing de facto control over much of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital passageway for large amounts of global energy and other commodity shipping.

The United States remains locked in a stalemate with Iran over the strait, with Iran denying access to much of the civilian shipping and the U.S. Navy mounting a blockade of Iranian ports in an attempt to cripple its economy.

"We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to," Mr. Trump told the cheering crowd of supporters and police.

World.title: PM Modi greets people on Independence Day
World.content:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday (August 15, 2026) greeted people on the occasion of Independence Day and said powered by 140 crore Indians, the country is scaling new heights of progress across different sectors.

Mr. Modi also paid tributes to the countless freedom fighters whose courage, sacrifice and unwavering commitment ensured the end of colonial rule.

Independence Day 2026 LIVE updates

"Warm greetings on the occasion of Independence Day. We remember with gratitude the countless freedom fighters whose courage, sacrifice and unwavering commitment ensured the end of colonial rule," the Prime Minister said in a post on X.

He said the dreams of the freedom fighters continue to inspire everyone as people work together to build a "Viksit Bharat".

"Powered by 140 crore Indians, our nation is scaling new heights of progress across different sectors. May this journey keep progressing at an even greater pace in the times to come," Mr. Modi said.

The country is celebrating its 80th Independence Day.

World.title: Telangana SIR: Botched-up enumeration phase leaves 94 lakh electors at the mercy of 119 EROs
World.content:
The promised three door-to-door visits, which did not happen as part of the Enumeration Phase in the Special Intensive Revision of Electoral Rolls, are set to cost dearly to the electoral officials in Telangana. With a large number of voters not filling in their details from the final electoral rolls of 2002 SIR as required in the Enumeration Forms, the work for the Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) has increased that much.

Also read | 78.3% voters enrolled in Telangana SIR; draft rolls to be published on August 17

After August 17, the date of publication of draft electoral rolls, the EROs will have to conduct hearings for verification of close to 94 lakh voters within two months’ time, which is next to impossible in practical terms.

Of the 94 lakh, more than 32 lakh are those who did not fill in their details in the first section pertaining to their entries in the rolls of 2002 SIR, or of their parents’ details from 2002 in the second section. They have all been categorised as unmapped voters, officials informed.

Also read | Over a fifth of the electors in Telangana might get deleted in SIR

The forms had three distinct sections: the first one for the electors’ details from 2002 SIR, the second for the relatives’ details for those who were minors in 2002, and the third one for the current details of the electors.

Many voters, not knowing the format, entered the current details as available on the Electoral Photo Identity Cards in the first section, leaving out the Polling Station numbers and Part Numbers blank.

Door-to-door visits by Booth Level Officers, which could have helped them understand the process, did not happen in many instances. BLOs in a large number of localities confined their roles to distributing the forms and collecting them back, sitting at a central location, instead of going from house to house.

Electoral officials, before the start of the Enumeration Phase, repeatedly asserted that the BLOs must visit each household at least thrice during the phase, once for distribution, a second time to explain how to fill in, and one last time to collect the forms back. However, the targets given were impossible for the BLOs, which became evident at the start of the distribution. Eventually, the officials made it the electors’ duty to return the filled in forms, extending the Enumeration phase twice to make that happen.

Of the total forms submitted at the end of the Enumeration Phase, a total of 61.4 lakh logical discrepancies/anomalies were reportedly discovered. When clubbed with the number of unmapped electors, nearly 94 lakh electors will have to be served notices to attend hearings before the EROs concerned, as per the directions from the Election Commission of India.

The notice period would begin on August 17, 2026, and continue up to October 15, 2026, leaving the EROs exactly 60 days to issue notices and conduct hearings. Even if the notices are served within the first fortnight, it would leave 45 days for hearings. With 119 EROs endowed with quasi-judicial powers set to adjudicate over 94 lakh cases in this short window, they would get less than a minute’s time to verify each elector even if they worked 24 hours a day. In a reasonable eight-hour workday with/without weekends and holidays, each elector would get just about 16-28 seconds!

Completion of the process with any reasonable time allocation, say 15 minutes per elector, will need seven to eight years’ time when done with utmost rigour.

EROs will also have to settle claims and objections simultaneously, apart from accepting fresh applications by electors deleted from the rolls.

With the number of anomalies/discrepancies uneven across constituencies, a few EROs will be more burdened than the rest, even with support from the Assistant EROs.

World.title: New administrative units ‘under serious consideration’
World.content:
• Top govt functionary thinks discussion could be precursor to proposed 28th Constitutional Amendment

• Proposals include bringing Karachi, Gwadar under federal control; splitting Punjab into three, KP into two units

ISLAMABAD: There is a serious debate underway in power corridors over the most feasible approach to creating new provinces, according to a top government functionary, who thinks the discussion is a precursor to the proposed 28th Constitutional Amendment.

The government source, who is privy to developments, was reluctant to say when the proposal — still said to be in the initial stages — could materialise.

He conceded, however, that turning the idea of new administrative into reality would not be easy, as building a consensus among major political parties, which appear opposed to the idea, would be a major challenge.

The functionary said discussions were focused on whether new provinces should be created and, if so, how many would suffice; whether more administrative units should instead be established; or whether the local government system should be revived and empowered.

According to the source, the most effective way to address the consequences of the 18th Amendment was to create new provinces. He said this could help resolve many of the problems faced by the federal government following the devolution of powers to the provinces.

Recently, while addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi urged all political parties to resolve key national issues, including the creation of new provinces, describing it as the only solution to improving the country’s overall condition, which he said had “collapsed”.

The issue gained momentum after the minister’s proposal drew strong reactions from government ministers, while the country’s leading lawyers’ bodies adopted divergent positions. The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) backed the proposal, whereas the Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) stressed that any such move must be pursued strictly within the constitutional fram­ework, through parliament and with national consensus.

Speaking at a Full Court Reference held at the Supreme Court in honour of Justice Musarrat Hilali on her retirement, SCBA President Haroonur Rashid said the association endorsed and supported the proposal to create new provinces.

He said the SCBA believed that any constitutional measure to create additional provinces would promote better governance through devolution and equitable administration at the grassroots level, create equal opportunities for balanced economic development and strengthen political stability.

The creation of more provinces, he added, would also help improve living standards by addressing the economic hardships faced by people.

The PBC, the apex representative body of the legal fraternity, meanwhile, said at its 250th meeting that all constitutional matters must be addressed strictly within the framework of the Constitution.

How many more?

The government functionary said that if it was ultimately decided that creating more provinces was the only solution to what the interior minister had described as a “collapsing system”, the next question would be how many provinces should be created.

Under one proposal being discussed, he said, Karachi and Gwadar could come under the administrative control of the federal government, while the rest of Sindh would remain a single province.

Similarly, Balochistan could be divided into two provinces, while Punjab could be divided into three. Khyber Pakhtun­khwa, however, presents a more complicated case beca­use of the merger of the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata) and the inco­rporation of areas previously administered under the Fata and Pata arrangements into the provincial constitutional, legal and judicial framework.

The source said KP could nevertheless be divided into Pakhtun and Hazara regions.

Stronger local govt

Alternatively, he said, if the decision was taken to strengthen the local government system, funds for local governments could be channelled directly through the federal government instead of the provinces.

Had the local government system introduced during the late President Pervez Musharraf’s tenure continued uninterrupted, he said, a large pool of experienced and competent councillors would have been available to address local issues effectively.

“Unfortunately, reaching that level of experience and building such a team will now take considerable time,” he added.

Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

World.title: Containers to stay off roads as transporters remain divided
World.content:
• Pakistan Transport Council ‘calls off’ wheel-jam after government accepts their eight demands

• Oil tankers association also dissociates itself from strike after Ogra agrees to terms

ISLAMABAD: A section of goods transporters on Friday called off its nationwide wheel-jam strike after reaching an agreement with the government, but major operators comprising container trailers, trucks and edible oil tankers remained off the roads, prolonging disruption to port operations and the country’s external trade.

Meanwhile, fuel oil tankers dissociated themselves from the strike after the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) accepted their key demands.

Oil Tankers Contractors Asso­ciation General Secretary Malik Shoaib Ashraf told Dawn that oil tankers were not part of the strike as their demands had been acce­pted by Ogra and a notification regarding an increase in freight charges was expected next week.

“The freight charges are adjusted after every two years, but it has been delayed for three years this time. An increase of 7-8 per cent is expected next week,” Mr Ashraf said.

Meanwhile, the Pakistan Transport Council, a constituent of the All Pakistan Goods Transporters Alliance, announced that it had called off the nationwide strike following what it described as successful negotiations with the government.

Addressing a press conference at the National Press Club, council office-bearers said movement of their goods carriers was being restored across the country.

The press conference was attended by Central President Tanveer Ahmed Jutt, Patron Muhammad Altaf, Founder Rao Tahir Khan, Central Vice President Ashraf Gujjar and other office-bearers.

The council leadership said goods transportation operations from Karachi Port and Port Qasim were also being restored with immediate effect.

They said a special committee formed by the prime minister and headed by Communications Minister Abdul Aleem Khan had held negotiations with the transporters.

As a result, eight of the transporters’ immediate demands had been accepted, while committees had been constituted to address the remaining issues.

The council said the agreement with the government carried the signatures of office-bearers representing 15 goods transport associations from across the country.

Among their demands were no increase in toll taxes for one year, removal of additional toll plazas and implementation of a modern automated system.

The council leadership also said an agreement had been reached for the immediate release, against bank guarantees, of vehicles detained under SRO 1619.

The committees established to address other long-standing issues would remain in contact with the relevant government institutions, they added.

However, All Pakistan Goods Transport Owners Association President Muhammad Owais Choudhry said only one segment of the All Pakistan Goods Transporters Alliance had broken ranks and that the strike by container trailers and trucks would continue as their key demands had not been met.

He said the strike, which had continued for the past six days, was adversely affecting port activities. “The smaller goods carrier vehicles have called off the strike, but the large vehicles that move between provinces and carry heavy loads are still off the roads,” Mr Choudhry said.

“The government is playing politics with us — buying time under the garb of negotiations while threatening our members through other means,” he alleged.

Edible oil tankers also remained on strike. Edible Oil Contractors Association President Tariq Sarbaz said operators were not lifting palm oil and palm olein from the ports for transportation to oil factories.

He said the best way out of the crisis was for the government to accept the transporters’ legitimate demands. Another meeting between the government and the striking transporters is scheduled to be held at the communications ministry on Saturday morning.

Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

World.title: Govt raises petroleum dealers’ margin to Rs9.98 per litre
World.content:
• PPDA calls off nationwide strike planned from today

• Higher margin to take effect from Sept 1

ISLAMABAD: In a move aimed at averting a nationwide strike by petroleum dealers, the Economic Coordination Com­mittee (ECC) of the federal cabinet on Friday approved a 15.5 per cent increase in dealers’ margins on both petrol and high-speed diesel, following which the dealers called off their protest planned from Saturday.

The decision raises the dealers’ margin on both fuels by Rs1.34 per litre, from Rs8.64 to Rs9.98 per litre. The revised margin is scheduled to take effect from Sept 1.

Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb chaired the ECC meeting virtually, while Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal attended in person at the Finance Division. The meeting was convened on a public holiday after petroleum dealers announced a nationwide strike from Aug 15, prompting the government to take up the matter on an urgent basis.

The Finance Division’s statement did not disclose the exact increase in dealers’ margins. However, officials confirmed that the ECC had approved the proposal submitted by the Petroleum Division.

“Yes, the ECC approved the same increase proposed by the Petroleum Division,” a senior official privy to the meeting told Dawn.

According to the summary submitted to the ECC, the dealers’ margin was proposed to be increased by Rs1.34 per litre to Rs9.98.

Soon after the decision, the Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) called off its plan to launch a nationwide strike from Saturday. The association had earlier given the federal government a 72-hour ultimatum, accusing it of failing to honour assurances made by the petroleum minister regarding its demands.

The dealers had sought replacement of the existing fixed margin with a variable margin linked to the retail prices of petrol and diesel, proposing that it be set at 8pc of the retail price of both fuels.

According to official sources, acceptance of that demand would have raised the dealers’ margin to around Rs26 per litre on petrol and Rs30 per litre on diesel at current retail prices, resulting in a substantially higher burden on consumers.

The ECC instead approved the 15.51pc increase in the fixed margin.

The margin of oil marketing companies (OMCs) remains unchanged at Rs7.87 per litre on both petrol and diesel. A proposal to increase the OMC margin by Rs1.22 per litre remains linked to the implementation of digitisation measures.

An official Finance Division statement said the ECC considered a summary submitted by the Petroleum Division and deliberated on the revision of dealers’ margins on motor spirit and high-speed diesel (HSD).

In December 2025, the ECC had approved an increase of Rs2.56 per litre in dealers’ margins on petrol and diesel. The decision was subsequently modified by the federal cabinet, prompting the PPDA to demand its implementation.

The shift from fortnightly to daily petroleum price revisions added another demand from dealers, who sought to link their margins to retail prices. The government, however, decided to retain the daily pricing mechanism.

Under the ECC’s December 2025 decision, 50pc of the proposed increase was to take effect from Dec 15, subject to a declining trend in petroleum prices, while the remaining 50pc was linked to achievement of digitisation targets set by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

On Dec 23, the federal cabinet modified the decision, making the increase conditional on completion of digitisation targets by OMCs and petroleum dealers.

With the digitisation drive still under way, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik held a meeting on July 22 with representatives of the All Pakistan Petrol Pump Owners Association and the PPDA following an earlier strike call. Senior Petroleum Division officials and the Ogra chairman also attended.

The dealers urged the government to delink the increase in their margins from digitisation, arguing that implementation of the initiative was primarily the responsibility of OMCs.

They also reiterated their demand that the fixed margin of Rs8.64 per litre be replaced with a margin equivalent to 8pc of the retail price of petrol and diesel.

Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

World.title: Presidency announces 355 civil awards on Independence Day
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: President Asif Ali Zardari on Friday approved several summaries sent by the prime minister, including the conferment of military and civil awards and a special remission of sentences for eligible prisoners.

According to the Presidency, President Zardari approved military awards for 1,172 personnel of the armed forces and civil armed forces in recognition of their services.

In addition, the president approved the conferment of national civil awards on 355 individuals on the occasion of the country’s Independence Day, honouring achievement across science, engineering, education, medicine, the arts, literature, sports, journalism, social welfare, philanthropy and public service, alongside a large slate of gallantry decorations dominated by personnel of the Federal Constabulary who were killed in the line of duty.

The awards, announced on August 14, will be formally conferred at an investiture ceremony on Pakistan Day, March 23.

Nishan-i-Pakistan

The country’s highest civil award for a foreign national goes to Sheikha Fatima bint Mubarak, Supreme Chairwoman of the Family Development Foundation, United Arab Emirates.

Nishan-i-Quaid-i-Azam

Two physicians who attended to the founder of Pakistan, Dr Jal Rattanji Patel (Late) and Dr Jal Daeboo (Late), are recognised more than seven decades on.

Nishan-i-Imtiaz

Six government figures and one literary personality will be conferred the award: poet and writer Asad Muhammad Khan, Ishaq Dar, Mohsin Naqvi, Muhammad Aurangzeb, Ahad Khan Cheema, Bilal Azhar Kayani and the late Austro-Hungarian Muslim scholar Muhammad Asad (Late).

Hilal-i-Pakistan

Six foreign dignitaries were recognised for their services to Pakistan: Prince Saud bin Nayef bin Abdulaziz Al-Saud, Yousef bin Abdullah Al-Benyan, Mohammed Al-Tuwaijri, Deemah Al Yahya, Russian Deputy PM Alexey Logvinovich Overchuk, and Hiroji Kataoka.

Hilal-i-Quaid-i-Azam

The award went to Carey Schofield, an educationist working in Chitral.

Sitara-i-Pakistan

Three Turkish ministers and a Spanish senator were honoured: Hakan Fidan, Yasar Gular, Omer Bolat and Senator Vicente Azpitarte.

Sitara-i-Quaid-i-Azam

The award went to six recipients drawn from China, Spain, France and Malaysia. They included Yang Baoning of the China Academy of Space Technology, Master Yuan Xikun, Professor Zhou Yushu, Antonio Gutierrez Limones, Pascal Allizard, and Dr Maszlee bin Malik.

Hilal-i-Imtiaz

The award was conferred on fifteen recipients across the realms of technology, higher education, medicine, broadcasting, letters, the senior bureaucracy and the diaspora.

These included Interactive Group CEO Dr Shahid Mahmud, NUTECH Rector Lt Gen (r) Moazzam Ejaz, renowned transplant surgeon Dr Faisal Saud Dar, HUM Network’s Sultana Siddiqi, and poets Ejaz Rahim and Khurshid Ul Hasan Rizvi.

Five senior public servants were also honoured, including DG IB Fuad Asadullah, AGP Mansoor Usman Awan, Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal, FBR chief Rashid Mahmood Lagrial, and Establishment Secretary Barrister Nabeel A. Awan.

The remaining awards went under the services to Pakistan head to Saudi Assistant Minister for Investment Ibrahim Al-Mubarak, and to three overseas Pakistanis: Dr Ghulam Murtaza in the UK, the late Prof Ahmed Ali in China, and Sardar Muhammad Ilyas Khan in Saudi Arabia.

Sitara-i-Imtiaz

In science and higher education, the award went to Kohat University of Science and Technology VC Prof Dr Syed Zafar Ilyas and Balochistan Public Service Commission member Prof Dr Mudassir Asrar, along with ICCBS Director and Unesco Chair Prof Dr Muhammad Raza Shah, FJMU Lahore VC Prof Dr Khalid Masood Gondal, PIDE VC Dr Rashid Amjad, and Taaleem Foundation founder Dr Zafar Iqbal Qadir.

Two of the five medical awards are posthumous, going to bone marrow transplantation pioneer Prof Dr Tahir Shamsi (Late) and infectious diseases specialist Dr Naseem Salahuddin (Late). The others went to SICHN Executive Director Prof Dr Syed Jamal Raza, Battagram neurosurgeon Dr Shah Khalid, and physician Prof Dr Muhammad Khurram.

Ten artists were recognised: actor Balqees Bano (Nisho Begum), comedian Iftikhar Ahmed Thakur, naat khawan Syed Fasih Uddin Soharwardhy, composer and compere Shakir Hussain, singer Taranam Naz, Sufi opera singer Saira John Peter, the late painter and art historian Abida Ehsan (posthumously), painter Raja Changez Sultan, theatre and TV artist Muhammad Naeem Tahir, and miniature painter Bashir Ahmed.

In literature, the award went to short story writer Shakeel Adilzada, Iqbal scholar Prof Brig (r) Waheed Uz Zaman Tariq, poet Maqsood Hussain Jafri, naat writer Riaz ul Haq Tahir Riaz Majeed, writer Muhammad Hafeez Khan, historian Prof Dr Muhammad Saleem Mazhar, novelist Hashim Nadeem, and poet Syed Ghulam Abbas (Muhsin Naqvi).

Boxing coach Atta Mohammad Kakar and martial artist and yoga pioneer Dr Waseem A Tai were honoured in sports, journalists Muhammad Saleh Zaafir and Haji Nawaz Raza in journalism, WHO technical officer Dr Maryam Mallick and Nayyab Ali in social welfare, and Shanawar Khan in philanthropy.

Twenty-eight public servants also received the Sitara-i-Imtiaz, while under gallantry and public service, the award went to Ahmad Arifeen and to three Punjab police officers recognised for the Kacha operation — IGP Abdul Kareem, DIG Waqas Hassan and DIG Tanveer Hussain Tunio. Danish citizen of Pakistani origin Justice Muhammad Ahsan and UAE-based Haji Khan Zaman Saroor were honoured for services to Pakistan.

Tamgha-i-Imtiaz

The Tamgha-i-Imtiaz is the largest single category on the list. In science, it went to One Health and AMR focal person Dr Sajjad Hussain, PIEAS Deputy Chief Scientist Prof Dr Aneela Zameer Jaffery and GIS specialist Dr Urooj Saeed, and in engineering to UET Peshawar VC Dr Muhammad Sadiq and PIEAS Principal Engineer Prof Dr Naeem-ul-Haq Tariq.

Sixteen educationists were honoured: Women University Mardan and Swabi VC Prof Dr Ghazala Yasmeen, AIOU VC Prof Dr Nasir Mahmood, LUMS Dean Prof Dr Faisal Bari, former LCWU VC Prof Dr Sabiha Mansoor, University of Loralai VC Prof Engr Dr Ehsan Ullah Kakar, IBCC chief Dr Ghulam Ali Mallah, TCF’s Riaz Ahmed Kamlani, retired FDE principals Sabah Faisal and Muhammad Rafique Malik, Cambridge Advisors Network co-founder Syed Azhar Afaq Rizvi, former Sindh High Court judge Qazi Khalid Ali, Diamer-Astore Education Director Faqir Ullah, Abdul Sattar, researcher Dr Ruhi Khalid, CPSP fellow supervisor Prof Dr Sardar Muhammad Ali Ayaz Sadiq, and educationist and philanthropist Yasmeen Dadabhai.

In medicine, the award went to CDA Hospital surgery head Dr Naeem Taj, Quetta cardiac surgeon Dr Abdul Wasay, Hashmanis Group chairman Dr Mohammad Sharif Hashmani, and bariatric and laparoscopic surgeon Dr Maaz Ul Hassan.

Twelve artists were recognised: actor and anchor Noor Ul Hassan Malik, host Shafat Ali, singer and composer Shiraz Uppal, singer Jabbar Abbas, painter Ali Saad, khussa maker Muhammad Ramzan, shoemaker Jahangir Khan, stone carver Ghulam Haider, Balochi chawat maker Rozi Khan, naat khawans Akhtar Qureshi and Khan Muhammad Chachar, and fashion designer Rubina Kazmi.

Ten literary figures were honoured: writer Farida Hafeez, novelist Agha Gul, writer Noor Khan Muhammad Hasni, writer and translator Khalid Fateh Muhammad, poet Haleem Qureshi, writers Manzoom Ali and Sherbaz Ali Khan Barcha, the late historian and archaeologist Muhammad Siddique G Memon (posthumously), Iqbal scholar Prof Dr Haroon-ur-Rasheed Tabassum, and author Qaiser Abbas Sabir.

Athlete Faiqa Riaz was the sole sports recipient. Seven journalists were recognised — Muhammad Riaz Khan, culture journalist Shoaib Ahmed, Ammar Masood, news anchors Dr Maria Zulfiqar, Adil Shahzaib and Hammad Hassan, and Tasawwar Arafat. Religious scholars Qari Rooh Ullah Madani, Hafiz Asad Ubaid, Syed Riaz Hussain Najfi and Bishop Humphri Sarfraz Peters were honoured under social welfare, while Haripur Chamber of Commerce President Atif Ikram Sheikh, National Forum of Women with Disabilities Chairperson Abia Akram and Pakistan Association of the Blind President Riaz Hussain Memon were recognised for philanthropy.

President’s Pride of Performance

Forty-six people will receive the President’s Award for Pride of Performance, most of them from the performing and visual arts.

Thirty arts recipients were named. Among the actors and directors are Mahmood Aslem, Sarfraz Hussain Ansari, M Ehtesham Warsi, Arshad Hussain, Ghazala Kaifi, Khawaja Saleem Ahmad, Shazma Haleem, Syeda Maria Wasti and Sania Saeed.

From music, the award went to sarangi players Ustad Mazhar Umrao Bundu Khan and Zohaib Hassan, singer Rafia Bano, classical musician Jahangir Iqbal (Ustad Ejaz Tawakal Khan), BJS Qawwal Group’s Nadeem Salamat, harmonium soloist Shahbaz Ali, ghazal singer Gulshan Ara Syed, the late folk singer Talib Hussain Dard (posthumously), singers Mushtaq Shifai and Zulfiqar Jabbar Khan (Zulfi), and choreographers Shaukat Hussain Samrat (Pappu Samrat) and Syed Wahab Hussain Shah.

In the visual arts and crafts, it went to painter and illustrator Aftab Zafar, painter and sculptor Tayyeba Aziz, artist Aleem Dad Khan, boreendo maker Allah Jurio, Kashmiri embroidery artist Sheikh Muhammad Yousaf, natural-dye block printer Ameer Buksh, painters Nasir Shahzad and Muhammad Imran Qureshi, and sculptor and cultural consultant Hidayat Ullah Khan.

Eight literary figures were recognised: Dr Shahida Shaheen, Ali Muhammad Farshi, Aslam Javed, Muhammad Muti-Ur-Rehman Mumtaz (Rehman Faris), Syed Farid Ullah Shah Hassas, Shafqat Ullah Mushtaq, Nizakat Kalsoom (Kalsoom Zeb) and Syed Wasi Ahmad Fatmi.

Six athletes made the list — wrestler Bashir Bhola, shooter Kishmala Talat, squash player Noor Zaman, ramp jumper Sultan Muhammad Golden, boxer Muhammad Waseem and cricketer Sadiq Muhammad — along with journalist Syed Hammad Ghaznavi and photojournalist Muhammad Amir Khan.

Gallantry awards

Security and law-enforcement personnel account for the single largest bloc on this year’s list, with 91 gallantry decorations approved in addition to the awards named above.

Forty-eight were conferred Sitara-i-Shuja’at awards, 24 received the Tamgha-i-Shuja’at while 19 officials were awarded the Tamgha-i-Imtiaz for gallantry and public service. These are separate from the military awards for 1,172 serving personnel of the Armed Forces and Civil Armed Forces approved by the president on the same day.

World.title: Chenab, Ravi nullahs may enter high flood category
World.content:
LAHORE: The Flood Forecasting Division (FFD) of the Pakistan Meteorological Department has warned of possible high flooding in storm-water nullahs linked to the Chenab and Ravi rivers from Aug 15 to 21 as flows in these waterways continue to rise.

The FFD said flows at major rim-gauging stations of the Chenab and Ravi were expected to remain at low flood levels during the period, while adjoining nullahs could experience low to medium flooding. However, a significant increase in flows in tributary nullahs could lead to high flood levels.

It forecast no significant increase in inflows at major gauging stations of the Indus, Kabul, Jhelum, Ravi and Sutlej over the next 24 hours, although several stations could reach low flood levels.

Flows at Taunsa, Marala, Khanki, Qadirabad and Sidhnai are expected to enter the low-flood range, while Tarbela, Kalabagh, Chashma, Guddu and Balloki are likely to remain at low flood levels. The FFD also warned of flash flooding in tributary streams of the Kabul River and hill torrents in the Dera Ghazi Khan division during the forecast period.

Tarbela at maximum conservation level as Mangla 67pc full

According to the FFD, Tarbela Dam, Kalabagh and Chashma on the Indus were experiencing low-level flooding on Friday evening, with flows of 268,200, 365,870 and 321,667 cusecs, respectively, recorded at 6pm on Aug 14.

The department forecast widespread rain, wind and thunderstorms, with isolated heavy falls, over the upper catchments of all major rivers during the next 24 hours.

The areas include Islamabad, Gilgit-Baltistan, Kashmir, upper Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and several districts of upper Punjab.

The FFD said Tarbela reservoir had attained its maximum conservation level, while Mangla was yet to reach its maximum, with the reservoir 67 per cent full.

Meanwhile, according to Wapda’s daily report for Aug 14, inflows and outflows at Tarbela were recorded at 274,100 and 273,300 cusecs, respectively. At Nowshera, inflows and outflows of the Kabul River were 32,700 cusecs each.

The Jhelum at Mangla recorded inflows of 28,400 cusecs and outflows of 7,000 cusecs, while the Chenab at Marala had inflows of 81,000 cusecs and outflows of 62,000 cusecs.

Tarbela Dam’s water level stood at 1,550 feet, its maximum conservation level, with live storage of 5.580 million acre-feet (MAF). Mangla’s level was 1,209.75 feet against its maximum conservation level of 1,242 feet, with live storage of 4.870 MAF.

Chashma lake was at 648.50 feet, just half a foot below its maximum conservation level of 649 feet, with live storage of 0.285 MAF.

Wapda said the inflows and outflows at Tarbela, Jinnah and Chashma, the Kabul at Nowshera and the Jhelum at Mangla were reported as 24-hour mean flows.

World.title: Gas supply disruption persists in Balochistan as repair work awaits security clearance
World.content:
QUETTA: Despite the passage of three days, repair work on the damaged gas pipeline could not begin as several cities and towns in Balochistan, including parts of the provincial capital, remained without gas supply on Friday.

The 18-inch-diameter main gas pipeline was blown up by unidentified people using explosives in the Bolan riverbed in Kachhi district on Wednesday night, disrupting gas supplies to several districts of Balochistan.

Officials said the relevant security authorities had yet to provide clearance for repair teams to enter the affected area and replace the damaged pipeline.

Gas supply was suspended to several towns and cities, including parts of Quetta, after the main pipeline was blown up in the Bolan area of Kachhi district.

Officials of the Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) confirmed the incident and said the pipeline had been badly damaged, disrupting gas supplies.

“The explosion occurred at the KMP-246 valve assembly in the Bolan riverbed area near Gorkat, around 700 to 800 metres from the main Quetta-Sibi Road,” officials said, adding that it was an 18-inch-diameter pipeline.

They said unidentified people had planted high explosives beneath the pipeline and detonated them using a remote control.

Flames and smoke were seen rising from the damaged pipeline following the explosion.

“After the pipeline explosion, gas supplies were suspended to Kolpur, Mach, Mastung, Kalat, Pishin, Ziarat and many parts of Quetta,” officials said, adding that consumers could face reduced gas pressure or disruption in supply.

SSGC officials said repair teams were ready to begin work but were awaiting security clearance before entering the affected area. The teams would be dispatched to the site immediately after clearance was granted, the company said.
