World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: Hundreds of jobs saved as coal mine granted six-year lifeline
World.content:
A major New South Wales coal mine has been given a lifeline by the state government, four months before it was due to close.

Mining approvals for MACH Energy's Mount Pleasant coal mine near Muswellbrook were due to expire in December.

The mine has been given a six-year extension while it fights to overturn a block on its plans for a 22-year expansion project in the High Court.

The approval also allows for an increase in the approved extraction rate from 10.5 to 12.5 million tonnes of coal per annum.

The mine is continuing its bid for a longer extension to 2048. (ABC Upper Hunter: Amelia Bernasconi)

The mine employs more than 500 people.

Upper Hunter MP Dave Layzell said the extension was crucial to secure those jobs as the expiry deadline loomed.

"It's quite damaging to people's psyche when they're constantly bombarded with this news that they could lose their job. People have mortgages, they've got families," he said.

"It is frustrating to have this project bailed up through environmental lawfare from a very small group.

"We hope that once it's dealt with in the High Court, people know that they've got a job for the next couple of decades."

Legal hold-up

MACH Energy applied for the six-year extension in October, after a legal challenge from a local environment group halted plans for a longer extension project.

MACH had previously secured approval to extend the mine's life by 22 years to 2048 as a State Significant Development.

The proposed expansion would allow the company to mine an additional 247 million tonnes of coal by 2048.

But the consent was later ruled invalid after the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) challenged the decision in the New South Wales Court of Appeal.

The court found that the state's Independent Planning Commission (IPC) had failed to take into account the project's impact on the environment and climate, specifically the impacts of greenhouse gases from exported coal.

The Court of Appeal ruling rendered the IPC's approval invalid.

Wendy Wales says the approval will worsen climate change. (Supplied: Wendy Wales)

DAMSHEG president Wendy Wales said the environmental impacts of the project would be extreme.

"We have to be winding back from coal," she said.

" We can't be incrementally adding to this burden every few years just because the industry has failed to plan for a transition. "

MACH Energy was granted special leave to appeal the ruling in the High Court of Australia last year, but sought the six-year extension to allow operations to continue while it awaits a decision.

Protesters gathered outside the High Court in Canberra when the case was heard earlier this year. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Ms Wales said she was "devastated" the six-year extension was approved while the High Court case was still active.

"This approval has pre-empted the High Court decision and provided them a pathway to continue if they lose," she said.

"We need to know what that decision is before we allow mining to continue."

In a statement following the High Court hearing in May, MACH said it was "actively pursuing all available options to ensure the continuity of this important project".

"MACH Energy welcomed today’s opportunity to appear as an appellant to the High Court and will continue to operate in alignment with existing approvals and conditions and seek to provide long-term continuity and certainty for its staff, contractors, customers and the local community," the statement read.

World.title: Seventy years of School of the Air celebrated in family recipe cookbook
World.content:
Coming together to share a meal can look a little different for those living on remote stations across Far West New South Wales, where even visiting the neighbours can involve hours of travel.

While catch-ups might be infrequent due to geographic isolation, their importance cannot be overstated, and neither can the tradition of sharing food.

Bessie Thomas from Burragan Station, who lives nearly 200 kilometres from the nearest supermarket, said cooking was what kept people connected in the bush.

"We're getting together for smoko in the paddock or barbecues to celebrate birthdays or nibbles on the verandah and drinks by the dam," Bessie says.

" Food is a way we connect with our families, connect with staff on our properties, connect with our friends and the whole community. "

Food is how families, neighbours and station workers connect on remote properties, Bessie Thomas says. (Supplied: Bessie Thomas)

These stories of food, connection and life out bush are celebrated in Dust Off and Dish Up, a fundraising cookbook published by the School of the Air (SOTA) Parent's and Citizens Association (P&C) to commemorate the school's 70th anniversary.

The cookbook shares recipes from remote families throughout the region, along with stories of SOTA throughout the decades, and advice for living out bush.

As well as being co-editor, all three of Bessie's children learn through Broken Hill SOTA, with classes taking place online.

"It's completely different to the type of school that I attended," Bessie says.

"The advancements in technology in the last few years and especially since COVID have just been incredible for the development of SOTA, and the kids now get so much face-to-face time on the computer that they can really form friendships with their peers and their teacher before they even get to Broken Hill and meet in person."

Bessie Thomas (centre) and members of the SOTA P&C selling the 70th anniversary cookbook, Dust Off and Dish Up. (Supplied: Bessie Thomas)

Sales from the cookbook will go towards funding bus trips, school camps and supplies for the Broken Hill campus.

"A big part of our school that makes it a bit different to other schools is just the distance kids are to accessing things they need to access," Bessie says.

"For example, most children have the ability to go to weekend sport every weekend. Our students don't necessarily have that."

Seventy years of remote education

The cookbook is the fifth iteration for the Broken Hill SOTA, with the tradition of releasing a cookbook every decade beginning in the 1980s.

Among the recipes are stories about the early days of remote education, tracking its progression from radio and tape recorders to the internet — the method by which students learn today.

This year's cookbook features Anny O'Connor's reflections on learning through SOTA in the late 1960s.

Located on Connulpie Downs Station, near Tibooburra, she recalls receiving lessons in the weekly mail and being taught over a transceiver.

Anny O'Connor learning via School of the Air from her family's station in remote NSW in the 1960s. (Supplied: Anny O'Connor)

"We couldn't see each other and could barely hear one another, depending on the weather," she says.

"Sometimes school was interrupted when our poddy foal Tiny Tim wandered off and we had to find him, or when we went with Dad checking waters and didn't come home for a day or two because we got caught up doing something."

Along with these anecdotes, the cookbook features recipes for classic country cooking; sausage rolls, quiche, brownie, sponge cake and pumpkin soup are just a few of the recipes, passed down over generations.

How to cook yabbies

For families who live hours from the nearest chemist or supermarket, bush wisdom in the form of home remedies and cleaning hacks can provide temporary solutions between town trips.

Some of these are also captured in the cookbook, with practical advice for finding and cooking local food too.

Lachlan Gall and his yabby catch at Langawirra Station (Supplied: Lachlan Gall)

Lachlan Gall, from Langawirra Station, provided tips for catching and cooking yabbies, with a dash of larrikin humour.

"Boil decent yabbies for five minutes and then carefully remove the bucket from the fire with a shovel," Lachlan writes.

"If they're monsters, give them another minute, but if they're all small you should have chucked them back into the dam and gone home for chops instead."

He also advises against cooking yabbies in the kitchen.

"You will stink the house out and she-who-must-be-obeyed won't be pleased at all."

Not quite picture perfect

The back cover photo of Dust Off and Dish Up. (Supplied: Ainsley Fuster)

Former SOTA student Ainsley Fuster, who photographed the cookbook cover, says not everything had gone to plan when it came to trying to capture images of food, much like life on the station itself.

"Out in the middle of the paddock, there's flies everywhere, it's warm so the cream in the sponge was starting to melt a little bit," she says.

"It looks great on the camera, but behind the scenes it was a lot of fanning the cream to make sure it wouldn't melt and swatting off flies and whatnot."

" I think most of the editing process was just me getting rid of all the flies. "

Cookbook sells out at Broken Hill stockist

The Broken Hill Bookshop has repeatedly sold out of the Dust Off and Dish Up since its release in March, and owner of the bookshop Amanda Murray isn't surprised.

"I think it's just the easy recipes," she says.

"I made the lemon slice and it was a big hit — I brought it into the shop and it sold out very quickly."

The 70th Anniversary School of the Air cookbook, Dust Off and Dish Up, has repeatedly sold out at the Broken Hill Bookshop. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

And it's not just locals snapping up copies, Amanda says she's been posting them to customers around the country.

"I've even posted them to Tasmania, South Australia [and] Mudgee [in NSW].

"I think people just love the country, and a lot of people I've sold them to have history with School of the Air, whether their children went through or they went through."

Cooking for community

Back at Burragan Station, about an hour's drive from Wilcannia, Bessie has been trialling recipes from Dust off and Dish Up for family, friends and contractors.

"At the moment, I'm obsessed with the Spring Hill Lamb … We had musterers out recently and I cooked that to make slow-cooked pulled lamb rolls with coleslaw. It was great."

Cooking often takes place outdoors, around a campfire, at Burragan Station. (Supplied: Bessie Thomas)

Living so remotely means grabbing takeaway for dinner isn't an option, but Bessie doesn't mind because she enjoys cooking — especially when it involves a catch-up.

"Food is such a celebration of community," she says.

"It's essential, but it's also really precious to a lot of people, and this is a real celebration of that. It's something that brings everyone together and something we all have to do, and this is a lovely way to grab little snippets from everyone's lives in a way that connects the broader community."

World.title: Hana and Wanda's unlikely friendship is helping tackle an insidious problem
World.content:
Anyone looking at Hana and Wanda can see they share a special friendship.

They chat, laugh, sing karaoke at Wanda's aged care home and even dance together in the local park.

You'd be forgiven for thinking they've known each other for decades.

Hana Byambadash has volunteered to spend time with elderly people. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

But their friendship began seven years ago when they met through a free program tackling loneliness among older Australians.

It is something estimated to affect one in six Australians and is more common among people with cognitive impairment.

Laughter and dancing

Hana Byambadash, 63, and Wanda Janus, 87, first bonded over a love of music and dancing.

They also share a love of Polish movies from Wanda's homeland, with Hana saying they even have the same favourite film.

"Wanda was in Poland, I was in Mongolia, it was something we had similar," Hana said.

Wanda Janus, who comes from Poland, stays in a nursing home. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

"[People] like to be with me because I'm funny and I'm joking with them, I have a good time and then they come again," Wanda giggled.

The program that brought the women together is offered by Umbrella Multicultural Community Care in Perth.

Borhan Milani of Umbrella Multicultural Community Care Centre says more volunteers are desperately needed. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

Chief executive Borhan Milani said it aimed to address the "significant and under-recognised issue" of social isolation and loneliness among the elderly.

"What we've realised is that one or two hours … playing a card game or having a cup of tea or a coffee or going for a walk, that alone has completely changed their life," he said.

"They have hope, they look forward to their next visit … and for the first time some of them are actually smiling and look forward to starting their day."

Isolation and disease

Social isolation is defined as a lack of connection and interaction with social networks, according to the Australian Institute of Family Studies (AIFS).

The institute said this had been linked to issues including poor mental health, declines in cognitive function and premature death.

Musical memories and magic moments in dementia-friendly choir Regional WA's only dementia-friendly singing group is helping people living with the degenerative condition to reconnect with their beloved musical memories.

Wanda has dementia and suffers from common symptoms of the disease, but Hana says music transforms her friend's mood.

"I've seen her very happy when she dances. She becomes a different person," she said.

The function room of Umbrella Multicultural Community Care center in Belmont is used to host weekly events for staff and clients. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

The Umbrella program currently oversees 183 matches, and with a growing waiting list, Mr Milani said more volunteers were desperately needed.

Rising cost-of-living pressures also mean more families are unable to spend as much time and resources as they would like caring for their elderly relatives.

"With the economic challenges and cost-of-living expenses … what we have found is as the aging population is growing, the demand for volunteers is growing, so have the time limitations," he said.

"Our volunteers have less and less time unfortunately because they have their own life priorities, they have to work and be able to pay the bills."

Umbrella also offers an inclusive space for clients and their volunteers to meet up, and also takes them out on weekly excursions.

Mr Milani said these gatherings are the only opportunity for connection for some clients.

'You gain more than you give'

Hana said she initially got involved in the program to give back to the community, but quickly found it filled her cup as well.

"My mum is a few years younger than Wanda. I miss my mum quite often, so to come and see Wanda I just feel like I'm seeing my mum," she said.

"When I go and see Wanda at the nursing home, I give her a hug and then I see the other seniors want to give me a hug as well."

Weekly outings are one of the options available to help seniors overcome social isolation. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

Hana encouraged more Perth residents to join the program, and said just one hour a week could make a huge difference.

"You will gain more than you give," she said.

World.title: What makes a great Aussie banger? The sausage kings aim to find out
World.content:
Chocolate, pistachio, baked beans and maple are just some of the inventive ingredients that continue to amaze the taste buds of sausage judge Gary Thompson

"There's nothing you can't put into a sausage, provided it's edible, and all the flavours have got to work," Mr Thompson said.

The sausages were examined before and after cooking. (ABC Capricornia: Russel Talbot)

The Brisbane-based sausage connoisseur has joined Queensland's best butchers who are experimenting with unconventional flavours for a shot at the title of the state's 'Sausage King'.

Nearly 600 entries from across the state have travelled to the state's beef capital, Rockhampton in Central Queensland, this week for the Australian Meat Industry Council competition — the largest of its kind in the country.

Independent butchers could enter six sausage categories and three burger categories, with industry and amateur judges scoring the products on workmanship, flavour and creativity.

All of the sausages were cooked in an oven for consistency. (ABC Capricornia: Russel Talbot)

Mr Thompson said butchers were transforming sausages from a cheap, everyday product to gourmet food they could put their own twist on.

"The butchers are actually getting their own signature in their own products, so they're a stand-out performer and something that other butchers don't sell," he said.

"So, they can separate themselves that way."

Fan-favourite snags

The main categories in the annual competition are traditional Australian, beef, pork and lamb sausages, as well as the Best Butcher's Burger.

This year, chicken, cherry and white chocolate, Wagyu, wasabi and soy, sticky BBQ pork belly and creaming soda, even camel and crocodile inspired sausages, were this some of the weird and wonderful flavour combinations dished up.

The sausages included a range of different meats, include unique types like camel and crocodile. (ABC Capricornia: Russel Talbot)

Spicy sausages with jalapeno were a favourite with judge Vicky Aubsich.

The Rockhampton local was one of the amateur judges, volunteering because of her love of food — and a sizzling snag.

"I prefer a finer-textured sausage rather than a coarser sausage," she said.

" Something spicy, throw it on the barbie, have it with a beer, nothing could be better. "

Greg Roberts (pictured left) and the judges had a line up of different flavours to try. (ABC Capricornia: Russel Talbot)

Greg Roberts, a fellow amateur judge, agreed.

"I'm looking for the spice, a pleasant taste, a pleasant mouthfeel and then a really nice aftertaste so that you know it's not too strong or too powerful."

Firsts for beef capital

This year's sausage competition is the first to be held in Rockhampton, and comes 262 days before the city's — and the country's — largest meat-related event, Beef Week.

The Australian Meat Industry Council is the peak industry body representing the Australian meat industry.

The council's Nicole Newman said the shift to Rockhampton from the competition's previous home in Toowoomba was to encourage more remote butchers, whose products were otherwise spoiled by the long travel, to participate.

"Logistically, it's really hard to get that many sausages around the state, so by having it in a more northern and rural location, it's meant more access to more product and more opportunity for some of the butchers that may not have featured previously," she said.

The panel of judges dissecting the meat, entering scores. (ABC Capricornia: Russel Talbot)

Ms Newman said organisers invited central Queensland locals to judge entries alongside experienced butchers.

She said the competition had also expanded to include evening events, so locals working during the day could participate.

Billy Gibney, a previous entrant and chef at this year's event, said the competition encouraged butchers to develop their craft and build connections with their local communities.

Billy Gibney in the kitchen. (ABC News: Jessica D'Souza)

"We are sort of a dying breed, I'd say … but people are starting to go back to the small business and local butchers because we care about what we do; we have pride in what we do," he said.

" The experience you get, not just in the quality meat you buy but that relationship you build with your butcher, is so important and your food will taste better. "

The Queensland competition winners will progress to the national finals in Melbourne, where the stakes are even higher.

World.title: 'Unusual' coffee delivery leads to woman's arrest, attempted poisoning charges
World.content:
A Tasmanian woman is set to face court after allegedly sending poisoned coffees to her ex-partner multiple times in a "targeted attack".

The 43-year-old woman from South Launceston was arrested yesterday and charged with two counts of attempting to unlawfully administer poison with intent to harm.

Tasmania Police Inspector Aleena Crack said the woman allegedly purchased the coffees, tampered with them, and then used the Airtasker app to deliver them to her former partner.

She said the alleged victim, a 47-year-old man, did not drink the first coffee and reported it to police, which launched a months-long investigation.

"The victim has received the initial coffee, found it to be unusual, and reported the matter to police and that's what's provoked the investigation," Inspector Crack said.

" Police will allege … the woman has caused several coffees to be sent to an ex-partner of hers, that she had tampered with and put an unknown substance into, with the intent to cause him some physical harm. "

Inspector Crack said police had some "early indications" of what the substance was, but they were awaiting a "full forensic analysis".

The woman was pulled over and placed into custody yesterday, ahead of her appearance at the Launceston Magistrates Court on Saturday morning.

Inspector Aleena Crack says it's an "unusual case" which she has not seen before in Tasmania. (ABC News)

Delivery people not linked, police say

Airtasker is an online platform which connects people looking to outsource everyday chores with independent local contractors bidding to complete the work.

Police said there was no suggestion the people who delivered the coffees had any involvement in the alleged scheme.

"At this stage, police don't believe the delivery people were aware," Inspector Crack said.

"It is pretty common that [they] would do little tasks like this and there's no reason to suspect they had any involvement."

She said police would allege the woman sent poisoned coffees multiple times over the last few months, in what she described as a "rare" case.

"Not one I see often and not something we see regularly in Tasmania, so it is an unusual case," she said.

World.title: Ozzy the orphaned long-nosed potoroo loves his peanuts
World.content:
Ozzy, the long-nosed potoroo, is living his best life in the eco-sanctuary of Tatachilla Lutheran College in the famous wine-growing region of McLaren Vale, just south of Adelaide.

In January, his life was in the balance after his mother became ill with a bacterial infection and had to be euthanised.

Still in the pouch, weighing 96 grams and having only just grown his first covering of fur, a team of staff, students and volunteers pulled together to help raise him.

Ozzy, the long-nosed potoroo, having one of his two-early feeds in the early days of his care when he weighed less than 100 grams. (Supplied: Tatachilla Lutheran College)

They included long-standing staff member Dolores Amos, who prefers to be known as Ranger Dee, who took on the two-hourly night feeds and resultant sleep deprivation needed to keep him alive.

During the day, other staff and volunteers kept up with his feeds, and students helped by crocheting pouches to keep little Ozzy feeling warm and safe.

Ozzy was orphaned after his mother developed a bacterial infection. (Supplied: Tatachilla Lutheran College)

Now Ozzy is a healthy one-kilogram juvenile.

Tom Hurley, the coordinator of the college's EcoSanctuary, said Ozzy's development was a testament to Ranger Dee's skills and knowledge.

" He's grown into a very robust young male. "

Ozzy is now one of 20 long-nosed potoroos living in the eco-sanctuary and now weighs one kilogram. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Growing independence

Now, in what could be called his teenage phase, Ozzy has moved out of the care centre and is becoming an independent resident of the school's 4.3ha eco-sanctuary.

While he is learning "how to be a proper potoroo", he still has an appetite for a peanut treat.

Ranger Dee and the other staff have to resist the urge to give Ozzy too many peanut treats. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

He still comes when called in the early morning, but it takes him a while to rouse after spending much of the night foraging for roots, fungi, grubs, and insects.

Recently, Ozzy has started making a nest for himself under a bus, a sign that he's starting to have female potoroos on his mind.

Hopefully he will find one amongst the nine other potoroos that live with him, in addition to the brush-tailed bettongs, tammar wallabies, and birds that can flourish away from the threat of cats and foxes.

Students at the college crocheted pouches to keep Ozzy warm and secure. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The college's eco-sanctuary is more than 20 years old and is on land that was once used to grow grapes and run sheep in the famous wine-growing region of McLaren Vale.

It's been revegetated with plants native to the local area and fenced to keep out cats, foxes and other predators, which is just as well for Ozzy and the other potoroos that call the sanctuary home, as Mr Hurley said they tended to be "incredibly naive" to these threats.

Ranger Dee, Tom Hurley and Tatachilla Lutheran College Principal Alison Thacker with Ozzy. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

The sanctuary is used as a teaching resource and as a place for students who want to learn about the environment, providing a contrast between what the area was once like and the vineyards that surround the school.

"This is as close to what it used to be like, as we can create," Mr Hurley said.

Lost to the wild in South Australia

Rob Brewster from the Invasive Species Council said he believed long-nosed potoroos were extinct in the wild in South Australia, due to land clearing and the introduction of feral predators.

Rob Brewster said long-nosed potoroos were believed to be extinct in the wild in South Australia. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

While they were able to cope with native predators such as quolls, the potoroos had not been able to withstand cats and foxes, as well as the loss of complex vegetation.

He said that while the school's population of potoroos was only small, it meant a lot to keep the species "on the radar" and show how they could be returned to South Australia "one day".

Letting go

The time will come soon when Ranger Dee calls for Ozzy, but he'll no longer respond as he gets on with his life, safe within the sanctuary, and she's not fazed.

Ozzy has graduated from two-hourly feeds to foraging for himself. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

"That's the way it should be," she said.

Holding the pouch she had made for Ozzy when he was smaller, Year 11 student Marlee felt the same way.

"To see him now, out with the rest of the animals, is so sweet."

World.title: Takeover of rare remaining community-owned nursing home
World.content:
Community generosity built the Proserpine Nursing Home four decades ago.

Sugarcane farmers in the small community about 120 kilometres north of Mackay gave up harvest profits, the Rotary Club raised money, and people joined street parties and community events to help fund the facility.

Farmer Edward Dray donated a cane paddock for the site and, once the home opened in 1986, it meant the town's older people no longer had to move 90 minutes' drive away.

Mr Dray's granddaughter, Genevieve Moller, said that many of the people who raised the money ended up living there themselves.

"It was a joy to go there; when you came home, you'd go to the nursing home because that's where the locals that you knew growing up were," she said.

"It was just such a wonderful community and family thing."

Proserpine Nursing Home opened in the 1980s. (ABC Tropical North: Liam McNally)

Future fears

After much speculation, ownership of the nursing home is set to be transferred to Tasmanian-based provider Respect Aged Care.

More than 100 current and former nursing employees, union delegates, and residents' families met in July, when the transfer was only rumoured.

The Proserpine Nursing Home is a registered charity and is governed by an association and a management committee.

The transfer is subject to a vote by the Proserpine Nursing Home Association on September 7.

The association, which had about 30 members, received more than 160 applications to join in recent months.

A petition that was circulated at the July meeting, urging the cancellation of any transfer, has also garnered hundreds of signatures.

A community meeting drew more than 100 people. (ABC Tropical North: Liam McNally)

Robin Van Niekerk's mother moved to the nursing home in November after dementia meant she could no longer care for herself.

Mr Van Niekerk said his mother was a former beautician who still loved makeup and jewellery.

"The staff are happy to do her makeup for her and make her feel special, put her jewellery on and make sure she goes out for her meals looking nice," he said.

Mr Van Niekerk said he was worried a transfer of ownership to a larger company from outside the community would change the home's culture.

"They might come out with lots of shiny things at the start to try and make it sound good but, in the long run, it's going to be a community asset that's no longer a community asset, and … I believe the quality of care will go down," he said.

Ownership transfer

Management board chair Marie Dickens announced on Wednesday that a deal had been struck to transfer ownership to Respect Aged Care.

The following day, in a letter to residents seen by the ABC, Ms Dickens said, subject to the association vote, Respect would be running the facility by mid-December.

No money is changing hands as part of the deal. In line with the nursing home's constitution, it can only be owned by another charity.

In the letter, Ms Dickens said residents would not be impacted, and that current staff would be offered continuing work.

Her reasons for the transfer included increased costs, tightening compliance regulations and challenges in hiring senior staff to regional roles.

Specialist aged-care consultant from Proserpine, Allira Griffiths, said these issues were causing consolidation across the industry.

"In 2018, we had 807 residential aged-care providers. In 2025, we were down to 636," Ms Griffiths said.

"It's a trend that we've seen for years now; providers are increasingly having to look at ways to improve their performance, how they can become more efficient.

"But, often, that requires a cash injection, which providers may not have readily available."

Respect has grown rapidly in the past decade, and it now owns 47 homes, acquiring its first eight Queensland homes last year.

Genevieve Moller and Geoffery and Margaret Dray are relatives of Edward Dray who donated the land for the aged care home. (ABC Tropical North: Liam McNally)

The Australian Workers Union said it would prefer the centre remained locally controlled.

"In our experience generally, what happens when a community loses control of an important institution like an aged-care home is it eventually results in worse services for the community," northern district secretary Jim Wilson said.

Respect chief executive Jason Binder said his organisation had an excellent standard of care, but he understood strong community sentiment.

"It was built and supported by generations of local people, and Respect takes very seriously the responsibility that comes with becoming the custodian of that legacy," he said.

"Our view is that becoming part of Respect does not mean it stops being a community asset."

World.title: Local family wins keys to $3.5m Bondi semi as bidder fails to show
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Local family wins keys to $3.5m Bondi semi as bidder fails to show Robyn Willis August 15, 2026 — 1:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A local family upsizing from an apartment bought a semi in Bondi for $3.5 million at auction on Saturday when they were the only ones to bid. Two parties registered to bid for 6 Miller Street, a three-bedroom semi, but only one was active, making an opening bid of $3.4 million. After some negotiation, the bidder, the local family, increased their offer to $3.5 million and the home sold under the hammer. A second registered bidder, who was on the phone, was a local who had sold a property earlier in the year but didn’t bid. A third person advised at the last minute that they would not be attending. “I had one registered bidder saying they would buy it on Monday, and they missed that opportunity,” McGrath Double Bay sales agent James Ledgerwood said.



Related Article Financing ‘Declare everything’: Why it may be harder to get a mortgage right now “Some buyers are sitting back assuming they will have something to negotiate post-auction.” The two-storey property has been fully renovated and has a north-facing backyard. It was one of 444 properties scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this Saturday. The home, which was a deceased estate, had a guide of $3.5 million, in line with the reserve. Ledgerwood said more than 50 groups had been through the property during the campaign. The Miller Street semi has a fully renovated kitchen and a north-facing backyard. Domain



Following buyer feedback, the guide was adjusted from $3.85 million to $3.5 million about 10 days before the auction. “At $3.5 million, that’s where we got engagement with buyers,” he said. In Pennant Hills a young couple, alongside extended family, won the keys to a five-bedroom house offered for the first time, paying $1.68 million. The brick home at 1 Lutanda Close had a guide of $1.6 million. It had a reserve of $1.68 million.



There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Two bidders registered and they were both active. Bidding for the property opened at $1.65 million. After three bids of a further $20,000, $5000 and a final $15,000, auctioneer Leon Axford’s hammer fell and the property sold. The vendors raised their family in the well-maintained Pennant Hills home, which was offered for the first time since it was built more than 50 years ago. Domain “In the hottest part of the market it would have sold for $1.7 million to $1.8 million, but we found a good buyer willing to offer fair market value,” sales agent for Ray White Upper North Shore Nathan Leuzzi said. The vendor is downsizing to an apartment. The underbidders were a young family searching for their first home. “They have missed out [on buying at auction] a few times now,” Leuzzi said.

World.title: ‘Un-Australian’: Smith drops sitter as Bangladesh take lead past 200
World.content:
Darwin: Steve Smith dropped the simplest of outfield catches as Australia failed to bowl out Bangladesh before lunch on day three of the first Test, with the visitors stretching their lead to an enormous 219.

Travis Head also put down a catch, albeit a much tougher one, to enable Mehidy Hasan Miraz (65 not out) to prolong the innings. Australia have now dropped five catches in the innings.

Mehidy finished the session by hooking Cameron Green for a huge six to leave absolutely no doubt which side had dominated the morning.

"It's very, very un-Australian, isn't it?" said Alyssa Healy in the Fox Cricket commentary box. "We've seen catches go down. We've seen us out in the field for 128 overs. A lot of talking points that I think Australia seemingly have brought upon themselves."

World.title: Bezos consortium buys a stake in Liverpool FC
World.content:
SportJeff Bezos Bezos consortium buys a stake in Liverpool FC Dominic King August 15, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Premier League with 4K on Stan Sport. Every match, live & on demand. Stream now

Liverpool Football Club have been valued at £5.5bn ($8 billion) after a consortium, that includes billionaire Amazon Founder Jeff Bezos, secured a 30 per cent stake in the six-time European Cup winners. There has been significant speculation for the past month that Fenway Sports Group (FSG), Liverpool’s owners, was in negotiations with a group led by Amit Bhatia, the former QPR chairman, and a point has been reached where the partnership has been confirmed. Jeff Bezos has made an investment into Liverpool FC. AP Bhatia, who will become Liverpool’s vice-chairman, recruited Bezos – the world’s third-richest man – along with Eduardo Saverin, the Facebook co-founder, and his wife Elaine Andriejanssen, to take a stake in the club. They did so through an investment vehicle called 1892 Holdings and, unlike at FSG, there are no faceless investors in the background. This is the Bhatia family, the Saverins and Bezos, who leads the K5 Sports Fund.



Bhatia will have no say in the day-to-day running of Liverpool’s football matters, even though their stake is worth more than Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s investment in Manchester United. Ratcliffe is ultimately responsible for football operations at Old Trafford. But FSG insists there is no change to how they have always conducted business on Merseyside and, crucially, maintains that this is not the beginning of the end of their ownership or a sign that Bhatia and co will one day take full control at Anfield. New owners are moving into Liverpool FC. Getty Images John W Henry, the lead figure at FSG, has never hidden the fact that he has always looked to secure outside investment. Bhatia is the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal – but the premise is the same: nothing will change about how Liverpool conduct their business.



There will be fervour that such substantial funding will lead to a boost to Liverpool’s transfer kitty for this window, but that is not the case. There is no new transfer budget for Andoni Iraola, the head coach, and there will not be a diversion from the plan the club has persistently followed. Mike Gordon, the FSG president, said in a statement: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world. “As we considered this opportunity, it became clear Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place.” Talks between Bhatia and FSG began in 2025 – sources close to the deal said it had been worked on for “multiple months” – after Bhatia was introduced to them by Will McDonough of the merchant bank Corestone Capital.



McDonough, who is the long-time agent of Tom Brady, a former American footballer, had a deep understanding of the Boston sport and business scene and felt Bhatia would be a good fit for what FSG was looking for. Bhatia, on behalf of 1892 Holdings, said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield. “To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership.” There is no indication yet whether Bhatia will be at St James’ Park for Liverpool’s opening Premier League fixture against Newcastle on August 23. The transaction remains subject to regulatory approval and customary closing conditions.

World.title: Rinehart almost doubles US shares to $8 billion, led by backing Elon Musk’s SpaceX
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaGina Rinehart Rinehart almost doubles US shares to $8 billion, led by backing Elon Musk’s SpaceX Christine Lacy August 15, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart, has almost doubled her bet on the US stock market, with her portfolio of shares there now worth an eye-watering $US5.7 billion ($8 billion). Filings to the US Securities Commission overnight reveal that Rinehart’s ownership of US shares increased from $US3.3 billion at the end of March to $US5.7 billion at the end of June. The massive jump in the value of her portfolio was driven in part by the $US1.4 billion value of her investment in technology billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Gina Rinehart, a SpaceX investor, has praised the business and its founder Elon Musk. Rinehart spent $US1 billion buying shares in the sought-after float on Nasdaq in June, equating to about 7.4 million SpaceX shares. The mining magnate’s friendship with Musk has evolved via their mutual support of Donald Trump during the 2024 US presidential election. Rinehart has described Musk as a “truly exceptional person”.



It has not, however, been one of Rinehart’s better investments, as SpaceX was floated at $US135 a share, peaked at $US201.80 in the days following the listing, but has traded as low as $US108 a share in recent weeks. It ended trading on Friday at $US140 a share. Related Article One Nation Aussie battler: Hanson joins Gina poolside on White Lotus holiday in Sicily The filing reveals that Rinehart also bought almost 600,000 SpaceX shares after the float, to take her stake to 8 million shares. The SpaceX float briefly made Musk the world’s first trillionaire. Rinehart’s stake in the rocket, artificial intelligence and satellite company is the single largest investment outside iron ore made by her private company Hancock Prospecting. Rinehart topped the 2026 Financial Review Rich List, with an estimated wealth of $39 billion. Her bet on Musk does not end with SpaceX. The latest disclosures reveal she retains almost 21,000 shares in Musk’s electric carmaker, Tesla. Rinehart’s stake there is worth just under $US9 million, and the market is now mooting that Musk’s next strategic move will be to merge SpaceX and Tesla into one company.



The quarterly filing to the United States Securities and Exchange Commission reveals Rinehart has also boosted her support for Trump, doubling her investment in the listed Trump Media and Technology, which owns the president’s Truth Social platform. Rinehart now has 870,000 shares in the company, compared with 430,000 at the end of March, and her stake is now worth $US6.7 million. Rinehart and friends at a rally for Donald Trump during the 2024 presidential election campaign. Along with her relationship with Musk and support for Trump, closer to home, Rinehart has emerged as a major financial backer of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. In April, Hanson confirmed Rinehart had bought One Nation a light plane to facilitate campaigning. The Queensland senator and the billionaire were recently photographed together poolside at a luxury resort in Sicily on a trip that Rinehart partially funded.



The filings overnight show Rinehart also has stakes in other US-listed tech companies including semiconductor giant Nvidia, the Jeff Bezos-controlled Amazon, Google’s owner Alphabet, and Microsoft. She also has shares in the Murdoch-family controlled Fox Corp, which is chaired by Lachlan Murdoch. Rinehart has also made a major $US832 million bet on rare earths miner MP Materials and has $US612 million invested in Canadian natural resources company Teck Resources. Hancock Prospecting was contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Local family wins keys to $3.5m Bondi semi as bidder fails to show
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Local family wins keys to $3.5m Bondi semi as bidder fails to show Robyn Willis August 15, 2026 — 1:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A local family upsizing from an apartment bought a semi in Bondi for $3.5 million at auction on Saturday when they were the only ones to bid. Two parties registered to bid for 6 Miller Street, a three-bedroom semi, but only one was active, making an opening bid of $3.4 million. After some negotiation, the bidder, the local family, increased their offer to $3.5 million and the home sold under the hammer. A second registered bidder, who was on the phone, was a local who had sold a property earlier in the year but didn’t bid. A third person advised at the last minute that they would not be attending. “I had one registered bidder saying they would buy it on Monday, and they missed that opportunity,” McGrath Double Bay sales agent James Ledgerwood said.



Related Article Financing ‘Declare everything’: Why it may be harder to get a mortgage right now “Some buyers are sitting back assuming they will have something to negotiate post-auction.” The two-storey property has been fully renovated and has a north-facing backyard. It was one of 444 properties scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this Saturday. The home, which was a deceased estate, had a guide of $3.5 million, in line with the reserve. Ledgerwood said more than 50 groups had been through the property during the campaign. The Miller Street semi has a fully renovated kitchen and a north-facing backyard. Domain



Following buyer feedback, the guide was adjusted from $3.85 million to $3.5 million about 10 days before the auction. “At $3.5 million, that’s where we got engagement with buyers,” he said. In Pennant Hills a young couple, alongside extended family, won the keys to a five-bedroom house offered for the first time, paying $1.68 million. The brick home at 1 Lutanda Close had a guide of $1.6 million. It had a reserve of $1.68 million.



There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Two bidders registered and they were both active. Bidding for the property opened at $1.65 million. After three bids of a further $20,000, $5000 and a final $15,000, auctioneer Leon Axford’s hammer fell and the property sold. The vendors raised their family in the well-maintained Pennant Hills home, which was offered for the first time since it was built more than 50 years ago. Domain “In the hottest part of the market it would have sold for $1.7 million to $1.8 million, but we found a good buyer willing to offer fair market value,” sales agent for Ray White Upper North Shore Nathan Leuzzi said. The vendor is downsizing to an apartment. The underbidders were a young family searching for their first home. “They have missed out [on buying at auction] a few times now,” Leuzzi said.

World.title: ‘Un-Australian’: Smith drops sitter as Bangladesh take lead past 200
World.content:
Darwin: Steve Smith dropped the simplest of outfield catches as Australia failed to bowl out Bangladesh before lunch on day three of the first Test, with the visitors stretching their lead to an enormous 219.

Travis Head also put down a catch, albeit a much tougher one, to enable Mehidy Hasan Miraz (65 not out) to prolong the innings. Australia have now dropped five catches in the innings.

Mehidy finished the session by hooking Cameron Green for a huge six to leave absolutely no doubt which side had dominated the morning.

"It's very, very un-Australian, isn't it?" said Alyssa Healy in the Fox Cricket commentary box. "We've seen catches go down. We've seen us out in the field for 128 overs. A lot of talking points that I think Australia seemingly have brought upon themselves."

World.title: Attorney General: Championing the rule of law
World.content:
Abraham Lincoln and Winston Churchill both successfully led hand-picked Cabinets that included their own fiercest rivals in order to forge a team of the most able.

That is unusual.

Many leaders are surprisingly brittle in the face of anything less than absolute agreement, and even a reasoned challenge may risk punishment for disloyalty.

But New Zealand's Cabinet includes a minister whose role specifically includes poking the bear - that minister is the Attorney General. Below are aspects of the role with commentary from its incumbent, Chris Bishop.

Attorney General: Championing the rule of law The House Download MP3 15m

"The Attorney General is the first Law Officer of the Crown," said Bishop, giving an overview, "and is essentially responsible for ensuring the government acts in accordance with the rule of law, and provides legal advice to the government on how they conduct themselves. And it is, in a funny sort of way, an apolitical role, certainly not party-political."

In fact, New Zealand Governments have an entire specific department of legal advisors (Crown Law), led by the Solicitor General, Anna Adams KC.

The Solicitor General, Anna Adams KC. (File photo) RNZ/Calvin Samuel

But the Attorney General (AG) is the minister in charge of that team, and the ultimate arbiter and deliverer of its advice - the sharp end of the Crown Law stick.

The Cabinet Manual describes the AG as the "senior law office" and the Solicitor General as the "Junior Law Officer". Bishop agrees that the junior tag is "a bit insulting for Anna Adams KC who is a very seasoned barrister and lawyer herself, far more experienced than me, obviously."

Cabinet critic in chief

The Cabinet Manual said the AG has "particular responsibility for maintaining the rule of law. The Attorney-General has a responsibility to notify Cabinet of any proposals or government actions that do not comply with existing law and to propose action to remedy such matters."

That role means that an AG is likely to be one of the loudest critics inside the Cabinet.

No government relishes being told that a great idea is not strictly within the rules.

Cabinet has the same first rule as Fight Club. "Obviously we don't talk about what happens in Cabinet," said Bishop, but he agrees with my description of the AG as "the person that has to say, 'Uhm, chaps, actually, that isn't what the Constitution's going to allow'."

Of course, governments, like any legal client, can ignore the AG, but they do so knowingly.

On such matters, the AG is not subject to the rule of Cabinet collective responsibility, which is formal language for "what happens in Cabinet stays in Cabinet".

Providing ammo to the enemy

If disagreeing in Cabinet isn't enough to make a minister unpopular, how about providing debating points to the Parliamentary opposition? The Cabinet Manual notes that "the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 requires the Attorney-General to report to Parliament if a bill appears to be inconsistent with this Act."

NOTE: The Bill of Rights (NZBORA) is a surprisingly recent addition (1990) to our constitutional quilt.

It guarantees the right to life, freedom of expression, movement, peaceful assembly, association, religion, thought, conscience and belief, and to seek and impart information. It guarantees the right to vote equally and secretly, and to represent others. Freedom from discrimination, and from unreasonable search or seizure, arrest or detention. Freedom from torture, and cruel, degrading, or disproportionately severe treatment or punishment. It is a crucial part of our democratic and societal underpinning and our national ethos.

If the AG determines that a new bill is inconsistent with NZBORA (with advice from the Ministry of Justice or Crown Law, depending on where a law bill is originating), they first advise Cabinet, and then (waiving privilege) also report that inconsistency to Parliament.

You can read reports here.

Advising Cabinet and Parliament that a bill is inconsistent with the Constitution does not kill that bill.

Many are passed into law regardless because Parliament is ultimately sovereign.

Bishop adds some background to the process.

"This is a [Sir Geoffrey] Palmer innovation like much of our modern constitutional architecture... [It] is an important job, you know. An overriding statutory duty to Parliament to do that, and I take legal advice in relation to that, …but the decision is mine as to whether or not a bill is consistent or inconsistent with the Bill of Rights.

He points to two recent bills where he has concluded there are inconsistencies. The Move-on Orders bill (now enacted into law), which he concluded contravened the freedoms of expression and of movement.

Also, a Member's Bill from National MP Tom Rutherford that would make it harder for people in prison for murder to get parole if they don't reveal the location of victims' remains.

He concluded this is inconsistent with the guarantee against arbitrary detention. Another inconsistent Members Bill currently under debate is New Zealand First's bill seeking to legally define two genders.

'Most sued man in New Zealand'

As the government's official lawyer, the AG, via Crown Law, looks after all the cases taken against the Government (the Crown). As such, Bishop agrees he is the "most sued man in New Zealand".

The Cabinet Manual said "the conduct of legal proceedings involving the Crown is the responsibility of the Attorney-General. In practice, the Solicitor-General, the Crown Law Office, or departmental legal teams, acting on the Attorney-General's behalf".

In theory, Chris Bishop could turn up in court to speak as the respondent in these cases.

Bishop notes that Chris Finlayson appeared "for the government before the International Court of Justice. I think in relation to the Japanese whaling case… He was obviously a very learned barrister and KC as well."

Bishop said he keeps threatening to do the same "half in jest". He would enjoy the chance, but his workload and restraint prevent it.

"There's obviously a huge amount of time and energy in preparation for that. And also, I would rate my legal skills, but not that highly."

The judge in Parliament's own court

The AG does some court-adjacent action, chairing Parliament's Privileges Committee. Privileges is currently meeting to consider the alleged misleading of a select committee by senior public servants.

During questioning of public servants, the contributions of the chair (Bishop) and his deputy (Labour MP and lawyer Duncan Webb) certainly felt quasi-judicial.

Privileges Committee Chair Chris Bishop and Deputy Duncan Webb consult during a 2023 hearing into whether MBIE Immigration officials misled Parliament. VNP / Phil Smith

Choosing and defending Judges

As legal advisor, the AG is the Executive's contact with the judicial aspect of government, and meets regularly with the Chief Justice. That relationship helps with the next part: the appointment of judges.

"The Attorney General recommends to the Governor General the appointment of judges in consultation with the Chief Justice." Cabinet is advised of choices, but Bishop stresses that Cabinet does not approve them.

"It's quite a process that we go through, and the great thing about New Zealand in comparison to other countries is it's not a political process.

"I would never want New Zealand to get to a situation where the appointment of judges was a political process, a situation where judges were approved by a select committee or approved by a panel of ministers or MPs, or anything like that, because that way lies politicisation [of the judiciary]. So I take it very seriously."

Certainly in some jurisdictions the judiciary has become a battleground.

"I look in some horror at the US, for example," said Bishop, "where law is political, and the politics is law, and the two are just completely fused.

"There is clearly a linkage, but making sure there's a separation between the politics of the judiciary and the political process is extremely important, extremely important."

Maintaining that separation falls within the AG's responsibility for protecting comity.

"Comity," said Bishop, "basically means everyone stays in their lane. Parliament legislates and debates things. Judges adjudicate and decide and issue judgements".

"Sometimes judgements occur that politicians don't like very much. And, you know, it's fine to disagree…, but you don't want to end up in a situation where politicians are criticising judges, particularly personally, because that would be very bad for the system.

"So part of the role of the Attorney is essentially sticking up for the judiciary, because judges can't fight back."

In short, if a politician starts hitting at judges for political gain, the AG punches back. Metaphorically.

Parliamentary Counsel Office

Along with Crown Law, the AG also oversees the Parliamentary Counsel Office(PCO), another separate team of lawyers that specialise in drafting legislation-both bills and regulations.

They also maintain the vast and growing body of New Zealand legislation.

"Really important role," said Bishop.

"Most people don't even think about it, but someone's got to actually go and write all the laws and the regulations, and all the things that actually make the statute book work.

"So the Chief Parliamentary Counsel, Cassie Nicholson KC, reports to me. We're very well served in New Zealand by very experienced apolitical, professional public servants who are legal drafters.

"We're very well served by PCO."

He adds that another contributor to the quality of legislation is the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee, "a group of lawyers from around Wellington, both public servants and outside counsel who provide advice on that as well and they do a good job."

Defending the rule of law

Many aspects of the rule of law and the constitution that the AG defends are not stipulated in statute, but defined by practice and convention.

That allows the role and the constitution to evolve, but provides less defence against malevolent intent, so a constitutional white knight is genuinely important.

Bishop said his "broad view is that our constitutional arrangements work. They reflect our history… and they work pretty well. There's always room for improvement, and… debates about the MMP threshold, how often we have elections… those debates will continue, and that's healthy in a democracy".

"Frankly, I think New Zealanders don't spend enough time thinking about our constitutional arrangements.

"Typically, New Zealand changes its constitution in big ways after crises…The fact that we haven't really changed much in the last 30 years probably indicates there hasn't been much of a crisis. So that's probably good."

World.title: Country Life: The Trust helping New Zealand's raptors take flight again
World.content:
Ten years in the game, and 551 raptors on the books.

"We started this, basically, in my backyard," Ron Lindsay said, "and it's built to where it is now."

Lindsay is a founding member of the NZ Raptor Trust, a group which takes in injured kāhu (Australasian harrier hawks, or swamp harriers), kārearea (New Zealand falcons) and owls.

Raptor rescues in Timaru Country Life Download MP3 19m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The volunteers look after the birds from recovery to release, taking them to vet checkups, feeding them, and housing them until they're strong enough to head back into the wild.

Lindsay's love of birds and wildlife photography led him to co-found the trust in 2016.

"I'd been breeding birds since I [was] about five or six, kind of bred from finches and budgies up to African greys, cockatoos."

In the early days, injured birds had no centre to go to - so volunteers would just bring them home.

"We were running rescue birds out of our garages, lounges.

"Then we got this place and we slowly started to build it."

Shipping containers and netted enclosures at the Trust's Timaru operations base now house birds through the later stages of their recovery.

The space also includes an education facility, where people can pay to learn about the birds - and also hold them.

The ruru nohinohi, or little owl, was introduced in the 1900s in an attempt to manage small pest birds on grain and fruit farms. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"We're getting tourists; we have people come in off the cruise ships," Lindsay said.

"But my main emphasis really - it's great to have the tourists in - but I want to educate New Zealanders on these birds ... the things that we're doing to them, the things that we're doing to their habitat."

Birds enjoying a highway carcass are the trust's most common visitors. Other have built their nests in farm machinery, found their way inside a chicken coop, or been poisoned by bullet lead after scavenging culled pests.

NZ Raptor Trust chairperson Jenni Fraser (right) carries out a welfare check on a kāhu alongside volunteer Angie Tidy. RNZ/Anisha Satya

Some birds cannot be saved, chairperson Jenni Fraser said.

"Our stats are, at the moment, one in three birds will be released.

"One bird will come in and it'll be so badly injured that we'll euthanise it immediately."

But for the birds who do get better and return to the wild, it's another shot at life.

"We're so happy, 175 we've released so far."

Fraser and fellow volunteer Angie Tidy, who both joined the cause in 2019, monitor the birds at home before bringing the strong ones into the centre for rehabilitation.

"Over the years we've built up and expanded and learnt more about the birds," Tidy said.

The most recent addition to the trust is a breeding centre for their live-in kārearea - not strong enough to return to the wild, but capable of making babies who are.

"We have four falcons here, one breeding pair already," Tidy said.

"These birds can't be released because they've been injured ... but their offspring can be."

The team hopes it will help rebuild the kārearea population, which sits between 5,000 and 8,000, according to DOC (although the website cites that as an "uncertain" number").

Two kāhu (harrier hawks) in the long flight enclosure. RNZ/Anisha Satya
